content:
'I'm not a quitter': Kim Kardashian on retaking the bar exam
Published
It was meant to be Kim Kardashian's triumphant debut as a leading actor - but last year's legal drama All's Fair was so universally panned by critics that it actually broke streaming records as audiences clambered to see what all the fuss was about.
Kardashian, who is best known as a media personality and businesswoman, tells the BBC she had no choice but to "lean into" the discourse and come back for a second series.
"We thought we were this law show, dealing with some really serious issues," she jokes.
But viewers mostly enjoyed its comedy value - with outlandish outfits and zingy one-liners from co-stars Sarah Paulson and Glenn Close sending the show straight into the pantheon of 'camp classics'.
'What choice do you have when you're getting criticised?'
Kim Kardashian has returned to her role as Allura Grant in Ryan Murphy's legal drama All's Fair
"We're a full comedy now," the 46-year-old admits, adding: "The beauty in producing a show with writers that are really tuned in to pop culture is they can see what the response is and write accordingly to that."
All's Fair, which was created by American Horror Story and Glee showrunner Ryan Murphy, became the Hulu network's most-watched scripted series debut of the last three years and was immediately renewed.
Following a group of divorce lawyers - played by Kardashian, Close, Paulson, Naomi Watts and Niecy Nash-Betts - the show was panned for bad acting, with Kardashian bearing the brunt of criticism.
The Hollywood Reporter called her "wooden", and the Times declared that the show "may be the worst TV drama ever".
But the hallmark of Kardashian's career has been her ability to back herself - whether that's going from years of being snubbed by Met Gala organisers to becoming its most anticipated guest, or overcoming backlash to the launch of her shapewear company to turn it into a $5bn (£3.7bn) brand.
Kardashian says: "What is the alternative, right? What is the other choice that you have when you're getting criticised?
"Do you just fall in and feel that, or keep your head down and try better, try harder and try a different path?"
Having been in the spotlight for more than 20 years, she's "always had a really good sense of my mental health", and says that comes from being able to "brush off" those who seek to bring her down.
"I always do things that are tough because I genuinely want to learn," Kardashian says.
Kardashian's co-stars Sarah Paulson and Naomi Watts have also returned for season two
While she was promoting the legal drama last year, Kardashian was waiting to find out if she had passed exams to become a lawyer in real life, after six years of studying for an apprenticeship that negated the need for a university degree.
Shortly after the first series aired, she found out she had failed the exam - but says that won't be the end of her pursuit of the qualification.
"If I don't pass something, if I don't do the best at something, then I'll get there," she says. "I don't worry. I just have to keep going."
But after her admission that she had used AI for legal advice, external, she does say she will change how public she is about her studies.
"I'm going to be a little more quiet about my journey until I get there," says Kardashian, who has four children with rapper Kanye West and is now in a relationship with British Formula 1 driver Lewis Hamilton.
"I know there was a lot of talk out there like, 'she's given up', and that's funny to me.
"I like people to think what they want to think and I'll take it again and let you guys know once I've passed. I'll be very vocal about that," she says.
'A realistic depiction of a lot of women'
All's Fair was criticised in its first series for bad acting, but Kardashian's co-stars say she has stepped up in the next iteration of the show
Audiences have only been given a glimpse of what to expect from the second series of All's Fair so far.
Co-star Watts, who also serves as a producer on the show alongside Kardashian, says they have "doubled down" on "the high fashion, high drama and heightened reality" that audiences enjoyed the first time around.
As for Kardashian's acting, Watts says she's on a "trajectory" that sees her "stepping up in the second season".
"She was improvising, riffing, doing all kind of things that I thought were deeply impressive," Watts adds, to which Kardashian jokes: "I think I'm just naturally so funny."
One of the positives that critics did cite was the show's desire to spotlight the duality of professional women who were both feminine and successful, which Kardashian says she "loves" because it is "a really realistic depiction of a lot of women I know".
"It doesn't mean that just because you're super smart that you can't be fashionable and into glamorous things as well," she adds.

content:
A photograph showing thousands of satellites cross-hatching the night sky over New Zealand appeared so extraordinary the astrophotographer who captured it is fighting accusations it was created by AI.
To create his spectacular image – now viewed millions of times online – Brendan Larsen spent two hours in September snapping hundreds of photographs of the night sky over Mount Taranaki in the North Island.
Larsen, 51, says he set his camera up to take an unlimited number of eight-second-long shots, with a two-second gap in between each photo. “I left her running for two hours and captured 578 photos … That was the easy part.”
The hard part came next. Larsen spent about 45 hours layering the individual photos – each of which contained about 25 satellites – over one another, using Adobe Photoshop. Much of the time was spent painstakingly erasing stars, to reveal the satellites.
“I could start to see the pattern emerging and realised: ‘Wow, this looks really awesome.’ I knew if I carried on it would look even better and more impressive in terms of satellite numbers.”
The resulting image shows the sky inundated with about 1,400 satellites and 14,000 trails forming a dense crisscrossing pattern above the mountain.
When Larsen uploaded the image to his social media channels in mid-October, it quickly went viral, gaining him 15,000 new followers, clocking up tens of millions of views and igniting thousands of comments.
Some viewers dismissed the photo as AI – but Larsen understands why. “AI generating software is becoming so good it is becoming difficult to tell AI images from real images … especially if you’re not familiar with the location or with astrophotography,” he says. Still, it is “frustrating”.
It is also exasperating, he says, to see his image downloaded and recreated by AI, with obvious flaws.
In anticipation of the AI accusations and backlash, Larsen documented his creative process on video, which he hopes will also allow viewers to form an emotional connection to the landscape.
As a child Larsen was “absolutely blown away” by the number of stars over parts of rural New Zealand. But he has noticed an increase in light pollution and the number of satellites over the six years he has been photographing the sky.
“It’s interesting and fascinating seeing satellites, but it’s also disturbing,” he says.
“I’ve got about 10,000 comments on my Facebook page … nine out of 10 of the comments are like: ‘Wow, beautiful photo, but horrifying, terrifying and really concerning about what’s happening to the night sky.’”
About 16,000 working satellites are circling the planet, alongside tens of thousands of defunct spacecrafts, rocket parts and debris from payloads breaking up.
Studies have warned that metal particles from space activities – such as rocket launches and satellite reentries – could affect atmospheric chemistry and the ozone layer, while the UN has warned increased space activity poses risks to ground safety, darkness and astronomy.
While satellites don’t yet overwhelm the sky to the naked eye, Larsen worries about the future state of the night sky. He hopes his image will ignite debate and reflection over how satellites can be used responsibly.
“We can raise awareness, and through that get a groundswell of support for protecting the night sky.”

content:
New blood tests designed to check for multiple cancers in one go will be offered to NHS patients in some 200 GP surgeries in England as part of a trial.
The aim is to detect hard-to-diagnose abdominal cancers, including liver, ovarian and pancreatic cancer, much sooner. These cancers are often found only after they have spread.
The tests look for proteins or fragments of DNA in the blood that may signal cancer. Results could help doctors decide which patients with vague symptoms need further investigations.
More than 20,000 patients aged 45 and over with symptoms such as pain or persistent bloating will be eligible to take part.
Hard-to-detect cancers
The government-funded trial, led by the University of Birmingham, will assess whether the tests are accurate enough for wider NHS use.
The idea of a blood test that can identify multiple cancers is not new.
A separate NHS trial of a test called Galleri recently failed to meet its main goal of reducing diagnoses of late-stage cancers, although researchers are still assessing its potential benefits.
Prof Peter Johnson, NHS England's national clinical director for cancer, said detecting abdomen cancer early was "notoriously difficult" because symptoms can easily be mistaken for other less serious conditions.
Earlier diagnosis gives patients a much better chance of successful treatment and survival.
Around 71,000 people in England are diagnosed each year with pancreatic, stomach, liver, ovarian or bowel cancer, and nearly 35,000 die from these diseases.
The new STRIDE-RCT trial, external is about detecting bowel, small bowel, stomach, oesophageal, pancreatic, liver, bile duct and gallbladder, ovarian, endometrial, kidney, bladder and prostate cancer.
Patients will provide one or two tubes of blood, taken at their GP practice, alongside routine tests.
Scientists will then analyse the samples for signs of cancer and, if present, may be able to pinpoint where in the body the tumour is located.
A positive result does not automatically mean there is cancer, and a negative result is not a guaranteed all-clear.
Health secretary Yvette Cooper said she hoped simple blood tests such as these would help identify patients needing urgent investigation much sooner.
Michelle Mitchell from Cancer Research UK said: "GPs have long needed better tools to help them navigate that uncertainty by identifying which patients require further testing and this trial in England is an important step towards addressing that need."

content: Researchers recently spotted the brightly colored Ghana cuckooshrike in Côte d’Ivoire’s Taï National Park. The “lost” bird hadn’t been seen in 13 years, reports Mongabay’s John Cannon. Stephanie Bartlett, a field research fellow with the International Bird Conservation Partnership (IBCP), took a photo of the cuckooshrike while Paulo Ditzel, also an IBCP research fellow, called out its movements to her. Bartlett told Mongabay she got the identifying photo of the bird first before she even saw it. “They’re scared of you,” Bartlett said. “You don’t get to get close to them, and so often you have to use the camera as a tool for identification.” Her photo revealed a small bird with an orange body and black and yellow wings. The photograph was the culmination of months of fieldwork and bird surveys supported by an instrumental team of West African researchers. “To say they were vital for this project is an understatement,” Ditzel said. The Ghana cuckooshrike (Lobotos lobatus) was last documented in 2013 in Ghana’s Atewa Forest. Ornithologists believe it’s range stretches across sections of West Africa, from Guinea to Ghana, within the Upper Guinean Rainforest. However, the bird’s likely habitat has been whittled away by logging and agriculture, leaving isolated patches of forest across its range. Ditzel and his colleagues noted that the cuckooshrike was listed by the Search for Lost Birds (SLB), a platform that documents bird species that haven’t been scientifically documented in more than a decade. After the Democratic Party swept to victory in the US midterm elections, we bring people together to share their experiences of one of the major issues for voters: The cost of living. When he was elected as President two years ago, Donald Trump pledged to reduce prices. But the opposite has happened. Household costs have gone up, especially for food and fuel. His decision to impose tariffs on some imported goods has made them more expensive. But much of the increase has been driven by a jump in the price of petrol and diesel due to America and Israel’s conflict with Iran. In our conversation, we hear from three young mothers in different parts of the world’s largest economy about their daily struggle to make ends meet. Single mother Lauren from New York tells us she often doesn't eat properly "I'm borrowing from Peter to pay Paul because there's nothing left". “You expect greatness from America,” Cass in Pennsylvania tells us. “The conversation we’re having right now is so common in more than half of this country and what we’re experiencing when it comes to financial hardships.” Presenter: James Reynolds BBC producer: Isabella Bull Boffin Media producers: Sue Nelson and Richard Hollingham Editors: Harriet Oliver and Arja Haikonen A Boffin Media production in partnership with the BBC World Service Outside Source team. content:
Nasa’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, which has spent two decades studying the most powerful explosions in the cosmos, is expected to re-enter the Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday, burning up in the process.
The satellite, which was designed to operate with its three telescopes for just two years, is no longer able to steer or observe, and its re-entry is uncontrolled.
The US Space Force predicts the 3,200lb spacecraft will hit the atmosphere at about 3.30am ET on 4 November. Nasa says most of the spacecraft will burn up, but some components are expected to survive.
“Re-entry locations of any surviving components can vary from hemisphere to hemisphere and depend on when it re-enters,” the agency said in a blogpost, adding that surviving fragments are limited between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude.
The agency added: “The risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely – approximately 1 in 2,100. NASA and Space Force will continue to monitor the re-entry and update predictions.”
The observatory was launched in 2004 to explore the universe’s most powerful explosions, called cosmic gamma-ray bursts, and quickly return its observations of location and strength to Earth.
Over the course of its operational life, the observatory detected and tracked more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) that are considered the most powerful explosions the universe has seen since the big bang.
Nasa says these bursts of energy occur approximately once per day and are brief, but intense, flashes of gamma radiation and come from all different directions, and can last from a few milliseconds to a few hundred seconds.
But scientists do not know what causes them – theorizing that they may be the birth of a black hole in a massive stellar explosion or produced by the collision of two neutron stars, or some other phenomenon.
Swift was launched as part of Nasa’s medium explorer, or Midex, program. In July, it observed a wandering mega black hole shredding star, which occurs when a star passes fatally close to a supermassive black hole.
“Crumbs of the splintering star heat up as they swirl around the black hole, creating a glow astronomers can see from far across the cosmos, and the black hole launches a relativistic jet into space,” said the agency.
The black hole, described as an “orphan”, lit up as it devoured the star on the outskirts of a galaxy, in what scientists call a “tidal disruption event”. Nearly every galaxy has a supermassive black hole at its center, and a tidal disruption occurs about once every 100,000 years.
The star-shedding event occurred 2,600 light-years from the center of the host galaxy, but the Swift team observed one more than 30,000 light-years away.
after newsletter promotion
“We were looking for these star-shredding events as a way to find otherwise invisible supermassive black holes wandering away from the galactic cores where they usually reside,” said Robert Stein, a research fellow at the University of Maryland, College Park, and Nasa’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, at the time.
A paper describing the results published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, said: “The tidal disruption event outshone its entire host galaxy in ultraviolet wavelengths, temporarily radiating with the light of about 10 billion suns.”
Still unknown is how the black hole came to drift so far. Stein said it could have started off in a small galaxy that merged with the big one, but the key question was how common are wandering black holes.
Nasa attempted to push Swift into a higher orbit last year using a private space contractor but the mission did not succeed after they failed to rendezvous. Last month, Swift was estimated to be orbiting 171 miles above the Earth and it was commanded to end operations to prepare for re-entry.
Nasa said Swift has “broadened our understanding of a wide variety of cosmic objects and events, from active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars undergoing X-ray flares, to supernova explosions and comets and asteroids in our own solar system”.

content: For a time during the 19th and 20th centuries, gray wolves were practically extinct across Western and Central Europe. Now, thanks to strict protection measures in countries across the region, their populations have risen over the past couple of decades — including a reported surge of 58% between 2012 and 2022. On the one hand, this is a conservation success story. On the other, however, it amplifies long-standing sociocultural challenges, namely human-wildlife coexistence with farmers. Wolves sometimes prey on livestock, which can cause financial harm to farmers. Joining the Newscast this week to unpack these sociocultural challenges is social scientist Emu-Felicitas Ostermann-Miyashita, from the Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology. Ostermann-Miyashita has studied the conflict between humans and wolves specifically in Germany, and has published suggestions for sustainable wolf-livestock coexistence. However, she says the problems are much less polarized than European media may portray them. “Some people hate wolves, some people love wolves, but that was also something which I wanted to look into whether that’s true or not,” she says. “And all of my studies which I’ve conducted so far on … the public perception or social side hint to a much more like gray [area regarding] public attitudes or public perception towards the species.” The European Union has voted to loosen the protected status of Eurasian gray wolves (Canis lupus lupus), which critics say could endanger the progress that has been made in the animal’s recovery. “Wolf populations have barely recovered after going extinct in most parts of…This article was originally published on Mongabay

content:
On the morning of October 15, 2025, a livestreamer known as Sisi stepped out of her apartment in Yongzhou, China, with her young daughter. On the shoe rack outside her door sat an unfamiliar package. When she picked it up, it exploded.
The blast burned Sisi’s face, neck and arms. Her daughter escaped serious injury, though part of her hair and backpack were singed. Police arrested a former viewer, then 27-year-old Liu Mouqiang, later that day. According to the indictment reported by Chinese media, the package was the fourth in a series of attacks prosecutors say Liu carried out against Sisi.
Before the bombing, Sisi had repeatedly rejected Liu, returned the money she received from his gifts, and taken him to court over his harassment. His pursuit continued across livestreams, social media accounts, and physical locations.
The case exposes the risks women creators face. Sometimes a viewer treats paid attention as a personal claim on the livestreamer’s life.
Liu first encountered Sisi through her livestreams. Sisi told The Beijing News that he had spent a little more than 1,000 yuan (around $150) on gifts for her. He later complained that he had reached “Level 28” through virtual gifting and was being treated “worse than a tourist.” Sisi explained that the level reflected his cumulative spending across multiple creators.
Liu eventually found Sisi offline and began pursuing her. According to Sisi, he offered 160,000 yuan if she agreed to marry him. She repeatedly rejected his advances. As she distanced herself, Liu left a revealing comment on her social media: “Female livestreamers all belong to the top donor.” He later created new accounts and posted insulting and manipulated content about her. Chinese media documented the messages and Sisi’s account of his marriage proposal.
Liu’s behavior reflects a dangerous logic in creator economies: spending can foster a sense of ownership. Livestreaming rewards creators for cultivating familiarity, attention, and interaction. For women creators, that commercial intimacy can collide with misogynistic expectations that male financial or emotional investment deserves female attention in return. Rejection can then become a trigger for retaliation.
Sisi transferred Liu 600 yuan, hoping he would stop pursuing her. The online harassment continued. According to detailed reporting on the case, the sum covered the roughly 500 yuan she had received after the platform took its share of his gifts, plus about 100 yuan he had spent on a meal.
On June 4, 2025, the Qiyang People’s Court registered Sisi’s civil lawsuit over Liu’s harassment. A subsequent court-mediated agreement required him to delete defamatory material, publicly apologize, and pay her 3,000 yuan in compensation. The legal process, however, carried its own hidden risk. According to reporting based on the investigation, the mediation materials contained Sisi’s home address, which Liu later used to locate her apartment.
Her livestreams provided additional information about her movements. Sisi told reporters that Liu had previously found locations where she was streaming and had used backgrounds visible in her broadcasts to track down her family’s business.
Prosecutors say Liu’s retaliation escalated over several months. In May 2025, he planted an explosive device above the entrance to Sisi’s parents’ shop and remotely detonated it after seeing through her livestream that she was there. In August, he placed a metal spike beneath her car tire. In October, he sprayed a corrosive liquid into her home. Eleven days later, prosecutors say, he left the disguised explosive package outside her apartment. The indictment describes all four attacks.
In March 2026, prosecutors charged Liu with endangering public safety by dangerous means. The case went to trial in June. At trial, Liu argued that the case involved a personal relationship dispute, an account Sisi rejected. The court said it would announce its verdict at a later date.
Liu’s claim that female livestreamers “belong to the top donor” laid bare the entitlement behind his increasingly aggressive actions. He believed spending money on virtual gifts was grounds for demanding a relationship. He continued to pursue Sisi after she rejected him and returned the money she had received. Her efforts to end contact were followed by continued harassment and, prosecutors allege, repeated attacks.
Sisi’s experience also exposes the limits of China’s legal remedies for online abuse. By the time Sisi’s civil case reached mediation, Liu had already staged on bomb attack, although she had yet to learn who was responsible. The settlement addressed his defamatory posts, but the harassment continued. Worse, the mediation materials gave him her home address, which he used to stage yet another attack. Seeking legal redress inadvertently led her harasser right to her doorstep – literally.
summary: When a fan thinks he owns you, online entitlement can morph into real-world violence.

content: The multilateral body charged with regulating fishing and protecting ecosystems in the Southern Ocean reached no agreements on establishing new marine protected areas or adopting new krill-fishing management measures at its recent annual meeting. The 45th meeting of the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) took place Oct. 19-30 in Hobart, Australia, bringing together the body’s 27 members: 26 countries and the EU. Months of press conferences, boycott campaigns, lobbying activities and bilateral meetings preceded the event. Attention focused particularly on the potential adoption of a new fisheries management system for Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) and the establishment of a marine protected area in a large swathe of sea, known as Domain 1, between the Antarctic Peninsula and the South Orkney Islands. Domain 1 is where krill fishing is concentrated and also contains important feeding grounds for wildlife populations that rely primarily on the small shrimp-like crustaceans for food. “CCAMLR Members did not reach consensus on either,” Javier Arata, spokesperson for the industry Association of Responsible Krill harvesting companies (ARK), told Mongabay by email, minutes after the meeting closed. “CCAMLR adopted no new measures for the krill fishery this year,” Arata said, adding that members “were closer this year than many expected.” He said his group will keep working with all CCAMLR members, scientists and other interested parties to get both measures adopted in 2027. content:
Across social media platforms, Karakalpak activists have increasingly found themselves on the wrong side of copyright and other complaints, leading to the removal of content and the disabling of profiles.
Recently, an unknown person presenting themselves as an editor for The Diplomat filed at least one fraudulent copyright complaint, which led to the removal of a post on Facebook. This one case is illustrative of a wider weaponization of copyright law, its uneven application, and the abuse of automated reporting systems to target activists.
“We are losing more than accounts and audiences,” Gulya Nur, a Karakalpak activist and president of the Via Serica Foundation, told The Diplomat. “We are losing documentation: testimony, interviews, records of abuse, and years of civil society work. After silencing outspoken people through repression inside Karakalpakstan, pressure on online voices threatens the remaining space for documenting and challenging that repression.”
On October 31, Nur contacted The Diplomat. A fellow activist, Aman Sagidullayev, had shared the text of an op-ed Nur had written, which was published by The Diplomat. Sagidullayev’s post had been reported to Meta as a copyright violation and Meta removed it, notifying Sagidullayev of the details of the complaint and his appeal options.
Sagidullayev is the leader of the Alga Karakalpakstan movement. In exile since 2012, his movement has long demanded a referendum on independence in Karakalpakstan. The autonomous republic – and the people who would like to see it attain complete independence – have a complex history with Uzbekistan, to say the least.
In the summer of 2022, a draft version of a then-proposed constitutional referendum was published. The draft scrapped an article that guaranteed Karakalpakstan the right to secede from Uzbekistan on the basis of a referendum. That perceived attempt to chip away at Karakalpakstan’s sovereignty sparked protests and a renewed crackdown. The constitutional referendum that passed in April 2023 retained the clause that the draft had cut. But although Karakalpakstan’s right to secede is technically still a constitutionally-guaranteed right (now under Article 89), in practical terms discussing it remains a taboo.
The notice Sagidullayev received from Meta stated that “The removal decision was made by our technology.”
Social media sites like Facebook use automated systems to assess content for violations, including copyright. Such platforms are motivated to move quickly, as failing to act expeditiously in response to a sworn takedown notice opens them to legal liability under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) in the United States. The law includes what’s known as a “safe harbor” provision that shields platforms from liability if they make a good-faith effort to respond to complaints. Automated systems speed up this process, but shift the burden onto the user to file a counter-notice when content is wrongfully taken down.
Sagidullayev has appealed Meta’s decision to disable the post.
***
When you file a DMCA complaint with a platform like Meta, which operates Facebook and Instagram, you attest under penalty of perjury that the information in the claim is accurate and that you are the copyright owner or authorized to act on their behalf. Under U.S. copyright law, only the legitimate copyright holder, or their authorized agent, has standing to file complaints.
As noted above, platforms are motivated to move quickly in response to complaints. As such, they do not assess the complainant’s standing to make the complaint in the first place before taking steps to remove content. This inadvertently opens the door for imposters to silence individuals using tools designed to protect copyright.
The complaint against Sagidullayev was submitted by an individual referring to themself as Jasmina Jasurova. In response to the form’s prompt inquiring how the affected work was infringed, the complainant wrote:
“I, Jasmina Jasurova, am an editor at The Diplomat (https://thediplomat.com/). The two reported fake profiles repeatedly steal and republish our editorial team’s original content without authorization, seriously infringing our copyright. I urge Meta to immediately remove all infringing content and take strict enforcement action against both profiles, including permanent removal, to prevent further violations.”
As managing editor of The Diplomat since 2017, and on staff since 2014, I can state with complete confidence that no person named “Jasmina Jasurova” has ever worked as an editor for The Diplomat. When The Diplomat contacted the email address used to file the complaint (a Gmail address), we did not receive a reply. Google searches of the name in English, Uzbek, and Russian yielded nothing significant.
The Diplomat has sought ways to file a counter-complaint with Meta, but there appears to be no mechanism by which a copyright holder can complain directly about an unknown individual impersonating them in making a DMCA takedown request. There are forms for copyright and trademark infringement, and forms for reporting accounts that may be impersonating another account and other abuses. But while we have the name and email address used to file the complaint, we do not know what Facebook account they are associated with – Meta does not provide that information. There are several dozen Jasmina Jasurovas on Facebook.
Questions sent to Meta’s press office inquiring about whether the company has systems in place to ensure that only legitimate copyright holders are able to file complaints and what mechanisms there are for redress when a fraudulent complaint is filed and acted upon went unanswered as of publication.
***
This is not Sagidullayev’s first run-in with copyright complaints. His YouTube channel “Civil Society of Karakalpakstan” was terminated following multiple copyright strikes. Many of those complaints appear to have been submitted under an email address bearing his own name, according to documents viewed by The Diplomat.
Sagidullayev told The Diplomat he has already lost previous Facebook accounts, “and, with them, my connection to thousands of followers.”
“It hurt to lose touch with people who counted on me for information about Karakalpakstan. Through those accounts, I helped people harmed by Uzbekistan’s authorities tell their stories and be heard,” he said. “I’m asking Meta to restore my previous accounts. If it shuts down my current profile, I could lose years of human rights documentation and once again lose contact with the people who rely on my work. It takes minutes to open a new account. It took years to build that archive and earn that trust.”
Jasmina Jasurova, the complainant fraudulently posing as a Diplomat editor, asked for a permanent removal of his account from the platform.
“Uzbekistan’s security forces used bullets and grenades to silence peaceful protesters in Karakalpakstan. Now Uzbekistan authorities are weaponizing Facebook and YouTube to silence the Karakalpak voices online,” Sagidullayev told The Diplomat. “I believe Uzbekistan’s security services are behind the repeated shutdowns of my Facebook accounts.”
Other Karakalpak activists have similarly reported being targeted with copyright complaints, sometimes even for reposting their own material to different platforms. Activists like Sagidullayev and Nur believe they know the source of these complaints, but hard evidence is difficult to come by given layers of online privacy rules and the use of sock puppet accounts.
Uzbek authorities have long denied targeting critics, at home or abroad.
This comes at a time when Uzbekistan, like many countries, is making a concerted push to invest in and expand its digital sphere.
“As Uzbekistan promotes digital cooperation abroad, Karakalpak defenders struggle to preserve their voices on those same global platforms,” Nur told The Diplomat.
In June 2026, Uzbekistan’s Minister of Digital Technologies Sherzod Shermatov met with Beth Ann Lim, director of public policy, strategy and campaigns for the Asia-Pacific (APAC) region at Meta, “to discuss the development of Uzbekistan’s digital economy, the expansion of bilateral cooperation, and the advancement of digital skills among young people,” according to a government readout.
“These partnerships deserve scrutiny alongside the use and potential abuse of platform complaint systems,” Nur argued. “American technology companies should be asking how their services protect people documenting repression.”
Nearly a decade ago, Freedom House highlighted “the rise of digital authoritarianism” in their 2018 Freedom of the Net report. “Digital authoritarianism is being promoted as a way for governments to control their citizens through technology, inverting the concept of the internet as an engine of human liberation,” the report warned.
Scholars summarize digital authoritarianism as the “use of digital information technology by authoritarian regimes to surveil, repress, and manipulate domestic and foreign populations.” Discussions of digital authoritarianism often focus on mass surveillance and control of information. This ranges from propaganda and disinformation – muddying the waters with false but neatly packaged narratives – and repressing authentic voices through “fake news” laws and the criminalization of defamation.
But this also includes the weaponization of copyright to achieve goals unrelated to copyright, such as censorship and retaliation. Tools designed to protect copyright can be easily deployed for ulterior purposes by a range of actors, from individuals to governments the world over, and ultimately shift the boundaries of public discussion. The very platforms that provide the avenues for free speech also provide the tools of repression. It’s a dark irony to be wrestled with.
summary: An individual claiming to be a Diplomat editor filed a copyright complaint with Meta against a Karakalpak activist. They were an imposter. The post was taken down anyway.
summary_th: บุคคลที่อ้างว่าเป็นบรรณาธิการของ Diplomat ได้ยื่นเรื่องร้องเรียนเรื่องลิขสิทธิ์กับ Meta เพื่อต่อต้านนักเคลื่อนไหว Karakalpak พวกเขาเป็นคนแอบอ้าง กระทู้ก็โดนลบไปแล้ว
title: With Copyright Complaints, Even Imposters Can Silence Karakalpak Activists
title_th: ด้วยการร้องเรียนเรื่องลิขสิทธิ์ แม้แต่ผู้แอบอ้างก็สามารถปิดปากนักเคลื่อนไหว Karakalpak ได้

content:
The China-Pakistan Information Corridor, or CPIC, has been promoted as a barrier against fake news. However, what it really does is give two governments with some of the world’s worst press freedom records a shared tool to decide what their citizens can read, what they can see, and how they should think.
CPIC was launched at the Pakistan-China Friendship Center in Islamabad on October 27, at an event organized by Pakistan’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting with China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning and Chinese Ambassador Jiang Zaidong in attendance. During the event, Pakistan’s Information Minister Attaullah Tarar thanked the Chinese embassy for supporting the project.
CPIC brings media organizations and think tanks together to share news, produce content, and respond to reporting the two governments consider misleading. Officials have described it as the “voice” of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), a multibillion-dollar program of Chinese investment and financing in Pakistan. Establishing cooperation in this arena was first raised by Tarar in March 2024, who asked for joint action against what he called fake news about CPEC. Back in 2021, a China-Pakistan Media Forum had already pledged a China-Pakistan Media Corridor and set up a network. The U.S. State Department, in a report, characterized this turn of events as China negotiating significant control over Pakistani media by establishing a jointly operated “nerve center” to monitor and shape Pakistan’s information environment.
Under the CPIC plan, 18 Pakistani and Chinese media outlets will share news and content. These include Pakistan’s state broadcasters and some private channels, alongside China’s Xinhua, China Media Group, and People’s Daily. A separate “fact-checking” unit will track and respond to stories that officials consider misleading. The Pakistan-China Institute will lead joint research and publications by think tanks, which Tarar said will help in “shaping narratives.”
According to the Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson, as Pakistan and China face “misinformation, fake news, and lies,” this will build a more favorable public-opinion environment and help counter propaganda against both countries, as China’s ambassador to Pakistan put it.
But CPIC arrives in a country where the words “fake news” can already put a reporter in prison.
In January 2025, the Pakistani government amended the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA). Section 26-A introduced penalties of up to three years in prison, a 2 million Pakistani rupee fine, or both, for deliberately spreading information known or reasonably believed to be false and likely to cause public fear, panic, or unrest. The amendments also gave a government-controlled regulator broad powers to block online content, including material considered against “the ideology of Pakistan.”
These powers have been subsequently turned against independent reporting. Within nine months of the amendments, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) had recorded at least nine journalists prosecuted under PECA. Raftar founder Farhan Mallick was among those arrested in March 2025 for PECA breaches. Pakistan’s National Cyber Crimes Investigation Agency (NCCIA) issued Dawn journalist Muhammad Akbar Notezai a notice over his 2024 investigation into corruption in Balochistan, the province where CPEC’s Gwadar port is located. Reporting on corruption had become grounds for pursuing the reporter.
By April 2026, the government had reported 187 cases registered under Section 26-A of PECA. Separately, Freedom Network documented 129 violations against journalists between April 2025 and March 2026, including 58 legal cases, most involving PECA. It identified the amended law as the most consequential instrument being used to restrict journalism and free expression. Its executive director, Iqbal Khattak, said the law had created a climate of fear in which journalists were censoring themselves to avoid prosecution.
This is the environment into which CPIC’s official “fact-checking” unit is being introduced.
RSF’s 2026 Press Freedom index placed Pakistan 153rd of 180 and said the authorities work to control, and sometimes suppress, what journalists publish. When the Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists asked the Islamabad High Court to suspend the PECA amendment, the court said in February 2026 that it could not do so by injunction.
Questioning CPEC was taboo in Pakistan long before CPIC. Foreign Policy reported in 2022 that criticizing CPEC was being treated like criticizing the army, with the military’s media wing warning journalists over WhatsApp when they cross the red line. A 2020 Brookings paper, “At All Costs”, described how both the Pakistani and Chinese governments guard the CPEC story.
Now add CPIC. A government that jails people for “fake news” has built an official unit, with a foreign state’s media inside it, to decide which stories about their flagship project are misleading. That unit gives the fake news law a target list. A reporter asking about CPEC debt, unpaid power dues, Gwadar protests, or attacks on Chinese workers can first be labeled misleading by the state, then charged under Section 26-A. In an environment like that, many reporters will not take the risk; instead they will stop asking such questions and reporting on these issues.
Now on the Chinese side, RSF’s 2026 index ranked China 178th of 180, above only North Korea and Eritrea. RSF called China the world’s largest jailer of journalists, with 121 media workers behind bars. Citizen journalist Zhang Zhan, first jailed for reporting from Wuhan during COVID-19, was sentenced again in September 2025 to four more years. China Media Group, a CPIC member, runs CGTN and China Radio International, the regime’s main voices abroad. Under CPIC, Xinhua, CMG, and People’s Daily help decide what counts as verified news in Pakistan.
This is a known playbook by China. Freedom House studied Beijing’s media influence in 30 countries in 2022. Officials in 19 of them had stepped up their own attacks on free expression since 2019, and officials in 12 had acted specifically to suppress coverage Beijing disliked. Freedom House’s first advice to newsrooms in those countries was to end content-sharing deals with Chinese state media. CPIC does the exact opposite and makes those deals official.
The central question is who gets to decide which narrative is misleading? Under CPIC, that judgment sits with the governments whose actions journalists are supposed to investigate. A report about debt, corruption, or abuse can damage CPEC’s image precisely because it is true. Yet the same officials defending that image can disguise their response as fact-checking. Once the governments’ version becomes the standard, a journalist must defend the right to report before anyone examines the evidence. This has always been how governments make people distrust journalists who question them; in a situation like that, the powerful become the judges of truth, while those who question them are treated as the problem.
Fact-checking is good in principle, necessary even. The issue is that governments cannot be reasonably expected to fact-check stories about themselves in an unbiased fashion; it’s a conflict of interest. Governments have reputations, policies, and political interests to protect and promote. When the institution being subjected to media scrutiny also decides whether the investigation is misleading, it is deciding its own case.
An honest fact-check should follow the evidence, even if it makes a government look bad. But CPIC is meant to protect the partnership’s image. That puts a journalist investigating wrongdoing up against the governments trying to defend themselves. If publishing a story could mean losing their job or getting arrested, a reporter may decide it is not worth the risk. The story goes unpublished, people never hear what the reporter found, and those responsible never have to explain themselves.
summary: CPIC arrives in a country where the words "fake news" can already put a reporter in prison.
summary_th: CPIC มาถึงประเทศที่คำว่า "ข่าวปลอม" อาจทำให้นักข่าวติดคุกได้แล้ว
title: The China-Pakistan Information Corridor Is Made to Silence Journalists

content:
For years, China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) has been presented as a set of trade routes. While infrastructure projects are crucial for growth, another part of China’s work in Central Asia gets much less attention: the links between universities and laboratories.
Uzbekistan is a good example. In October 2026, the second meeting of the Uzbekistan-China Expert Council convened in Tashkent to discuss “Digital Partnership: Artificial Intelligence and the Next-Generation Data Economy.” The meeting demonstrates that China’s engagement with Central Asia does not neglect knowledge networks and scientific cooperation. This matters because scientific partnerships often outlast commercial projects and can shape who trains future researchers and provides access to advanced technologies. Indeed, such meetings start a recurring mechanism through which Chinese and Uzbek academics and technology specialists formulate ideas, standards, and research priorities together.
According to Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, trade with China reached $13.07 billion in 2024. Uzbekistan exported goods worth $2.64 billion and imported goods worth $10.43 billion. Yet trade figures alone reveal only part of the relationship. Increasingly, Beijing and Tashkent are investing in knowledge production. In September 2025, the two governments signed a cooperation program that links the “Uzbekistan–2030” strategy with the BRI. They also signed agreements on training people and on the digital economy.
In November 2025, Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Higher Education, Science, and Innovation reported that universities in the two countries had launched 29 joint study programs in 2024-2025. Another development was the creation of the Muhammad al-Khwarizmi International Mathematical Center at Urgench State University, in partnership with Peking University.
Universities can train talent but their impact ultimately depends on the infrastructure available to convert research into practical outcomes. This is where laboratories are becoming increasingly important. In May 2025, Uzbekistan’s national news agency reported an agreement with a Chinese agricultural technology company to set up a food safety laboratory center. It also reported talks on a laboratory with the Tashkent Institute of Chemical Technology and Xi’an Petroleum University.
We should read such news with care. An agreement or a plan is not the same as a working laboratory that produces research. Still, these reports show where institutions plan to spend their time and money.
By 2026, laboratory initiatives had become part of a broader institutional effort to define priority areas. At the seventh meeting of the Uzbekistan-China subcommission on science and technology cooperation, officials agreed to expand joint projects in artificial intelligence (AI), digital technologies, agricultural biotechnology, new materials, and green energy. They also agreed to work on research facilities, systems that help turn research into business, joint funds, technology parks, and exchanges for young researchers. The key question now is how many of these plans will become real programs with clear results.
Building scientific capacity also requires systems that can protect and commercialize new ideas. Intellectual property (IP) is therefore another important part of the picture. In July 2026, during the meetings of the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) in Geneva, China’s National Intellectual Property Administration signed two documents with Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Justice. The first is a memorandum on IP cooperation. The second is a Patent Prosecution Highway agreement, which helps patent offices in both countries review applications faster. These agreements open the door to closer patent cooperation. But on their own, they do not show that the two countries now file more joint patents or sell more joint technologies. The official sources used for this article do not give regular data on joint patents, licensed technologies, or research results that have reached the market.
The same shift from traditional cooperation to knowledge-based cooperation is visible in emerging technologies. In July 2026, Uzbekistan became a founding member of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization. This should not be seen as only a China-Uzbekistan success, because the organization includes many countries. More directly, in October 2026, Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Digital Technologies met China’s ambassador to discuss cooperation in AI, data security, and university training. On October 19, the second meeting of the Uzbekistan-China Expert Council in Tashkent discussed AI rules, digital infrastructure, technology transfer, investment, and skills.
Yet, as elsewhere in the partnership, discussions and agreements remain easier to identify than measurable outcomes. It is important to separate three things: an agreement, an activity that has started, and a measurable result. Announcing a new research center shows ambition. A joint degree program shows that work has begun. Patents, published papers, trained graduates, new technologies used by companies and income from licenses show real results. Without reliable and detailed data, it is too early to say that one country has pushed another out of Uzbekistan’s science system.
One of the most widely used indicators is scientific co-authorship. Chinese universities increasingly promote international co-authorship to expand research networks, raise global visibility, and strengthen their presence in leading scientific databases. When researchers in Uzbekistan collaborate with Chinese institutions, Chinese universities gain not only publications but also a stronger position in setting research agendas, defining priority fields and coordinating long-term research networks. Scientific leadership today is often built through repeated collaboration, access to funding, laboratory infrastructure, doctoral training and publication networks. Co-authorship therefore serves not only as a measure of cooperation but also as a mechanism for accumulating scientific influence over time.
The United States and European countries still play an important role in Uzbekistan’s universities and science ecosystem. A fair comparison would need the same kind of data for each partner: joint publications, citations, researcher exchanges, scholarships, jointly funded laboratories, patents, and links between universities and industry. This data should also be open to checking. It should state which database was used, how author affiliations were counted, which years were covered and when the data was collected. This article does not attempt such a comparison, but future studies should.
For Beijing, science cooperation is a way to stay engaged in the region over the long term. It is less visible than a railway, but it may last longer. For Washington, Brussels, and other partners, it is a reminder that their role in Central Asia should be judged not only by infrastructure loans or security talks, but also by the opportunities they offer young researchers and universities. These partnerships do not exclude each other. Uzbekistan can benefit from science cooperation with many countries at once.
summary: Scientific and educational cooperation may be less visible than a railway, but it may also have longer lasting and broader results.
summary_th: ความร่วมมือด้านวิทยาศาสตร์และการศึกษาอาจมองเห็นได้น้อยกว่าทางรถไฟ แต่อาจมีผลลัพธ์ที่ยั่งยืนและกว้างกว่าด้วย
title: How China Is Building Influence in Central Asia, One Laboratory at a Time

content:
แพนเค้ก ไม่นอยด์ เดอะเฟซ ถูกมองอ่อม-เผยยังรักเคารพ ‘บุ๋ม ปนัดดา’ เหมือนเดิม เชื่อมีหลายเรื่องที่ต้องรอคำตอบ
หลังจากที่มาร่วมงานเปิดตัวซีรีส์ออริจินัลแห่งปี ‘The Remarried Empress การแต่งงานครั้งใหม่ของจักรพรรดินี’ ณ ลาน ATRIUM 1 ชั้น G ศูนย์การค้า SIAM CENTER นางเอกสาว แพนเค้ก เขมนิจ ก็ได้เปิดใจถึงกรณีรายการ The Face Thailand ปีซีซั่นนี้โดนติว่าอ่อม ไม่มีซีนฟาดจนเป็นมีมเหมือนซีซั่นก่อน รวมถึงเรื่ององค์กรทำดี ของ บุ๋ม ปนัดดา วงศ์ผู้ดี ที่เจ้าตัวเคยไปช่วยการกุศลอยู่หลายครั้ง
ตอนนี้กระแสหลายคนบอกว่าเมนเทอร์ฝีมือตก เพราะยังไม่ชนะสักที?
“เด็กอยู่ครบนะ (ไม่โดนตัดออก?) ก็เป็นกำไร เราต้องพลิกวิกฤตให้เป็นโอกาส”
เขาบอกว่าซีซันนี้ดูซอฟต์ลง?
“ซอฟต์ลงเหรอ เพราะยังไม่เห็นชุดละสิ ก็สลับไป แพนว่ามันไม่ง่ายเลย ยากทุกครั้ง พูดตั้งแต่คราวที่แล้ว ที่รู้สึกแฮปปี้มากคือน้องๆ ในทีม แพนมีอะไรใหม่ๆ ขึ้นมา เราเลือกทุกคนที่ค่อนข้างเฟรซ สดใหม่ อาจไม่ใช่คนที่มาถึงปั้งๆ ได้เลย แจ่ทุกคนพยายาม เราจะได้เห็นการพัฒนาของทุกคน”
ทำไมแชมป์ไม่ฟื้นสักที?
“รอดูค่ะ (หัวเราะ)”
กดดันไหม เพราะหลายคนบอกว่าแอนโทเนียเขามา ตั้งใจจะมาเพื่อมาแก้เกม?
“แอนทำดีมาก ชื่นชมน้องมาก เรารู้วึกว่าแพ้ชนะมันเป็นส่วนหนึ่งแหละ แต่เรื่องการทำงาน การให้อาวุธน้องไปทำงานต่อ มันเป็นอีกเรื่องหนึ่ง อาจเป็นรายการเป็นเกม แต่เราอยากให้น้องได้อะไรไปทำต่อจริงๆ สำหรับแอนเอง แพนชื่นชมน้องมาก เก่งมาก”
ฟีดแบ็กจากคนดู ดูว่าสะใจทุกอีพี ที่พี่มานั่งดูคนทะเลาะกัน?
“แพนก็ซ้ายทีขวาที เราก็นิ่งๆ สวยๆ เดี๋ยวรอดูว่ามงจะมาตกที่เราหรือเปล่า”
จะมีแมตช์ที่เราได้ร่วมวงไหม?
“มีค่ะ”
มีดีลลับกับแอนโทเนียไหม เพราะตัดอีกทีมออกค่อนข้างเยอะมาก?
“รู้ได้ยังไง ยังสิมันไม่ถึง ทุกอย่างเกิดขึ้นเร็วมาก ถ่ายทำกันเร็วมาก เดี๋ยวรอติดตามดีกว่าว่าจะเป็นยังไง”
ได้ติดตามกระแสซีซันนี้บ้างไหม?
“มีบ้าง มีคนให้กำลังใจ ส่งมาถาม ความเผ็ดร้อนอาจแตกต่างกันไปแต่ละอีพี แต่ละซีซัน”
อีกหนึ่งอย่าง หลายคนบอกว่าแต่ละอีพีดูอ่อมไม่ฟาดเหมือนซีซั่นก่อนๆ คนดูเลยผิดหวัง?
“สำหรับคนทำงานเราเต็มที่ทุกอัน อยู่ที่คนคาดหวังอยากเห็นอะไรจากตรงนั้น ดูตามสถานการณ์ตรงนั้น ถ้าอยู่ๆ ปรี๊ดป๊าด อารมณ์สวิงนิดนึง”
มีการปรับเบื้องหลังการทำงาน?
“ทีมงานทุกคนทำงานเต็มที่ พยายามทำในสิ่งที่ทำได้ ทำงานกับพี่ซินดี้หรือน้องแอน เราแฮปปี้ (อาจต้องรออีกนิดนึง?) ขึ้นอยู่กับความชอบของแต่ละคน”
กระแสอีกหนึ่งเรื่อง ตัวแพนมีส่วนเกี่ยวข้องกับกลุ่มในมูลนิธิ?
“จริงๆ มีโอกาสได้ช่วยกัน มีโอกาสร่วมกับพี่บุ๋มในบางกิจกรรม บางโอกาสได้เจอกัน”
ส่วนใหญ่เป็นงานร่วมกิจกรรม?
“จริงๆ เวลามีกิจกรรมการกุศลหรือกิจกรรมที่ต้องลงไปช่วยเหลือ เราก็จะไปเจอพี่บุ๋มและทีมที่ไปช่วยกัน”
เราได้บริจาคบ้างไหม?
“ส่วนใหญ่น่าจะเป็นสิ่งของ ที่ไปร่วมบุญด้วยกัน”
ร่วมกิจกรรมที่ผ่านมาเป็นยังไงบ้าง ได้เห็นภาพอะไรบ้าง?
“แพนรู้จักพี่บุ๋มมานานมาก (เราสายบุญเหมือนกัน?) ใช่ๆ ได้ทำบุญด้วยกันมานานมาก เป็นพี่ที่น่ารักเสมอ เราจะได้เห็นว่าพี่บุ๋มเป็นผู้หญิงสตรอง ขับเคลื่อนในการทำสิ่งต่างๆ ในมุมพี่สาวที่เราได้เห็นมาตลอดเราก็นับถือในมุมที่เขาที่มีความตั้งใจทำสิ่งต่างๆ ในหลายๆ เหตุการณ์ที่ผ่านมา”
พอเห็นข่าว ความรู้สึกเราเป็นยังไงบ้าง กับภาพที่เราเคยไปเห็น?
“ในส่วนของความเป็นพี่สาว ยังไงก็นับถือรักและเคารพเหมือนเดิม ในส่วนอื่นรอติดตามไปตามสถานการณ์”
แพนได้ส่งข้อความหาไหม?
“ยังไม่ได้ส่งไป ก็ขอให้ทุกอย่างผ่านไปได้คลี่คลาย ผ่านไปได้ในทางออกที่ดีที่สุด”
การทำดีมาตลอดของบุ๋มเลยทำให้คนไม่อยากจะเชื่อ?
“เราก็พยายามแยกแยะกันเนอะกับมุมที่เราได้เจอพี่บุ๋มมาโดยตลอด แล้วก็ในสิ่งที่พี่บุ๋มทำเพื่อสังคมหลายส่วน แพนว่ามันก็มีอะไรมากมายที่แกก็เป็นตัวอย่างที่ดีให้กับทุกคน เราก็ค่อยๆ พิจารณาสิ่งต่างๆ ไปดีกว่า แพนเชื่อว่ามันมีหลายอย่างที่เราอาจจะต้องการคำตอบในช่วงเวลาตรงนี้แต่ว่าเราในฐานะน้องที่รัก ณ ตอนนี้ก็คือให้กำลังใจแล้วค่อยๆ พิจารณาสิ่งต่างๆ กันไปดีกว่า”
การรักษาความดีมันอาจจะยาก ถ้าในมุมของแพนเรารักษาความดีของตัวเองยังไง?
“มันก็ทุกคนทำได้แหละ แต่อาจมีอะไรหลายอย่าง มีซ้ายบ้างขวาบ้างตามเรื่องราว แม้กระทั่งตัวเราเอง แต่ถ้าเราพยายามให้ตัวเองอยู่ในเส้นที่คิดว่าเหมาะควร ที่เราสามารถทำได้ ไม่กระทบกระเทือนใคร นั่นคือสิ่งที่ตั้งใจในการทำงานมาโดยตลอด แต่มันไม่มีใครเพอร์เฟกต์ไปหมด ไม่พลาดเลย คงเป็นไปไม่ได้”
ในวันที่อาจจะมีสิ่งยั่วยุเข้ามา เรามีการดำรงตัว หรือรับมือยังไงบ้าง?
“สำหรับตัวแพน ก็คงกลับมาที่ครอบครัว โชคดีที่มีคุณพ่อคุณแม่ เราอยู่ด้วยกันเดินมาตรงนี้ด้วยกัน มีการตบซ้ายตบขวากันตลอด ช่วงเวลาไหนมากไปน้อยไป แม่คอยกระตุกนิดนึง เรายังอยากทำงานเส้นทางนี้เป็นอาชีพ อยากทำงานอยู่ตลอด เราก็ต้องดูแลตัวเองในเส้นทางของเรา (คนรอบข้างสำคัญ?) สำคัญมาก สภาพแวดล้อมสิ่งแวดล้อมก็นำพากันไป อย่างเราทำงานในฐานะสื่อ สิ่งที่พูดเราพยายามระวังและพิจารณาตลอด ก็เป็นกำลังใจให้กัน สำหรับทุกคนและทุกเรื่องค่ะ”

content:
The Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) has largely become associated with the overall health of the global artificial intelligence ecosystem in recent months, owing to the dominance of its two largest companies, Samsung and SK Hynix. The two semiconductor giants now account for around 50 percent of the entirety of the KOSPI – and the index has become especially vulnerable to industry-related volatility due to their high market capitalizations.
At this stage, it’s important to highlight that artificial intelligence has still been an exceptionally strong tailwind for the KOSPI. Growth related to the technology’s rapid evolution paved the way for the South Korean index to more than double in value since the beginning of 2025. The KOSPI’s six-quarter growth rate between January 2025 and the beginning of July 2026 sat at more than 231 percent.
However, since its June peak, the index has shed more than a third of its value, and there’s been little sign of a recovery. Worryingly, the downturn appears to have been driven by a global slowdown in investor enthusiasm for AI stocks. Fears are growing over the seismic capital expenditures of hyperscalers, which are projected to reach $1 trillion in 2026 alone.
In the United States, investors have also seen an AI slowdown, with the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF slipping 5.39 percent in value since the beginning of the third quarter of 2026.
South Korea unveiled ambitious AI infrastructure plans this summer. President Lee Jae-myung announced plans to commit $880 billion to rejuvenate the economies of areas outside the capital, Seoul. The package will focus on three areas: chip production hubs, data centers, and robotics technology.
But the announcements came in late June. Since then, the KOSPI’s value has slipped by 35 percent – over one-third – although it’s still up 37 percent since the start of 2026. South Korea’s tech outlook appears to be changing at a rapid pace. While memory demand has remained resilient, foreign selling has pushed Korean shares to six-month lows in recent weeks.
The negative sentiment has even spread beyond tech stocks and into domestic automakers and tech stocks, which suggests that the bearish outlook could linger for longer.
This downturn has seen Goldman Sachs cut 25 percent off of its target price for the KOSPI, chopping its 12-month forecast from 12,000 to 9,000 in a note posted in late October. However, Goldman’s chief equity strategist for Asia, Tim Moe, has also provided a timely reminder that the recent sell-offs haven’t made much of a dent in the KOSPI’s long-term growth, maintaining a “strong buy” status on the index.
Even at a lower price target of 9,000, the KOSPI’s implied upside still represents a 60 percent growth rate from current levels. That indicates a clear continuation of South Korea’s artificial intelligence boom period.
At this stage in its development cycle, it’s certainly worth taking stock of the potential gains. Estimates hold that the South Korea AI infrastructure market is set to rally from a value of $2.58 billion in 2025 to $26.75 billion by 2035, representing a CAGR of 26.35 percent. This growth will be driven primarily by the nation’s advanced semiconductor market, as well as AI computing, cloud platforms, AI manufacturing, and the construction of high-performance data centers.
This aptitude for AI growth can help to compound South Korea’s infrastructure initiatives. Developments in the technology can pave the way for new efficiency brought by operational AI agents, which can identify and work toward solutions while identifying bottlenecks in the buildout process.
Critically, South Korea is earning global support for its AI ambitions. Semiconductor giant Nvidia, which is currently the world’s largest company with a market capitalization of $5 trillion, announced plans during the summer to expand South Korea’s sovereign AI factory infrastructure through planned investments that will grow its Nvidia DSX AI factory deployment to 200 megawatts. The move would see the facility at the GAK Sejong data center more than triple its capabilities from an initial 55 megawatts. Collaborators on the project, Naver and Brookfield, are eyeing a 1 gigawatt facility in the future.
The KOSPI remains integral to the scale of South Korea’s AI ambitions. Although the index has shed more than a third of its value since the summer, it’s clear that expectations remain high thanks to its high concentration of semiconductor superstars in Samsung and SK Hynix. With an ambitious $880 billion AI infrastructure buildout already taking shape, it’s important for the KOSPI, as a barometer of the overall health of the AI landscape, to begin displaying some more resilience. But with a strong domestic innovation pipeline, we’re likely to see a symbiotic relationship form as more industry innovations drive investor optimism.
As things stand, South Korea’s AI ambitions aren’t under threat. If the KOSPI can recover to reach new highs of 9,000 over the next year, we might see the nation stake a claim as one of the world’s most important emerging artificial intelligence ecosystems.
summary: South Korea has emerged as one of the world leaders in the AI buildout. But now, as investor sell-offs continue to force the KOSPI lower, are its AI ambitions under threat?
summary_th: เกาหลีใต้กลายเป็นหนึ่งในผู้นำระดับโลกด้านการสร้าง AI แต่ตอนนี้ ในขณะที่นักลงทุนขายออกยังคงบังคับให้ KOSPI ลดต่ำลง ความทะเยอทะยานด้าน AI ของบริษัทกำลังถูกคุกคามหรือไม่?
title: Amid Stock Troubles, Is South Korea’s $880 Billion AI Infrastructure Buildout Under Threat?

content:
On October 28, Taiwanese media reported that the Secretary for Relations with States of the Holy See, Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, addressed the progress of negotiations regarding a Vatican office in China at an event with journalists in Rome. When a reporter asked about the status of these talks, Monsignor Gallagher responded: “The idea is to have some type of cultural presence in Beijing. But, as with everything in a negotiation, there would be a price to pay and, for the moment, we are not willing to pay that price.”
The report drew significant attention in Taiwan and Hong Kong media. This was partly because it cited earlier reporting by the Italian daily Corriere della Sera that, during the tenure of the late Pope Francis, the Vatican’s Secretariat of State repeatedly expressed a long-standing desire to establish a “permanent office” in China. Corriere della Sera also noted that Beijing proposed a precondition, demanding that the Vatican first sever diplomatic ties with Taiwan.
The Taiwanese news outlet ETtoday followed up, using the headline, “Beijing Proposes ‘Severing Ties with Taiwan’ in Exchange for an Office? Vatican Foreign Minister: Not Prepared to Pay the Price for Now.” Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s TVB provided an in-depth report headlined, “Vatican Foreign Minister: Sino-Vatican Bishop Agreement Flawed, Holy See Has No Intention of Setting Up Office in Beijing.” Archbishop Gallagher’s remarks about establishing an office have undoubtedly struck a sensitive nerve in cross-strait relations.
However, while Archbishop Gallagher mentioned that “there would be a price to pay,” he did not explicitly state what that “price” entails. A report by INFOVATICANA simply noted, “The archbishop did not wish to specify what the demands would be to reach such an understanding. Currently, the Holy See maintains diplomatic relations with Taiwan and has a study mission in Hong Kong, but does not have official diplomatic representation in the People’s Republic of China.”
Reuters’ reporting focused solely on Gallagher’s admission of the provisional agreement’s flaws, quoting him as saying: “It’s not easy, the dialogue is not easy. The imperfections of the agreement are evident, but there is a commitment to persevere in dialogue… and that is what will continue to happen.”
Comparing Chinese and English media reports, the assertion that the “price” the Holy See must pay – but is currently unwilling to – involves severing ties with Taiwan seems to be an interpretation by Chinese-language media of past Italian reporting, which in turn reflected the Chinese Communist Party-led government’s stated position.
Beyond the political maneuvering between Taiwan and China over formal Vatican recognition, what is the Holy See’s real motive for establishing an office in China? Is it to forge diplomatic relations, or is it a procedural step in negotiating the agreement on the appointment of bishops?
I believe it is necessary to clarify the significance of this “office” through the lens of the Holy See’s pastoral mechanism for China – specifically, the appointment of bishops. The Vatican’s effort to establish a presence in Beijing should not be oversimplified as “the Holy See rejecting China’s demand to break ties with Taiwan” or “the Holy See currently having no intention of opening an office in Beijing.”
As to whether this issue will return to the Sino-Vatican negotiating table, some scholars believe that the issue of setting up an office is unlikely to be discussed in near-term negotiations, now that the policy position is clear. I disagree; establishing an “office” will almost certainly remain an active topic of discussion. My primary argument is that an on-the-ground presence is necessary to properly implement the Sino-Vatican agreement. A Papal delegate’s presence in Beijing is necessary for good governance over the episcopal appointment process. Beijing is deliberately misinterpreting the purpose of this “office” as a matter of diplomatic negotiation over cross-strait relations, masking its true reluctance to loosen its control over the Catholic Church’s religious freedom.
While traveling in a devoutly Catholic European country, I had the privilege of attending its National Day reception. During the event, I met a senior Holy See diplomat assigned to that nation. Out of curiosity, I asked, “Father, what does your daily work entail? Being in such a devout Catholic country, is your work fairly smooth?” The diplomat replied, “Not exactly. 90 percent of my work involves investigating bishop appointments. I need to understand the backgrounds of so many clergy members to determine who is suitable to become a bishop.” This Holy See diplomat’s statement truthfully outlined the core mission of a papal diplomat. Fulfilling pastoral care in a local Catholic Church includes vetting candidates for the episcopacy as a primary task.
The Holy See and the People’s Republic of China signed a provisional agreement on the appointment of bishops in 2018, and renewed it in 2024 for another four years, until 2028. Since the signing of the agreement, the Pope has appointed several bishops in China, resulting in an increasingly rejuvenated Chinese Catholic episcopate. However, the process by which China selects bishop candidates remains a black box. Because there is no true religious freedom in China, the Catholic Church remains under severe control of the Chinese Communist Party’s United Front Work Department.
Scholars note that, even without a formal Holy See-Vatican office in China, certain civic organizations operated by religious orders may play intermediary roles. Yet these unofficial mechanisms are far less institutionalized than establishing a direct, official office in Beijing. Regarding the Holy See’s process for selecting bishop candidates, a significant concern is whether the background of every episcopal candidate can be vetted in a diverse and transparent manner. If the Holy See does not have an official delegate in China – and if that representative cannot investigate freely while possessing completely uncontrolled personal liberty – then establishing a Holy See-Vatican office in Beijing is a false proposition, one that merely falls into the CCP’s diplomatic narrative of coercing the Holy See over whether to sever ties with the Republic of China (Taiwan).
In the article “Diplomacy and Divided Nations: The Holy See’s Approach to China and Taiwan,” published in the journal Issues & Studies, Yun Wang and I analyzed the distinction between a Papal Delegation and an Apostolic Nunciature. The core differences lie in the presence of “Diplomatic Recognition” and whether the primary counterpart for engagement is the “local government” or the “local church.” These two terms represent entirely different tiers of diplomatic tools the Vatican uses across varying political environments and historical periods. Whether the Holy See-Vatican is pushing to establish a Papal Delegation or an Apostolic Nunciature in Beijing becomes clearer when we look at another Asian communist state the Holy See engages with: Vietnam.
The office in Beijing is truly intended to be a Papal Delegation, an ecclesiastical rather than diplomatic office. However, the CCP cleverly conflates the two. When the Holy See proposes a Papal Delegation to China, Beijing counters that establishing an Apostolic Nunciature requires “first severing ties with Taipei.” This is a malicious interpretation to disguise China’s basic lack of religious freedom.
This year marks the 400th anniversary of Catholicism’s arrival in Taiwan. The Chargé d’Affaires of the Apostolic Nunciature to China (Taipei), Monsignor Stefano Mazzotti, has attended multiple events marking the anniversary. “This year marks the 400th anniversary of the arrival of the first Catholic missionaries in Taiwan to evangelize,” he said in one such speech. “Today, the Catholic Church has taken deep root and become an indispensable part of Taiwan’s diverse society. The Holy See will work hand in hand with the international community, including Taiwan, to continue to develop and consolidate the Church’s mission within the framework of ‘security and freedom,’”
As my previous article “Taiwan-Vatican Ties: The Dynamic Interplay Under Pope Leo XIV” indicated, amid shifting Sino-Vatican dynamics, Taiwan has no reason to worry. In the eyes of the Holy See, Taiwan remains an undeniably “precious” presence. I firmly believe Taiwan can be decoupled from the Sino-Vatican negotiation narrative, and indeed, it must be. Neither Taiwan nor the Holy See should fall into the narrative trap maliciously set by the Chinese Communist Party.
summary: Archbishop Gallagher’s remarks about the “price” of setting up an office in Beijing have struck a nerve in Taiwan. But the two aren’t actually related.

content:
บลู พงศ์ทิวัตถ์ เคลียร์ความสัมพันธ์ ‘ลิซ่า’ สนิทเพราะแก๊งเพื่อนเดัยวกัน ยันหัวใจยังโสด จีบได้
หล่อออร่าพุ่ง กับการปรากฏตัวในงานเปิดตัวซีรีส์ “The Remarried Empress” สำหรับพระเอกหนุ่ม “บลู พงศ์ทิวัตถ์” ที่งานนี้เจ้าตัวได้ออกมาเปิดใจอัพเดตสถานะหัวใจ พร้อมตอบประเด็นที่แฟนๆ จับตาความสัมพันธ์กับซูเปอร์ตาร์สาว “ลิซ่า” โดยหนุ่มบลูเผยว่า สนิทกันเพราะอยู่แก๊งเพื่อนกลุ่มเดียวกัน ไม่ได้กดดันที่ถูกจับตามอง และมั่นใจว่าหัวใจยังโสดสนิท พร้อมเอ่ย “จีบได้” ส่วนโปรเจ็กต์คู่มีเพียงงาน ททท. เท่านั้น พร้อมสยบข่าวลือเล่น MV ให้ลิซ่า ยืนยันไม่ใช่ตนแน่นอน!
อัพเดตหัวใจหน่อยสีชมพู่ไหม?
“เป็นสีบลูครับ เพราะว่าแฟนคลับผมชื่อด้อมว่าบลูด้า”
อาการมันเป็นยังสีบลู?
“ก็เป็นอย่างนี้ครับ (ทำท่าน่ารัก)”
หัวใจตอนนี้คนจับต้องได้ไหม?
“จับต้องได้ครับ”
ช่วงนี้ดูเรามีความสุข?
“ช่วงนี้ผมรู้สึกว่าผมเอ็นจอยและรู้สึกว่าโฟกัสงานและเตรียมเพลงด้วย เพื่อมาให้ทุกคนฟัง”
ไปต่างประเทศเพื่อไปเก็บประสบการณ์มาทำเพลง?
“ต่างประเทศไปทำงาน ไม่ว่าจะที่ประเทศไทยหรือต่างประเทศก็เป็นประสบการณ์หมด ขึ้นอยู่กับสิ่งที่เราเจอ”
หล่อขนาดนี้จีบได้ไหม?
“จีบได้ครับ”
มั่นใจว่าโสด?
“มั่นใจครับ”
หลายคนมองว่าเราหล่อขนาดนี้ไม่น่าโสด
“จริงหรอครับ”
ได้ดูกระแสข่าวเราไหมที่หลายๆ คน จับตาความสัมพันธ์กับ “ลิซ่า”?
“มีเห็นบ้าง ส่วนตัวผมก็ปกตินะครับ คือช่วงนี้เตรียมเพลงจริงๆ โฟกัสเพลงกับทีมที่ค่าย”
รู้สึกยังไงคนจับตามอง?
“จริงๆ ผมก็ทำตัวปกติ ใช้ชีวิตปกติ”
กดดันไหมจะไหนก็มีภาพถ่ายออกมา?
“จริงๆ ก็ไม่ได้เกร็งอะไร ก็ใช้ชีวิตปกติ”
หลายคนโฟกัสความสัมพันธ์เรากับลิซ่า?
“คือผมกับพี่เขาก็สนิทกันเพราะว่าเพื่อนๆ พี่ๆ อยู่แก๊งเดียวกัน”
กดดันไหมมีคนจับตามองขึ้น?
“ก็ไม่ได้รู้สึกกดดันเพราะผมก็ปกติ”
เพื่อนๆ มีแซวบ้างไหม?
“ยังไม่มีครับ”
แสดงว่าเราก็ยังไม่ได้ข้ามโซนที่ใครเข้าใจกันใช่ไหม?
“ก็อย่างที่บอกเลยครับว่าสนิทกัน เพราะว่าเพื่อนๆ พี่ๆ ก็เป็นแก๊งเดียวกัน”
เราจะมีโปรเจ็กต์ร่วมกับลิซ่า?
“โปรเจก็ต์ร่วมกันก็มีททท.ครับ ทางด้านเรื่องเพลงก็ยังไม่มีร่วมกัน”
หลายคนไปจับตาว่าเราไปเล่น MV ให้กับลิซ่า ?
“ไม่ใช่ผมครับ”
summary: บลู พงศ์ทิวัตถ์ เคลียร์ความสัมพันธ์ ‘ลิซ่า’ สนิทเพราะแก […]
title: บลู พงศ์ทิวัตถ์ เคลียร์สัมพันธ์ ลิซ่า สนิทเพราะแก๊งเพื่อนเดัยวกัน ยันหัวใจยังโสด จีบได้

content:
The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
Date:
November 3, 2026
Source:
McGill University
Summary:
A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.
Share:
The brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but new research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
For years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.
In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.
"Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," said senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD."
How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear
To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.
The researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.
At the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.
"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," said Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.
Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger
Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an important evolutionary purpose.
The experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.
Such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.
"The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters."
The ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The new findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.
A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD
The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.
For someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.
The researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too quickly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.
"Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," said Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'."
Because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.
Study Details and Funding
The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.
The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.
