content:
Thailand has long prided itself on its foreign policy acumen and its status as the only nation in Southeast Asia that avoided colonization by the West. At the center of this is the notion of “bamboo diplomacy” – a form of diplomacy that prioritizes pragmatism and flexibility in pursuit of the national interest. However, in a recent article, Pongkwan Sawasdipakdi argued that memories of past Thai diplomatic successes had become a trap, that an idealized vision of its own past had the potential to restrict the country’s foreign policy – in particular, its response to the growing
Pongkwan, a lecturer in international relations at Thammasat University in Bangkok, spoke to The Diplomat’s Sebastian Strangio about the origins of “bamboo diplomacy,” and how history informs Thailand’s present diplomatic behavior, and the potential for the country to become trapped by its own past successes.
To begin with, what are the main principles of “bamboo diplomacy”? To what extent does it even constitute a coherent doctrine?
Bamboo diplomacy draws on the analogy of bamboo bending with the wind. Rather than standing rigidly against strong winds and risking being broken, bamboo survives by adapting to changing conditions. Applied to foreign policy, the analogy emphasizes prudence, flexibility, and the ability to gauge the direction of great power competition before committing to a particular course of action.
In the language of modern international relations, bamboo diplomacy can encompass both bandwagoning and hedging, depending on the circumstances. When the winds blow strongly in one direction, Thailand may find it necessary to align itself with the dominant power. When the balance of power is less clear, Thailand may instead hedge by maintaining relations with competing powers and avoiding firm commitments to either side.
This is also why I would hesitate to characterize bamboo diplomacy as a coherent doctrine. It is better understood as a broad diplomatic philosophy that prioritizes adaptability and survival rather than a clearly defined set of foreign policy principles. Its flexibility allows Thai policymakers to justify different, and sometimes contradictory, strategies under the same label. In this sense, bamboo diplomacy tells us more about how Thailand understands its approach to navigating great power competition than about the specific policies.
Your article explores how memories of past Thai diplomatic successes – in particular, Thailand’s avoidance of colonization by the West and its management of relations with the Allies in the aftermath of WWII – have shaped Thai diplomatic practice, trapping the country in “a pattern of light hedging and ambiguous foreign policy positioning.” Why do you think these memories have exercised such a hold, and how much can they be attributed to Thai efforts, as opposed to circumstances beyond Thailand’s control?
Broadly speaking, these two historical episodes are influential because they shape how Thailand understands its own survival during existential crises. They are remembered as critical junctures at which Thailand successfully navigated the challenges posed by great powers. The avoidance of colonization, in particular, has a powerful place in the Thai national narrative because it is closely associated with the prudence and diplomatic skills of King Rama V. This narrative has also been repeatedly glorified as part of the broader effort to legitimize and institutionalize the monarchy.
I am not suggesting that diplomacy played no role in Thailand’s survival. Rather, my concern is that these historical narratives tend to overemphasize Thailand’s diplomatic agency while overlooking the external circumstances that contributed to its success.
Take the avoidance of colonization, for example. It is true that Siam undertook significant modernization efforts, adopted Western institutions, pursued closer relations with Western powers, and opened its economy to international trade. These were important diplomatic and political choices. But timing and geography also worked in Siam’s favor. Its position between the British and French colonial territories gave both powers an interest in maintaining Siam as a buffer. Moreover, as European powers became increasingly preoccupied with rivalries on the continent, further expansion into Siam carried the risk of provoking tensions with other colonial powers. In other words, Siam’s survival cannot be explained by diplomatic skill alone.
The Second World War is somewhat different. Unlike the colonial episode, the popular narrative does not necessarily attribute Thailand’s survival to a single individual. There are references to the Free Thai Movement, although its role in helping Thailand avoid the consequences of being treated as a defeated country is not always clearly articulated. What tends to be remembered, however, is that Thailand once again managed to navigate a major international crisis successfully. This narrative often overlooks the broader geopolitical context, particularly Thailand’s strategic value to the United States in the emerging Cold War order.
The problem with these narratives is that they place too much emphasis on agency and too little on structure. By attributing Thailand’s historical successes primarily to its own diplomatic prudence, they risk creating the impression that the same approach can be replicated regardless of changing international circumstances.
How and when were these episodes enshrined as a coherent doctrine, and for what purpose? By what process have they come to shape how policymakers interpret contemporary challenges?
According to Jittipat Poonkham, the author of “A Genealogy of Bamboo Diplomacy” (2022), these historical episodes were retrospectively incorporated into a coherent narrative of Thai diplomacy through the efforts of prominent foreign policymakers in the late 1960s and 1970s, as well as international relations scholars during the period.
As Jittipat explains, Thai policymakers faced considerable challenges in moving away from their rigid alignment with the United States toward a more flexible diplomatic approach, particularly as they sought détente with China and the Soviet Union. To justify this shift, proponents of flexible diplomacy invoked Thailand’s historical experiences, particularly its avoidance of colonization, as evidence of a long-standing tradition of diplomatic flexibility. This helped legitimize a significant departure from Thailand’s previously rigid anticommunist foreign policy by presenting it as a continuation of the country’s established diplomatic tradition rather than a radical change.
As for how this narrative shapes policymakers’ interpretation of contemporary challenges, I am still collecting evidence and would hesitate to draw definitive conclusions at this stage. What I would argue, however, is that bamboo diplomacy has become something of a script of survival for Thailand. It has become the default foreign policy approach in the absence of deliberate efforts to develop an alternative foreign policy strategy. As Jittipat argues in his article on “hedging by default,” what appears to be a carefully calibrated hedging strategy may actually reflect the absence of coherent strategic planning. In this sense, bamboo diplomacy may continue to shape Thailand’s foreign policy because it has become an established way of thinking about how Thailand should survive amid great power competition.
Can you give some examples of how this “script of survival” has influenced the country’s diplomacy in the current era?
One obvious example is Thailand’s 20-Year National Strategy (2018-2037) and its accompanying Foreign Affairs Master Plan, which reflect the principles of bamboo diplomacy by emphasizing the importance of maintaining balanced and neutral relations with major powers and adapting to changes in the international environment. However, as with bamboo diplomacy more generally, these plans remain broad, without clearly identifying specific foreign policy priorities or concrete steps to achieve their objectives.
We can also see this script of survival at work in Thailand’s response to intensifying competition between China and the United States. Successive Thai governments have sought to maintain good relations with both powers without clearly articulating or communicating their strategic priorities or policy red lines. This tendency to avoid firm commitments is also reflected in Thailand’s abstentions on several UN resolutions concerning Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
The underlying problem is that the belief in diplomatic flexibility as a means of survival, as reflected in the Foreign Affairs Master Plan, may lead policymakers to pay insufficient attention to changing external circumstances and the constraints they impose. By treating flexibility and neutrality as inherent diplomatic advantages, Thailand risks overlooking the possibility that intensifying great power competition may increasingly limit its ability to maintain such a position.
How well suited do you think “bamboo diplomacy” is to the current international environment? In what ways do these memories of past successes constrain Thailand’s diplomatic options today?
I am not suggesting that Thailand needs to pick a side amid intensifying geopolitical competition. After all, hedging remains a viable strategy for many small and middle powers. What I am arguing, however, is that predictability may be an increasingly important diplomatic advantage, if Thailand wants to position itself as a leading hub of international engagement, as envisioned in its Foreign Affairs Master Plan. The problem with bamboo diplomacy is that its emphasis on flexibility does not necessarily translate into clear foreign policy commitments, making it difficult for other countries to anticipate what Thailand is willing or unwilling to do.
For example, while Thailand’s Foreign Affairs Master Plan emphasizes neutrality as a diplomatic advantage, the highly publicized displays of close relations between Thai leaders and China, along with repeated references to China as an “elder brother,” may raise questions about Thailand’s actual position. When a country’s intentions and commitments are unclear, foreign partners may find it more difficult to regard it as a predictable and reliable partner. This could, in turn, constrain Thailand’s ability to play the international role it aspires to.
All in all, Thailand does not need to choose a side, but it does need to communicate clearly what it wants to achieve, what it is willing to do, and where its limits lie. Greater predictability could help Thailand build trust with its partners and enhance its relevance in international affairs.
Are there any competing narratives in Thai diplomatic history that offer a counterpoint to “bamboo diplomacy,” and do you see the potential for a shift in Thailand’s approach?
I am not sure whether these alternative approaches have developed into coherent narratives comparable to bamboo diplomacy, but there have been several attempts to pursue different policy directions. These include economic and trade diplomacy under Chatichai Choonhavan and Thaksin Shinawatra, the middle-power diplomacy recently advocated by Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow, and the emerging emphasis on science and technology diplomacy under the current administration.
Some of these approaches share overlapping ambitions. For example, Thaksin’s trade diplomacy sought to enhance Thailand’s regional leadership through initiatives such as the Asia Cooperation Dialogue (ACD) and greater regional economic integration. Similarly, the recent emphasis on middle-power diplomacy seeks to enhance Thailand’s relevance and influence in international affairs.
However, these approaches do not necessarily pose a direct competition with bamboo diplomacy. Trade diplomacy, for example, can coexist with flexible relations among major powers. The more meaningful departure would be a shift from treating survival and autonomy as Thailand’s principal diplomatic objectives toward defining the specific international roles Thailand wants to play and the contributions it seeks to make.
As for whether these approaches can produce a lasting shift, I remain uncertain. As the emergence of bamboo diplomacy in the 1970s demonstrates, establishing a dominant foreign policy narrative requires sustained efforts from both policymakers and the academic community. In today’s polarized domestic political environment, compounded by rapid geopolitical changes and ongoing tensions with neighboring countries, sustaining such efforts may prove particularly challenging. As a result, alternative approaches may struggle to become institutionalized and outlast the governments that introduce them.
summary: "Its flexibility allows Thai policymakers to justify different, and sometimes contradictory, strategies under the same label."

Indonesia has officially urged Russia to stop recruiting Indonesian citizens into its armed forces following a report last week that an Indonesian national was killed while fighting in Ukraine.
According to a report in the state news agency Antara, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang said on Sunday that Jakarta had conveyed its objection to Moscow through diplomatic channels.
“The Indonesian government has asked the Russian government to take the necessary steps to ensure that Indonesian citizens are not recruited into the Russian military or other military-related formations through any channel,” Yvonne said.
She added that Jakarta had asked Moscow to formally designate Indonesia as a country whose nationals are excluded from military recruitment, which other nations, including India, Sri Lanka, Colombia, and South Africa, have already done.
The past year has seen growing numbers of Indonesians drawn into the Russian army. As per Antara, the move came after Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) reported on October 27 that an Indonesian identified by the initials MT, born in 1978 and formerly employed as a taxi driver in Jakarta, had been killed on the frontline in Ukraine. The man “reportedly signed a one-year military contract but was killed approximately one week after being deployed to the battlefield,” it reported.
Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service (FISU) also said on August 27 that it had documents on at least eight Indonesians who were recruited into Russia’s army. It stated that Indonesia “has joined the list of countries that the Kremlin has turned into yet another source of cheap manpower for the war.”
As Radityo Dharmaputra wrote in a recent feature for The Diplomat, in many cases these people have been attracted to Russia by the prospect of civilian employment, only to find themselves tricked or forced into joining the armed forces. This has been complicated by the fact that Indonesian institutions opened a formal labor channel to Russia this year, as relations between the two nations have grown warmer.
“The scheme Moscow uses to recruit foreign cannon fodder has already been tested in dozens of other countries,” the FISU claimed in its August 27 statement. “Promises of high pay, non-combat duties, expedited Russian citizenship, and social benefits attract people who, more often than not, have no idea where they are actually being sent.”
As Radityo wrote in early October, the issue had previously been overlooked despite (or because of) the increasingly close relationship between President Prabowo Subianto and Russian president Vladimir Putin. Jakarta “counts the personal closeness between Prabowo and Putin as an asset, yet it has made no public use of that closeness to aid the citizens caught in this recruitment trap,” he wrote, contrasting it with other nations that had intervened with Russia at the highest level to stop their nationals being recruited by the Russian military.
The report that Indonesia has now made an official protest with Moscow is a sign that Indonesia is finally taking concerted action to protect its citizens abroad. One security analyst who has researched the issue said in a post on X that Jakarta’s announcement was a “significant development on a topic that went unacknowledged for a long time.”
In Sunday’s press conference, Yvonne urged Indonesians considering overseas employment to exercise caution, verify job offers through authorized institutions, and avoid signing contracts that they do not fully understand, Antara reported. She also said that prospective workers should be suspicious of any job offers promising unusually high compensation.
summary: In recent months, reports have surfaced of Indonesian nationals fighting on the frontlines in occupied Ukraine.

content:
It could be the opening of a Jurassic Park rip-off: scientists examining ancient dinosaur bones find what appear to be fossilised red blood cells, and traces of the molecule that gives the beast’s blood its distinctive crimson hue.
But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-eastern Brazil 115m years ago.
Electron microscope images of the dinosaur bones revealed small, round structures that resemble red blood cells in fine channels where blood vessels once ran, while chemical tests identified the presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around the body.
Such claims are controversial because biological tissues and molecules can break down fast, leaving little or no trace in ancient fossils. But if confirmed, it would open up entirely new avenues for scientists, allowing them to investigate dinosaur blood, metabolism and even their activity levels.
“We are seeing a mineral and molecular echo of the dinosaur’s original biology,” said Prof Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Western Australia who led the research team. “Fossilised red blood cells with distinct chemistry related to heme have never been found in situ in any fossil, let alone a dinosaur. This is a world first.”
The fossilised remnants of the Aratasaurus were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil, where researchers continue to study them. While analysing the dinosaur’s hind leg bones, Grice spotted the structures that resembled red blood cells.
The scientists’ suspicions that they were looking at red blood cells were bolstered when chemical tests came back positive for heme and its breakdown products. Tests also found traces of the amino acid building blocks for collagen, a key protein in connective and other tissues.
If the structures really are fossilised red blood cells, as the researchers contend, it raises the question of how they were preserved. According to Grice, a manganese compound called hausmannite, which formed in and around the blood cells, may have lent a helping hand by stabilising them prior to fossilisation. The same process might have helped preserve the amino acids, she added. The study appears in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
The work is already stoking debate. Prof Mary Schweitzer at North Carolina State University in the US, who has discovered remnants of blood vessels and soft tissues in dinosaur fossils, is not convinced Grice and her colleagues have found red blood cells. One reason for her doubt is that the dinosaur’s red blood cells should have a “nuclear bulge” making them appear dome-like on both sides. The structures Grice found are concave, suggesting they might be something else.
Schweitzer was more persuaded by the discovery of heme and collagen amino acids in the bone and said there was so much more to learn from exceptionally well-preserved fossils. Schweitzer added: “The conventional wisdom in palaeontology that all endogenous organics would disappear in a million years or less is being routinely challenged, and will continue to be as technological approaches to palaeontological specimens are more routinely applied.”
Another question the research raises is what other biological material might lurk in fossils collections around the world. On this, Grice urges extreme caution, adding that her work does not imply that large biological molecules such as proteins or DNA live on in ancient fossils. “Any extraordinary claim needs extraordinary analytical evidence,” she said. “The aim isn’t to find Jurassic Park DNA, it’s to determine how much genuine molecular information deep time can preserve.”
“The really exciting implication is that extraordinary molecular information may already be sitting in museum collections around the world, waiting for us to ask new questions of old fossils,” she added.

But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-eastern Brazil 115m years ago. summary_th: การทดสอบทางเคมีบนกระดูก Aratasaurus ระบุว่ามีฮีม ซึ่งเป็นสารประกอบอินทรีย์ที่ช่วยให้ฮีโมโกลบินในเลือดนำออกซิเจนไปทั่วร่างกาย อาจเป็นจุดเริ่มต้นของการฉ้อโกงของ Jurassic Park นักวิทยาศาสตร์ที่ตรวจสอบกระดูกไดโนเสาร์โบราณพบสิ่งที่ดูเหมือนจะเป็นฟอสซิลเซลล์เม็ดเลือดแดง และร่องรอยของโมเลกุลที่ทำให้เลือดของสัตว์ร้ายมีสีแดงเข้มที่โดดเด่น แต่นั่นคือสิ่งที่นักวิจัยอ้างว่าได้ค้นพบหลังจากวิเคราะห์กระดูกขาหลังของไดโนเสาร์กินเนื้อขนาดเล็กที่เรียกว่าอาราตาซอรัส ซึ่งอาศัยและตายในพื้นที่ซึ่งปัจจุบันคือทางตะวันออกเฉียงเหนือของบราซิลเมื่อ 115 ล้านปีก่อน อ่านต่อ...
title: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists
title_th: นักวิทยาศาสตร์เผยฟอสซิลเม็ดเลือดแดงในกระดูกไดโนเสาร์อายุ 115 ล้านปี

content:
‘หญิง ธิติกานต์’ เปิดใจปม ‘บุ๋ม ปนัดดา’ ยืนยันไม่เคยยุ่งเรื่องเงินมูลนิธิ เป็นแค่จิตอาสา เผยเห็นทำงานหนักจนซึม ลั่นไม่เหยียบคนกำลังล้ม ผิดจริงไม่เข้าข้าง วอนสังคมใจเย็นรอฟังข้อเท็จจริง
นักร้องลูกทุ่งสาว “หญิง ธิติกานต์” มาร่วมงานกาล่า ภ.กะเทยไทบ้าน ตอนไวรัสล้างโลก ที่สยามพารากอน และเปิดใจหลังเกิดประเด็นร้อนเกี่ยวกับ “บุ๋ม ปนัดดา” และมูลนิธิองค์กรทำดี ยอมรับตกใจและช็อกกับเหตุการณ์ที่เกิดขึ้น เพราะหลายเรื่องก็เพิ่งทราบพร้อมกับทุกคนในวันที่มีการแถลงข่าว เผยตัวเองเข้าไปร่วมงานในฐานะศิลปินจิตอาสา ไม่เคยเกี่ยวข้องกับระบบการเงินหรือการบริหารจัดการภายใน ยืนยันไม่กังวลหากถูกเรียกตรวจสอบ พร้อมเล่าถึงสิ่งที่เห็นจากการลงพื้นที่ เคยสังเกตเห็นบุ๋มเหนื่อยและมีอาการซึม แต่ไม่เคยปรึกษาปัญหาส่วนตัวให้ฟัง ย้ำยังขออยู่เคียงข้างในความดีที่เคยทำ แต่หากตรวจสอบพบว่าผิดจริงก็ไม่เข้าข้าง วอนสังคมใจเย็นๆ รอฟังข้อเท็จจริงและกระบวนการทางกฎหมาย
หญิง ธิติกานต์: “อันดับแรกเลยตกใจ หลายๆ เรื่องก็คือรู้พร้อมๆ กันกับทุกคนตอนที่แถลงข่าวนั่นแหละค่ะ หลายๆ เรื่องเลย แล้วก็รู้สึกช็อกว่ามันเกิดเหตุการณ์นี้ได้ยังไง ก็ได้ติดตามข่าวบ้าง พอสมควร ก็ทั้งทำงานด้วย แล้วก็อยากรู้ความคืบหน้าด้วยว่ามันเป็นยังไง แล้วมันจะจบตรงไหน ซึ่งหญิงมองว่ามันค่อนข้างที่จะหนักพอสมควร แล้วก็ไม่รู้ว่าจะไปจบตรงไหน แล้วก็วันไหน”
เราทำงานกับกับพี่บุ๋มค่ะ ไปในฐานะจิตอาสา หรือว่ามีส่วนอะไรในในองค์กรไหมคะ?
“ในส่วนของหญิง ก็คือหญิงจะแฮชแท็กตัวเองตลอดว่าเป็นศิลปินจิตอาสา มูลนิธิองค์กรทำดี เพราะว่าทำไมหญิงถึงเข้าไป ก็เห็นแม่บุ๋มนี่แหละว่าแกลงพื้นที่จริง รวดเร็ว แล้วก็ทำจริง แล้วเวลามีเหตุเพศภัยอะไร แกถึงพื้นที่ตรงนั้นเร็ว ทำให้เรามีความรู้สึกว่าในฐานะที่เราก็เป็นศิลปินคนหนึ่งที่อาศัยอยู่บนผืนแผ่นดินไทยก็เลยอยากที่จะไปร่วม ก็เลยเข้าไปร่วมกับมูลนิธินี้ แต่ในส่วนของเส้นทางต่างๆ ที่เราได้เห็นกัน อันนี้หญิงไม่รู้จริงๆ เป็นเพียงศิลปินจิตอาสาเท่านั้น”
แสดงว่าพี่หญิงไม่เคยเข้าไปถึงขั้นแบบว่าระบบการจ่ายหรือว่าเข้าไปช่วยอะไรขนาดนั้น?
“ไม่เคยค่ะ แต่ว่าเวลาที่เราลงพื้นที่ เวลาที่แม่ไป เราเห็นแม่จะคุยกับน้องๆ ที่ไปด้วยกัน แม่จะพูดตลอดเลยว่าพวกลูกๆ ทำให้ดีนะ ไม่ว่าจะเรื่องอะไรก็ตามอย่าให้เสียชื่อมาถึงแม่นะเว้ย แม่จะพูดคำนี้ตลอด แล้วก็บ่อยมาก อันนี้คือสิ่งที่หญิงได้เห็นได้สัมผัสด้วยตัวเอง ก็จะเห็นประมาณนี้”
แล้วส่วนเรื่องการใช้จ่ายเงินในองค์กรหรือของที่นำไปบริจาค เรามีส่วนในการเข้าไปจัดการอะไรยังไงบ้างไหมคะ? หรือว่าช่วงที่พี่บุ๋มบริหารจัดการข้างในเวลาก่อนที่จะออกไปสู่จากเราได้อยู่ตรงนั้นบ้างไหม?
“ถ้าในเรื่องของการซื้อของ ไม่ว่าจะเป็นของเข้ามูลนิธิ หรือว่าการซื้อของเข้าไปบริษัท อันนี้หญิงไม่ทราบเลย หญิงจะทราบแต่เพียงว่าว่างไหมมาช่วยแพ็คถุงยังชีพหน่อย ว่างไหมไปช่วยลงพื้นที่หน่อย ไปช่วยจ่ายถุงยังชีพหรือทำอะไรเพื่อสาธารณสังคมมากกว่า ถ้าในเรื่องลึกๆ การเงินนี่หญิงไม่ทราบจริงๆ”
ทุกครั้งที่ไปช่วยงานพี่บุ๋มเนี่ย เราเคยเจอคุณก๊อตบ้างไหม?
“หญิงเคยเจอคุณก๊อดน่าจะครั้งหนึ่งวันที่บวงสรวงที่มูลนิธิแค่นั้น แล้วก็แค่สวัสดีเฉยๆ ค่ะ ไม่ได้คุยอะไรกันเยอะ เพราะว่าดูพี่เขาค่อนข้างยุ่ง เดินประสานงานจุดนั้นจุดนี้แค่นั้นเอง”
แสดงว่าไม่มีโอกาสคุยเรื่องแบบคุยกันเป็นการส่วนตัว หรือเจอกันบ่อยๆ เลยใช่ไหม?
“ไม่มีค่ะ”
ความสนิทสนมของพี่หญิงกับแม่บุ๋ม พอแล้วได้เข้าไปทำงานเป็นจิตอาสานี้แ ล้วเนอะ แล้วสนิทสนมถึงขั้นแบบรู้ไหมว่าแม่เขา จิตใจเป็นยังไง?
“จริงๆ แล้วถึงแม้ว่าหญิงจะเจอแม่บ่อย ลงพื้นที่บ่อย แต่มันเหมือนหญิงเองก็ต้องมีระยะให้กับแม่เหมือนกัน เพราะว่าหญิงเห็นแม่ทำงานเยอะมาก บางทีไปลงพื้นที่พร้อมกัน แต่แม่ต้องรีบกลับไปถ่ายรายการ ไปเป็นพิธีกร ก็เลยทำให้ไม่ได้คุยอะไรกันเยอะ แต่ด้วยพื้นฐานที่หญิงเจอ แม่จะเป็นคนที่มีน้ำใจ แล้วก็ดูแลน้องๆ ในทีมงานองค์กรอยากเท่าเทียมกัน อันนี้คือสิ่งที่เห็น”
ก่อนหน้านี้พี่บุ๋มได้มาปรึกษา หรือได้มาแบบปรับทุกข์อะไรกับเราบ้างไหมคะ? เวลาออกไปทำงานอะไรที่พอเราจะรับทราบ วันนี้มีข้อเนี่ยที่มันเอ๊ะอ๊ะอะไรไหม?
“ไม่มีเลย แม่เป็นคนที่มีความอดทนเก่งมาก เป็นคนที่ไม่ปริปากพูดเลย จนช่วงหลังๆ มาก็สังเกตเหมือนกันว่าดูแม่น่าจะทำงานเยอะ ดูแม่เหนื่อยๆ บางช่วงเหมือนแกจะซึมๆ เราก็คิดว่าคงจะทำงานเยอะ และเมื่อไม่นานมานี้ก็เพิ่งเจอแม่ แล้วก็ดูแกซึมๆ ดูตาแดงๆ บ้าง”
แล้วเราเคยเจอ เราเจอพี่บุ๋มน้องสุดท้ายเมื่อไหร่คะ?
”เจอแม่ล่าสุดเลยก็คือวันที่เผาน้องฟองเบียร์ ซึ่งเป็นทีมงานองค์กรทำมูลนิธิเหมือนกันค่ะ เห็นแม่ดูเหนื่อย ดูตาแดงๆ วันนั้นเลย”
ช่วงนี้เขาจะทยอยเรียกพวกคนที่เคยบริจาคเงินหรือคนที่เคยร่วมงานอะไรอย่างเนี่ย พี่หญิงเราเรากังวลใจไหมกับเรื่องนี้?
“ไม่กังวลค่ะ เพราะว่าหญิงไม่ได้มีส่วนรับรู้ หรือว่าทราบในเรื่องของภายใน โดยเฉพาะเรื่องการเงินหญิงไม่ทราบเลย หญิงเพียงแต่เอาแรง แล้วก็ความรู้สึกของหญิงลงไปช่วยพื้นที่แค่นั้น ไม่กังวลค่ะ”
ก่อนหน้านี้เราเคยมีบริจาคให้กับมูลนิธิองค์กรทำดีไหมคะ?
“ช่วงแรกๆ มีค่ะ ห้าพัน หมื่นนึง ก็ตามกำลังของหญิง แต่ว่าด้วยส่วนตัวหญิงจะเอาแรงของตัวเองลงไปช่วยมากกว่า”
ซึ่งถึงตอนนี้เนี่ยความศรัทธาในตัวพี่บุ๋ม ความเชื่อมั่นเชื่อใจ มันยังมีเท่าเดิมไหมคะ?
“ในความไว้เนื้อเชื่อใจ เวลาที่หญิงเจอกับแม่ สัมผัสกับแม่ หญิงก็ยังคงขออยู่เคียงข้างแล้วกัน ในสิ่งที่แม่เคยทำ ในความดีที่เขาเคยมีให้กับสังคม แต่ถ้าในเรื่องที่เราตรวจสอบแล้วว่ามันผิด มันไม่ถูกต้อง ไม่โปร่งใส หรือเรื่องที่ต้องแก้ไข อันนี้ก็จะไม่เข้าข้างเช่นเดียวกัน ถูกไปตามถูก ผิดก็ไปตามผิดเลย หญิงเองก็มีโอกาสได้พูดไปบ้างแล้วบางส่วน ว่าเราคิดแบบนี้ แล้วหญิงก็โพสต์ที่จะให้กำลังใจแม่ในจุดนี้เหมือนกัน แม่ก็มาอ่าน แล้วแม่ก็ได้มาคอมเมนต์บอกว่า ขอบคุณนะลูก แล้วก็อีโมจิร้องไห้ ก็แสดงว่าแม่รู้แล้วว่าเราเคียงข้างนะ แต่ถ้าผิดไม่เข้าข้าง”
แล้วหญิงเนี่ย เป็นพยานจิตอาสาอย่างเนี้ยค่ะ ได้มีการพูดคุยกันไหมคะ ถ้าเกิดเป็นเรื่องใหญ่โตกัน มีการพูดคุยไหม?
“ก็จะมีพี่ลำยองที่ไปด้วยกันบ่อยๆ แล้วล่าสุดก็เจอกันถุงยังชีพ ก็ได้มีการคุยกันบ้าง แต่ว่าเราก็รู้เท่าที่ทราบเหมือนกัน เราก็คุยกันแค่นั้น”
คุยกันแล้วมีเศร้า มีซึมบ้างไหมคะ พอรู้ข่าว คนที่เคยคลุกคลีกับพี่บุ๋มเนี่ยค่ะ รับข่าว?
“มีค่ะ ก็เป็นธรรมดาค่ะ เพราะว่าเราเองก็ยังไม่รู้ข้อเท็จจริงในเรื่องที่มันเกิดขึ้น ไม่รู้ว่ามันมาก ไม่รู้ว่ามันจริง เท็จแค่ไหน แต่ถ้ามันจริง เราก็เสียใจนะ แต่ถ้ามันไม่จริง หญิงก็เชื่อว่าหลายๆ คน หรือว่าสังคมก็พร้อมที่จะให้โอกาสกับแม่ได้พิสูจน์ตัวเองเหมือนกัน”
หลายคนกลัวว่ามันจะไม่มีมูลนิธิดีๆ แล้วนะ จะไม่มีคนทำดีแล้วนะ?
“ตรงนี้ก็มีสิทธิ์ที่จะคิดได้ค่ะ หลายๆ คนก็มีความคิดที่แตกต่างกัน เอาเป็นว่าเราสะดวกใจแบบไหน อย่างไร เรื่องอะไร ก็แล้วแต่สิทธิ์ของบุคคลแล้วกันค่ะ แต่ในส่วนตัวของหญิง ก็ถือว่าเป็นเรื่องที่จะทำให้เป็นบรรทัดฐานที่มันเข้มแข็ง และหนักแน่นมากขึ้น สำหรับมูลนิธิที่กำลังมีอยู่ในตอนนี้ หรือกำลังจะเกิดขึ้นในอนาคต รวมถึงคนที่เป็นสะพานบุญ เป็นกระบอกบุญด้วย ก็จะได้รู้ว่าการกระทำแบบนี้ ถ้าคุณทำไม่ถูกต้อง วันหนึ่งคุณจะต้องโดนอะไรบ้าง เพราะฉะนั้น เริ่มต้นดีตั้งแต่ตอนนี้ ติดกระดุมไม่ถูก จะได้ไม่ต้องเกิดปัญหาค่ะ”
ก็หลังจากนี้เรา เวลาจะไปช่วยเหลือจิตอาสากับมูลนิธิไหน มันมีความระแวดระวังหรือมันมีความนอยด์ตรงนี้ไหมคะ?
“จริงๆ แล้วหญิงก็เป็นคนที่ช่วยด้วยตัวเองมาล่วงหน้าอยู่แล้ว แต่ว่าช่วยตามกำลังตัวเอง แต่ว่าพอมาเห็นมูลนิธิองค์กรทำดี เขาทำในพาร์ทที่มันใหญ่มากขึ้น แล้วก็กระจายการช่วยเหลือได้มากขึ้น ก็เลยลงมาช่วย แต่ว่าหลังจากนี้ก็ขอดูสถานการณ์ก่อน เหมือนกับที่ทุกคนมองนั่นแหละค่ะ ว่ามันจะอย่างไร
ตอนนี้หลายๆ คนตัดสินค่อนข้างเยอะมาก คือหญิงอยากจะบอกว่า ตอนนี้ข้อเท็จจริงที่เราได้เห็นกันทั้งหมด หรือว่าหลักฐานที่มันเกิดขึ้นทั้งหมด เรายังไม่สามารถบอกได้นะคะว่าเขาผิดจริง เพราะว่ายังไม่ได้เข้าสู่กระบวนการทางกฎหมาย ตอนนี้แม่บุ๋มเหมือนคนกำลังล้มอยู่แล้วยังลุกไม่ได้ สำหรับตัวหญิง หญิงจะไม่ข้าม จะไม่เหยียบ เพราะว่าหญิงมองเห็นในสิ่งที่เขาเคยทำเอาไว้ให้กับสังคม ทำให้กับคนที่ยากไร้ มันไม่ได้แค่เฉพาะเพื่อนมนุษย์ด้วยกันนะคะ กับสัตว์ต่างๆ หญิงก็ได้ลงพื้นที่กับแม่ ว่าแม่ช่วยจริง และก็การเข้าถึงเร็วมาก อันนี้คือเรื่องจริงเลย สำหรับแม่บุ๋ม สำหรับองค์กรทำดี อันนี้คือสิ่งที่หญิงได้เห็นกับตัวเอง เพราะฉะนั้นก็อยากให้ทุกคนฟังความไปก่อน ถ้ามันผิดจริง เราก็บล็อกไป ยังไงเข้าสู่กระบวนการอยู่แล้ว และคนผิดก็ต้องได้รับโทษทางกฎหมายอยู่แล้วนะคะ อยากให้ใจร่มๆ กันก่อน”
คนที่สละเรือ เทแม่กันเลย ?
“ตรงนี้ก็เป็นสิทธิ์ของเขาอีกเช่นเดียวกันว่าเขาจะคิดยังไง หรือว่าจะแก้ไข หรือว่าจะยังไงต่อไปกับสิ่งที่มันเกิดขึ้น หญิงก็ไม่อยากพูดอย่างนั้นหรอก มันอาจจะได้รับผลกระทบกับตัวเขาก็ได้ หรือว่าหน้าที่การงานของเขา ทุกคนก็มีเหตุผลของตัวเอง เพราะฉะนั้น ถ้าจะสละเรือ หรือว่าไม่ยอมอยู่เคียงข้างแล้วก็ไม่เป็นไร แต่ว่าหลังจากนี้ เราก็คอยดูกันต่อไป ว่าคนในชีวิตเราจะเหลืออีกกี่คนแค่นั้นเอง”
summary: ‘หญิง ธิติกานต์’ เปิดใจปม ‘บุ๋ม ปนัดด […]
title: หญิง ธิติกานต์ เปิดใจปม บุ๋ม ปนัดดา ยันไม่เคยยุ่งเรื่องเงิน ลั่นไม่เหยียบคนล้ม วอนสังคมใจเย็นรอฟังข้อเท็จจริง

content:
Two decades ago, a dear friend called me in a trembling voice. Was there hope for his young nephew, whose cancer had spread to the brain? Sadly, “no”, I said. But today, for such patients, there are options that were unimaginable back then.
Recently, researchers at the European Society For Medical Oncology presented the latest chapter results from a randomised controlled trial of a bespoke cancer vaccine for patients with high-risk melanoma. The trial involved 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed but remained at high recurrence risk. They received either pembrolizumab, an established immunotherapy, or pembrolizumab combined with an experimental mRNA vaccine, designed to help the immune system recognise and attack targets unique to the patient’s tumour.
At two years, 82.2% of those who received the combination were alive without their cancer returning, compared with 70% of those given pembrolizumab alone – a difference of about 12 percentage points. The combination also reduced the relative risk of distant metastasis or death by 38%.
These results raise the prospect that personalised vaccines could become an important addition to cancer treatment. Whether they will deliver similar benefits in other cancers remains to be established.
Overall survival data are not yet mature, so we don’t know whether the combination helps people live longer. Fever, injection-site pain and fatigue were common with the vaccine combination. Rates of severe treatment-related adverse events were similar between the groups; quality-of-life data is not yet available.
The standing ovation for the researchers was deserved, as was praise for the pharmaceutical companies that backed an idea that was once a pipe dream. Yet as cancer treatments become more effective, another question gains importance: what is life like for the people who receive them?
Treatment can delay a cancer’s return but can impose a considerable burden. Side-effects, fatigue, impaired mobility, psychological trauma, financial strain and the disruption of family and career all shape the experience.
In my work, I am often sobered by the juxtaposition of scans showing no cancer with a patient who cannot sleep, work or enjoy what others take for granted.
Recently, a retired academic approaching 90 told me: “My dear, the best thing you could do for me is get me safely home.” For this patient, their priority was clear; pursuing intervention would have caused a serious decline in their quality of life.
That does not mean some people should automatically be offered less treatment, or that the value of treatment depends on age alone. But it does mean oncologists must understand what each person hopes treatment will achieve, and explain what they may have to endure to get there.
My experience with elderly patients has made me more conscious of my other patients who are mid-career, raising children or caring for relatives.
The parent whose persistent nausea makes school drop-offs impossible.
The hairdresser who can’t work due to neuropathy.
The executive dismayed by cognitive fog.
A treatment that offers a cure or extra months of survival may be worthwhile to one person, even with significant toxicity. Others may place greater value on earning an income, caring for a child or living independently. These are not competing definitions of success: they are individual priorities that good medicine should respect.
Yet quality of life is often reported less rigorously than response, recurrence and survival. Less than a third of trials report quality-of-life measures in the primary publication, which most professionals read, and just half publish them at all.
Patient-centred care demands that information about quality of life should appear alongside the main findings, not years later in a separate publication, or not at all. When patients ask, “Doctor, how will this treatment affect my life?”, the information gap can become an indirect permission for oncologists to skim over the granular details.
A recent paper in The Lancet Oncology urges better reporting of health-related quality of life in trials of adjuvant treatments (treatments given after surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence). The researchers argue that average scores conceal important differences between patients: trials should instead report how many people experience a clinically meaningful deterioration, how long it lasts, and whether and when they recover.
Collecting quality-of-life data is not simple but, when data is missing, we should know why. Questionnaires are burdensome for sick patients and doctors have a different notion of quality of life from their patients. Of course, for a patient facing a life-threatening diagnosis, a chance at cure may reasonably outweigh significant toxicity concerns, but imperfect measurement is a reason to improve the status quo, not to look away.
From where I sit, I see immense gratitude for modern therapies but not inconsiderable decisional regret: “If only I had known.” We should empower patients to ask and be ready to tell them not only how likely a treatment is to work but also what it may cost them in daily life. Far too often, they find out later that treatment can bring months, years or even a lifetime of adverse effects.
None of this downplays scientific progress. Many treatments are now extending lives and personalised medicine may bring further gains. But the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curve. Researchers must collect quality of life outcomes diligently, clinicians should discuss them openly and health systems should treat them as central, not optional, to care.
While writing this column, my thoughts returned to the young man and his family, whose happiness for today’s melanoma patients is tinged with regret for their own loss. Today’s advance stands on the shoulders of the patients who generously volunteered to a take part in a study not knowing if they would themselves benefit. They deserve our gratitude.
Our ambition should be not only to keep people alive but to protect the lives they want to live, and to recognise that the true cost of treatment is measured in more than money.

Extra weight may be aging your brain faster than you think
Date:
November 2, 2026
Source:
University of Georgia
Summary:
A major 24-year study involving more than 8,200 adults suggests that excess body weight may accelerate brain aging, leading to faster declines in memory, concentration, and decision-making skills. The connection was particularly strong among people over 65, raising concerns about the long-term effects of obesity on brain health.
Share:
Carrying excess weight may affect more than physical health. New research from the University of Georgia suggests that having a higher body mass index may also speed up cognitive decline, potentially causing memory and thinking abilities to deteriorate more quickly with age.
Some cognitive changes are a natural part of getting older. Remembering information, thinking clearly, and processing new details can become more difficult over time. For healthy adults, however, these changes are usually relatively mild and develop gradually.
The new findings suggest that excess body weight may accelerate this process. Researchers found that people with higher body mass index (BMI) experienced faster declines in memory, overall cognitive performance, and executive functioning. These abilities are essential for everyday activities such as concentrating, planning, organizing tasks, and regulating emotions.
To investigate the connection, the research team analyzed data from a nationally representative study that tracked more than 8,200 adults over age 50 for 24 years.
Higher BMI Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline
The results revealed a consistent relationship between body weight and cognitive health. Each one-point increase in BMI was associated with a faster rate of cognitive decline, suggesting that even relatively small differences in body weight could matter over time.
The association was strongest at the eighth year of the study, and adults older than 65 showed the most pronounced effects.
Despite the concerning findings, researchers also identified a potentially encouraging opportunity to protect brain health. Managing body weight may help slow cognitive decline, with possible benefits becoming apparent within just two years.
"We found that if people managed their weight, they could significantly lower their rate of cognitive decline in just two years," said Suhang Song, the study's lead author and an assistant professor at the University of Georgia's College of Public Health. "That makes BMI one of the most easily modifiable risk factors when it comes to aging well."
How Excess Weight May Affect the Aging Brain
Obesity, generally defined as a BMI of 30 or higher, has been associated with poorer brain health. However, scientists are still working to understand exactly why carrying excess body weight may interfere with memory and other cognitive abilities.
Several biological processes could help explain the connection. Excess weight may promote inflammation, impair blood circulation, and contribute to insulin resistance. Together, these changes could increase the likelihood of cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease, and other forms of dementia.
The findings are particularly relevant given how widespread obesity has become in the United States. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, approximately two in five Americans meet the criteria for obesity when BMI is used as the sole measure.
Some scientists argue that BMI alone does not provide a complete picture of obesity. They support a broader definition that also considers waist measurements and medical conditions associated with excess weight. Using those additional criteria, the estimated proportion of Americans classified as having obesity rises to 75%.
Weight Management Could Help Protect Brain Health
The potential connection between obesity and cognitive decline is especially concerning as dementia becomes increasingly common. More than 7 million Americans currently live with dementia, and researchers expect that number to double by 2050.
Although the study does not establish that excess weight directly causes cognitive decline, its findings highlight body weight as a potentially important factor in maintaining cognitive health. Because weight can be managed, researchers believe it could offer an opportunity to reduce the risk of worsening memory and thinking abilities as people grow older.
"There are no cures for dementia," Song said, "which is why it is critical to identify and address any modifiable risk factors we can find to prevent it."
The research was published in the Journal of Neurology. Coauthors from the University of Georgia College of Public Health include Meng Hsuan Sung, Zhuo Chen, Janani Rajbhandari, Grace Bagwell Adams, Mahmud Khan, Ye Shen, and Xiao Song. Qianhui Xu and Xia Song also contributed to the study.

content:
IceCube detects ghost particles with 10 billion times the energy of solar neutrinos
Date:
November 2, 2026
Source:
University of California - San Diego
Summary:
Mysterious particles called neutrinos constantly stream through our bodies, and scientists are now detecting incredibly powerful versions arriving from distant cosmic sources using a massive observatory buried in Antarctic ice. These elusive “ghost particles” could hold extraordinary clues about the Big Bang, extreme cosmic events, and some of the universe’s greatest mysteries.
Share:
An enormous number of invisible particles are constantly traveling through Earth, passing through our bodies and continuing into space as though almost nothing stands in their way. Known as neutrinos, these mysterious particles are among the most difficult objects in the universe to detect. Yet scientists are finding ways to capture evidence of their passage, opening new opportunities to investigate the cosmos and its most extreme environments.
Neutrino research has played a remarkable role in modern physics. Discoveries involving these particles have contributed to five Nobel Prizes in Physics. This year, physicist Francis Halzen received the prestigious award "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin."
George Fuller, a Distinguished Professor of Physics at the University of California San Diego, has studied nuclear physics, particle astrophysics, and cosmology for decades. He also collaborated with Halzen on an early scientific paper about IceCube. His expertise helps explain what makes neutrinos so unusual and why scientists built an enormous observatory deep within the Antarctic ice to study them.
What Makes Neutrinos So Mysterious?
Neutrinos belong to a group known as elementary particles, which scientists believe have no smaller components. They come in three varieties, called electron, muon, and tau neutrinos. Unlike electrically charged particles, neutrinos have no electric charge. They do have mass, but it is extraordinarily small, potentially around 10 million times less than the mass of an electron. Their exact masses remain unknown, as does the mechanism responsible for producing them.
Another remarkable characteristic is their ability to travel through matter with almost no resistance. Because neutrinos interact so rarely with other particles, they can cross vast distances at speeds approaching the speed of light.
Neutrinos originate from many different places, including the Sun, distant regions of space, and sources scientists have yet to identify. They are also astonishingly abundant. Estimates suggest the universe contains roughly 1089 neutrinos, equivalent to approximately one billion for every atom in existence.
"Neutrinos are truly ghost-like particles," stated Fuller. "It's hard to stop them. It's hard to catch them. How do we even know they exist or where they are?"
Ghost Particles That Pass Through Almost Anything
Despite their elusive nature, neutrinos occasionally interact with matter through a fundamental force known as the weak interaction. This force is approximately 20 orders of magnitude weaker than electromagnetism. Such interactions can cause neutrinos to scatter or be absorbed, providing scientists with a way to detect them. However, these events are so uncommon that observing them requires exceptionally sensitive equipment.
Their ability to move through dense material also makes neutrinos valuable messengers from otherwise inaccessible regions of the universe. They can escape from environments surrounding collapsing stars and black holes, carrying information that other forms of radiation might not reveal.
The scale of this invisible activity is staggering. Approximately 100 billion neutrinos pass through every square centimeter of your body each second, almost entirely unnoticed.
"Because the interaction is so weak, neutrinos can get through almost anything," said Fuller. "Light years of lead -- depending on their energy, they would go right through it."
How Scientists Learned to Detect Neutrinos
The search for neutrinos began long before technology existed to observe them. During the 1930s, physicist Wolfgang Pauli proposed that an unknown particle might explain why energy appeared to be missing during certain forms of radioactive decay. He initially used a different name for the hypothetical particle (he called them "neutrons" at the time).
Pauli understood how difficult it would be to verify his idea. He famously acknowledged the problem by saying, "I have done a terrible thing, I have postulated a particle that cannot be detected."
For decades, neutrinos remained beyond the reach of experiments. That changed in 1956, when physicists Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines successfully detected them in an experiment known as "Project Poltergeist."
The breakthrough established that neutrinos were real, but detecting them remained an enormous challenge. Scientists needed increasingly sophisticated instruments to investigate the rarest and most energetic neutrinos arriving from space.
Why Antarctica Is Ideal for Hunting Cosmic Neutrinos
During the 1990s, Halzen recognized that the South Pole offered an extraordinary natural environment for neutrino research. Far below Antarctica's surface, immense volumes of ice are exceptionally clear, with relatively few bubbles or contaminants to interfere with the detection of faint flashes of light.
His vision eventually led to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a gigantic scientific instrument embedded within roughly one cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice. To construct it, researchers drilled deep holes and lowered long strings of sensitive light detectors called photomultiplier tubes.
These instruments search for brief flashes of blue light produced through a phenomenon called Cherenkov radiation. The light appears when a neutrino interacts with matter in the ice and produces a charged particle traveling faster than light can move through that material.
By recording these flashes, researchers can identify evidence of neutrinos that would otherwise pass through Earth without leaving a detectable trace.
Extraordinary Particles From Deep Space
IceCube is particularly important for studying neutrinos that arrive from distant cosmic sources with extraordinarily high energies. Unlike the enormous quantities of relatively low-energy neutrinos produced by the Sun, these powerful cosmic visitors are extremely rare. The observatory detects only a few dozen of the most energetic examples each year.
When one of these neutrinos interacts with the ice, it can produce a rapidly moving electron or muon. A muon, for example, generates a cone of Cherenkov light as it travels through the ice. Scientists analyze the resulting pattern of light to estimate the neutrino's energy and reconstruct the direction from which it arrived.
For Fuller, these exceptionally energetic neutrinos are among IceCube's most exciting discoveries because their origins and the physical processes responsible for accelerating them remain poorly understood.
"Some ultra-high-energy neutrinos detected at IceCube have roughly 10 billion times the energy of a typical neutrino from the Sun. One detected by a similar experiment has an energy 200 times higher than that. We don't really know where that neutrino came from," he stated. "The fact that it got here at all may be saying something profound about the universe. In that sense, Halzen really is at the frontier of experimental fundamental particle physics."
Neutrinos Could Reveal Secrets of the Big Bang
The scientific effort to understand neutrinos extends far beyond Antarctica. Researchers at UC San Diego are also involved in another major observatory that could offer new insights into these elusive particles and the universe's earliest history.
Located high in Chile's Atacama Desert, the Simons Observatory is gathering information about the cosmic microwave background, the ancient radiation left over from the early universe. Often described as the oldest light in the cosmos, this radiation provides a valuable record of conditions that existed shortly after the Big Bang.
UC San Diego helped establish the observatory, and Brian Keating, a Distinguished Professor of Physics at the university, serves as its principal investigator.
Although the observatory primarily studies ancient light, its measurements can also reveal information about neutrinos from the earliest stages of cosmic history. The project could provide an enormous amount of new data related to these ancient particles, potentially offering insights that other experiments cannot obtain.
Fuller believes the anticipated observations could improve scientists' understanding of the Big Bang, the early evolution of the universe, and other fundamental questions about how the cosmos developed.
"Halzen's work, and the work of those he inspired with his vision, was foundational in giving humanity a new window on the universe and on the mysterious and notoriously slippery neutrino," he stated.

content:
Experts say high blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation
Cutting back on salt may not be enough to get the greatest benefits for blood pressure.
Date:
November 2, 2026
Source:
University of Vermont
Summary:
Scientists are calling for a major rethink of how we manage high blood pressure, suggesting that eating more potassium could be just as important as cutting back on salt. A new report finds that combining increased potassium intake with reduced sodium consumption may offer greater benefits for blood pressure control than sodium reduction alone.
Share:
For decades, one of the most common recommendations for lowering high blood pressure has been simple: eat less salt. But a new scientific report suggests that this advice may be missing an equally important part of the equation.
Researchers say that increasing potassium intake, rather than focusing only on reducing sodium, could lead to better blood pressure control. By addressing both nutrients together, this approach could strengthen efforts to prevent hypertension and reduce the risk of serious cardiovascular problems.
The potential impact is enormous. High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, affects more than 1.28 billion adults worldwide and is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, including heart attacks and strokes. Although public health recommendations have traditionally emphasized cutting sodium, researchers now argue that getting enough potassium deserves just as much attention.
Why Potassium Matters for Blood Pressure
Sodium and potassium are essential minerals that help regulate fluid balance, nerve signaling, and muscle function. Both also influence blood pressure, but they affect the body in different ways.
Eating too much sodium can cause the body to retain additional fluid, increasing the pressure inside blood vessels. Potassium helps counter some of sodium's effects by supporting the kidneys in removing excess sodium through urine. It also contributes to the normal functioning of blood vessel walls, which plays an important role in maintaining healthy blood pressure.
In a new report, physicians and health experts argue that dietary recommendations should address these two minerals together. Rather than treating sodium reduction as the primary solution, they propose combining it with greater potassium consumption to achieve stronger results.
"It is time to view dietary interventions holistically because food components interact and physiology is integrative across systems," said Naomi Fukagawa, M.D. Ph.D., professor of medicine emerita at the Robert Larner, M.D. College of Medicine at the University of Vermont and first author on the report. "Growing evidence shows that increasing dietary potassium as well as reducing sodium intake work together to better manage hypertension."
A Major Rethink of Blood Pressure Guidelines
The report, published in the peer-reviewed American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, was supported by the IAFNS Sodium in Food and Health Implications Committee.
The researchers examined the scientific evidence underlying current sodium and potassium recommendations, along with practical ways to reduce sodium consumption and increase potassium intake. They also explored the obstacles to implementing these changes and identified areas where additional research and updated public health policies could help improve outcomes.
One of the central concerns is that many people consume too much sodium while getting nowhere near enough potassium. Both dietary patterns can contribute to elevated blood pressure, making them important targets for prevention and treatment.
Despite widespread efforts to encourage people to limit salt, average sodium consumption continues to exceed recommended levels. Meanwhile, potassium intake remains "far below optimal levels in both developed and developing nations," according to the authors.
This imbalance suggests that focusing primarily on what people should eat less of may be overlooking an important opportunity to improve cardiovascular health by encouraging them to consume more of a beneficial nutrient.
How to Get More Potassium in Your Diet
Potassium is naturally present in many familiar foods, including fruits, vegetables, legumes, and dairy products. Bananas, potatoes, beans, leafy greens, and yogurt are examples of foods that can help increase potassium intake.
Another possibility is replacing some sodium chloride, the main ingredient in ordinary table salt, with potassium salts. These substitutes can help reduce sodium while simultaneously increasing potassium, potentially addressing both dietary goals at once.
However, creating these products presents challenges for food manufacturers. Adding too much potassium salt can produce an unpleasant metallic taste, limiting how much can be used without affecting flavor. Manufacturers must therefore find a balance that improves nutritional content while keeping foods appealing to consumers.
Increasing potassium is also not appropriate for everyone. People with kidney disease or those taking certain medications may have difficulty regulating potassium levels, so potassium supplements and potassium-based salt substitutes should be used with medical guidance when these concerns apply.
A New Strategy for Fighting High Blood Pressure
The researchers emphasize that reducing sodium remains essential. Their proposal is not to abandon existing advice, but to expand it by recognizing that potassium intake is another major factor in blood pressure regulation.
The authors conclude that "dietary sodium reduction is a foundational strategy for hypertension prevention and management. However, new evidence supports a broadening of the current approach that focuses solely on sodium reduction and provides equal emphasis on increasing potassium intake."
For the more than one billion people living with hypertension, this shift in thinking could have significant implications. Instead of concentrating almost exclusively on reducing salt, future dietary recommendations may increasingly emphasize the combined benefits of consuming less sodium and more potassium.
The underlying message is straightforward: better blood pressure control may depend not only on what people remove from their diets, but also on what they add.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Vermont. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
Naomi K Fukagawa, Paul A Welling, Janice Johnson, Kristin Reimers, Soo-Yeun Lee, Patricia Zecca. Rethinking the impact of dietary sodium and potassium on blood pressure to advance public health. The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 2026; 124 (2): 101396 DOI: 10.1016/j.ajcnut.2026.101396

content:
New diabetes implant uses electricity to lower blood sugar and promote weight loss
Date:
November 2, 2026
Source:
ETH Zurich
Summary:
Researchers have developed a remarkable new electronic implant that could transform type 2 diabetes treatment by lowering blood sugar without insulin or traditional drugs. The device uses a special electrically powered catalyst to convert excess glucose into a substance that the body eliminates through urine, potentially preventing unwanted energy from being stored as fat. In diabetic mice, the implant precisely controlled blood sugar and promoted weight loss.
Share:
An experimental electronic implant could offer an entirely new way to treat type 2 diabetes. Rather than relying on insulin or conventional medications, the device uses electricity to convert excess blood sugar into a substance that the body can eliminate. In early tests with diabetic mice, the technology successfully regulated blood sugar and also led to weight loss.
The development comes as type 2 diabetes continues to affect a growing number of people worldwide. Unlike type 1 diabetes, type 2 is frequently associated with obesity, limited physical activity, and consuming more energy than the body needs over long periods.
Insulin injections can help reduce blood sugar by allowing muscle cells to absorb glucose from the bloodstream. However, insulin does not eliminate the underlying problem of excess energy. When the body does not use the glucose it absorbs, the surplus can eventually be converted into fat. This helps explain why some people with diabetes continue gaining weight even while receiving treatment.
Researchers led by Martin Fussenegger, a professor in the Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering at ETH Zurich in Basel, have developed an implant designed to address this problem differently. Their findings were published in the journal Science.
A New Diabetes Treatment Powered by Electricity
Fussenegger and his colleagues have spent years developing technologies capable of controlling blood sugar. Their previous designs used engineered genetic networks, but these systems depended on living cells and other biological materials.
That dependence introduced several complications. Biological components can create challenges involving immune compatibility, long-term stability, production, and regulatory approval.
The researchers have now taken a different approach by creating a catalyst made entirely from inorganic materials. It performs its function without requiring living cells, enzymes, or other biological components.
At the heart of the implant is a piece of graphite felt covered with tiny clusters of gold. These gold structures are coated with even smaller platinum particles, creating a specially engineered surface that enables the chemical reaction needed to process glucose.
The researchers designed this nanoscale surface themselves. According to Fussenegger, the materials also demonstrated excellent biocompatibility during experimental testing, suggesting they can interact with living tissue without causing significant adverse reactions.
The system includes an electronic controller enclosed in a 3D-printed housing. Instead of relying on a conventional wired power connection, the implant receives energy wirelessly at a frequency of 13.56 MHz. This frequency is internationally allocated for industrial, scientific, and medical applications.
How the Implant Removes Excess Blood Sugar
The technology works by transforming excess glucose into gluconate, a substance that can be eliminated from the body through urine.
Normally, glucose provides energy for cells. When more glucose is available than the body needs, some of that excess energy can ultimately be stored as fat. By converting part of the glucose into gluconate, the implant prevents that portion from being metabolized and stored in tissues, potentially helping reduce fat accumulation.
The entire process is designed to happen automatically, responding to changes in blood sugar as they occur.
A conventional glucose sensor, similar to those worn on the upper arm by many people with diabetes, continuously measures glucose concentrations in tissue. When levels rise too high, such as after a meal, the sensor communicates through Bluetooth with a smartphone or smartwatch.
The connected device then activates the implant, supplying the electrical energy needed for the catalyst to convert glucose into gluconate.
Once glucose levels return to the desired range, the implant automatically shuts down. This feedback system, known as closed-loop control, is intended to prevent blood sugar from dropping dangerously low.
Blood Sugar Control and Weight Loss in Diabetic Mice
To evaluate the technology, the researchers first conducted a laboratory experiment using a reservoir containing 5 liters of a nutrient solution with glucose. That volume is approximately equal to the amount of blood circulating in an adult human body.
The experiment demonstrated that the catalyst could convert glucose in a solution of this scale, an important step toward assessing its potential for medical applications.
The researchers then implanted the system in diabetic mice. The results showed that the device could precisely regulate the animals' blood sugar levels. The mice also lost weight, suggesting that converting excess glucose rather than allowing it to contribute to fat storage could offer an additional metabolic benefit.
Over six weeks of testing, the implant continued functioning reliably and was well tolerated by the animals.
"The system operates at a very low voltage, and our experiments showed no evidence of tissue damage from either electrical or thermal effects," says Fussenegger.
Although these findings are promising, the device has not yet been tested in humans. Additional research will be necessary to determine whether the technology can operate safely and effectively in people with diabetes.
Could Electronics Transform the Future of Diabetes Treatment?
Fussenegger believes the technology could represent a fundamental change in how diabetes is managed. Rather than using medications to influence how the body processes glucose, an electronic device could directly control the amount of glucose available.
"For decades, we have treated diabetes by telling the body how to manage glucose. We are now showing that we can take control of glucose directly, using electronics rather than drugs," he says. "And the catalyst only activates when glucose levels are too high."
The approach also creates opportunities to connect medical treatments with digital technologies, including the Internet of Things. This refers to networks of devices that exchange information and respond automatically to changing conditions.
The researchers envision electronically controlled treatments that could be manufactured at scale and integrated with existing digital health systems.
Their next objective is to turn the experimental implant into a medical device suitable for further development and eventual clinical testing.
One potential advantage is its relatively simple glucose conversion mechanism. Because the catalyst does not rely on cells or enzymes, the researchers believe some of the technical challenges associated with biological treatments could be easier to overcome.
Much of the supporting technology is also already available. Wireless power transmission systems and external electronic controllers are commercially established, meaning the team would not need to develop every component from scratch.
If future studies demonstrate similar benefits in humans, this approach could open the door to a new class of diabetes treatments in which smart electronic devices help regulate blood sugar directly, potentially reducing reliance on conventional medications.
Journal Reference:
Debasis Maity, Preetam Guha Ray, Peter Buchmann, Ghislaine Charpin-El Hamri, Martin Fussenegger. Wireless electrocatalytic closed-loop system for drug-free management of diabesity. Science, 2026; 394 (6822) DOI: 10.1126/science.ady8560

The device uses a special electrically powered catalyst to convert excess glucose into a substance that the body eliminates through urine, potentially preventing unwanted energy from being stored as fat. In diabetic mice, the implant precisely controlled blood sugar and promoted weight loss.

content:
Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice
Date:
November 2, 2026
Source:
McGill University
Summary:
In a surprising discovery, scientists found that certain diets associated with obesity can make cancer immunotherapy more effective in mice, challenging traditional assumptions about diet and cancer treatment. The findings suggest that the secret may lie in how food interacts with gut bacteria to strengthen the immune system's response to cancer.
Share:
Scientists have uncovered an unexpected connection between diet and cancer treatment. In a surprising finding, certain diets typically considered "unhealthy" or "fattening" actually improved responses to a common form of cancer immunotherapy in mice.
The discovery suggests that the success of cancer treatment may depend not only on which bacteria live in the gut, but also on the foods that help those bacteria thrive.
"There is a synergistic relationship between the bacteria that reside in our GI tract, and the food we eat," said Daniela Quail, Associate Professor in the Department of Physiology and Principal Investigator at the Rosalind & Morris Goodman Cancer Institute.
"Even with the right composition of bacteria in your gut, the foods you eat to nourish those populations can determine whether or not you respond to treatment," said Quail.
Quail co-led the research, which examined how diet influences the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors. These widely used immunotherapy drugs help the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. Other senior researchers involved in the study included McGill scientist Logan Walsh and CR-CHUM collaborators Bertrand Routy and Arielle Elkrief. The findings were published in Nature.
Why Unhealthy Diets Produced Surprising Results
One of the most unexpected discoveries was that some diets associated with weight gain appeared to make immunotherapy more effective, challenging assumptions about the relationship between nutrition and cancer treatment.
"Our findings were surprising because they highlighted a benefit of some obesogenic diets," she said. "That tells us the relationship between diet and cancer treatment is more complex than a simple message to eat healthy and exercise."
However, the researchers emphasize that these results should not encourage cancer patients to consume diets that promote obesity. Excess weight carries established health risks, and the findings do not demonstrate that adopting such diets would improve cancer treatment in humans.
Instead, the scientists want to understand how different foods influence the gut microbiome, the enormous community of trillions of bacteria that inhabit the digestive system. Identifying the mechanisms responsible for the improved treatment responses could eventually help researchers develop safer ways to make cancer immunotherapy more effective.
A New Explanation for Cancer's Obesity Paradox
The investigation grew out of a longstanding puzzle in cancer research known as the "obesity paradox."
Obesity is generally linked to a greater risk of developing cancer and dying from the disease. Yet several studies have found that cancer patients with a higher body mass index (BMI) sometimes respond more favorably to immune checkpoint inhibitors.
To investigate this apparent contradiction, the research team tested 12 different diets in mice. Surprisingly, some diets associated with obesity improved the animals' responses to immunotherapy, even when they were consumed for relatively short periods.
These results suggest that the apparent treatment advantage associated with obesity may not be primarily caused by excess body weight. Instead, the explanation could involve the combined influence of diet and gut bacteria on the immune system.
By uncovering how these interactions affect cancer treatment, researchers hope to identify new approaches that reproduce the beneficial effects without exposing patients to the health risks associated with obesity.
About the Study
The study, "Diet-microbiome synergy underlies obesity-associated immunotherapy efficacy," was published in Nature by McGill PhD graduate Lysanne Desharnais, Daniela Quail, and their collaborators.
Funding was provided by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Canadian Cancer Society, the Terry Fox Research Institute, the Canada Foundation for Innovation, and philanthropic supporters including La Vie en Rose and the Bachynski Family Foundation.
Story Source:
Materials provided by McGill University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
Lysanne Desharnais, Anikka Swaby, Meriem Messaoudene, Samuel Doré, Miranda W.
