content:
Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months
Date:
October 30, 2026
Source:
European Association for the Study of Diabetes
Summary:
A promising new study suggests that more than half of younger adults with type 2 diabetes could achieve remission in just six months through a combination of a low-calorie diet and structured exercise. Researchers found that 54% of participants under age 45 who followed an intensive diet and exercise program achieved remission, compared with just 4% receiving usual care.
Share:
A carefully structured combination of diet and exercise may offer a powerful way to put type 2 diabetes into remission in younger adults. In a new clinical trial, more than half of participants who followed an intensive lifestyle program achieved remission within just six months, compared with only 4% of those receiving standard care.
The findings, presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas, suggest that a low-calorie diet paired with regular exercise could significantly change the course of early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) (aged under 45 years).
The research was conducted by Professor Kaberi Dasgupta, Director of the Division of General Internal Medicine at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, Professor Thomas Yates of the University of Leicester in the UK, and their colleagues.
Why Early-Onset Type 2 Diabetes Is Especially Dangerous
Type 2 diabetes diagnosed at a younger age can be particularly aggressive. People with early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) often experience a faster decline in blood sugar control, develop complications earlier in life, and face a shorter life expectancy than those diagnosed at older ages.
Previous research has shown that very low-calorie diets (LEDs) can lower blood sugar enough for some people to achieve remission without diabetes medication (T2D remission). Remission means blood sugar has fallen below the threshold used to diagnose diabetes and remains there without glucose-lowering drugs. However, it does not necessarily mean the disease has been permanently cured.
Researchers wanted to find out whether adding structured exercise could make this approach even more effective. Beyond helping regulate blood sugar, physical activity could improve fitness, protect muscle during weight loss, strengthen heart function, and reduce insulin resistance.
To investigate, the team tested whether combining a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise could achieve remission after 24 weeks, compared with standard medical care.
An Intensive Diet and Exercise Program
The randomized clinical trial took place at three research centers in England and Canada (affiliated with the University of Leicester, UK, McGill University (Montreal), and the University of Alberta, Edmonton). It enrolled adults aged 18 to 45 who had early-onset type 2 diabetes and obesity but were not using insulin.
The trial was open-label, meaning participants and researchers knew which treatment each person received, although the assessment of the main outcome was blinded.
One group continued receiving usual care. The other followed an intensive program that combined a daily intake of 800 to 900 calories with supervised aerobic and resistance exercise twice per week, plus one independent exercise session each week (weeks 1-12). Participants then transitioned to a diet designed to maintain their weight loss while continuing to exercise independently (weeks 13-24).
The researchers measured how many participants achieved diabetes remission after 24 weeks. To qualify, participants needed an HbA1c level below 6.5%, equivalent to 48 mmol/mol, and must have taken no glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks. HbA1c is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.
The analysis included everyone assigned to either group. When remission data were missing, researchers conservatively counted those participants as not having achieved remission. They also examined changes in cardiovascular fitness, body composition, and heart structure.
What Participants Ate During the Study
At the beginning of the intensive program, participants discontinued medications used to lower blood sugar and blood pressure (in the absence of albuminuria), under the study's medical supervision. Albuminuria refers to the presence of a protein called albumin in urine and can indicate kidney damage.
Their restricted diet provided 800 to 900 calories daily (30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, 20% fat). Participants were encouraged to drink at least two liters of calorie-free fluids each day and were given access to a fiber-based laxative when needed.
During the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). From weeks three through 12, participants maintained the same calorie limit but gained more flexibility in their food choices (Optifast in UK and ProtiDiet in Canada).
This second phase allowed one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables (60 to 90 g protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, two portions of non-starchy vegetables).
After the first 12 weeks, participants shifted toward maintaining their weight loss rather than continuing rapid weight reduction.
More Than Half Achieved Type 2 Diabetes Remission
Between September 24, 2021, and June 6, 2025, the researchers enrolled and randomly assigned 96 participants (40 UK, 56 Canada). The group included 50 people assigned to the intensive intervention and 46 receiving standard care (24 female, 26 male intervention group; 21 female, 25 male control group; mean age 38 years, BMI 35·2 kg/m2).
Of those enrolled, 86 (90%) completed the final assessments.
The results revealed a striking difference between the groups. After 24 weeks, 27 of the 50 participants following the diet and exercise program had achieved remission, representing 54% of the intervention group. In comparison, just two of the 46 participants receiving standard care reached remission, or approximately 4%.
After accounting for relevant statistical factors, the researchers calculated that participants in the intensive lifestyle program were 21 times more likely to achieve remission than those receiving usual care.
Weight loss was also substantially greater among participants following the combined program.
Among the 47 intervention participants with available weight data, average body weight fell from 100.7 kg to 92.3 kg, a reduction of 8.4 kg over 24 weeks. The 43 control participants with available weight data started at an average of 103.2 kg and lost just 1.2 kg, reaching 102.0 kg.
After statistical adjustment, the intervention group lost an average of 7.5 kg more weight than the control group. Importantly, this included an additional 6.6 kg of fat loss, indicating that much of the difference came from reduced body fat.
Promising Results With Manageable Side Effects
No severe adverse events were reported during the trial. However, side effects were more common among participants following the intensive diet.
At least one adverse event occurred in 43 of the 50 intervention participants, compared with six of the 46 participants receiving standard care. Most problems appeared during the early stages of the restrictive diet and included symptoms such as constipation, headaches, dizziness, and fatigue (e.g., constipation, headache, dizziness, fatigue). These effects generally resolved.
The researchers believe the findings demonstrate that a combined diet and exercise intervention can produce meaningful improvements beyond blood sugar control alone.
The authors say: "Our findings demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low energy diet in early-onset type 2 diabetes, supporting its potential to deliver substantial and holistic health and well-being benefits alongside diabetes remission.
"Our remission rates are at the upper end of those previously reported in the literature for trials of similar duration, reinforcing the potential of structured lifestyle interventions to support clinically meaningful remission, while demonstrating for the first time that such effects can be achieved in a multi-ethnic population with early-onset type 2 diabetes through a combined low-energy diet and structured exercise intervention."
Why Preserving Muscle During Weight Loss Matters
One particularly important aspect of the study was its emphasis on protecting muscle mass during rapid weight loss.
The researchers explain that most people who complete weight loss programs eventually regain some or all of the weight they lost. This is especially relevant when using very low-calorie diets to achieve diabetes remission.
Losing weight through calorie restriction alone typically reduces both fat and fat-free mass, which includes muscle. Some evidence suggests that when weight returns, the body may regain proportionally more fat than lean tissue.
Over time, repeated weight loss and regain could therefore contribute to a gradual reduction in muscle mass and increase the risk of sarcopenia, a condition characterized by declining muscle mass and strength.
To address this problem, the researchers incorporated resistance training into the most intensive phase of weight loss. Their results suggest that it is possible to achieve substantial fat loss while preserving muscle, potentially making the approach more beneficial for long-term metabolic health.
They say: "Our RESET for Remission study targeted muscle during the intensive weight loss phase through resistance training, and our findings indicate fat-free mass and muscle preservation is achievable with rapid weight loss. Preserving muscle during remission-oriented weight loss may have important implications for long-term metabolic health, physical function, and disease trajectory. This requires examination in a longer-term study."
A Potential New Approach to Treating Type 2 Diabetes
The findings could be particularly important as type 2 diabetes becomes increasingly common among younger adults worldwide.
People who develop the condition earlier in life face more years of exposure to elevated blood sugar, increasing their lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease and other complications. Finding effective ways to achieve remission early could therefore have substantial health benefits.
The researchers emphasize that their intervention did more than lower blood sugar. It also reduced body fat while protecting muscle, improved muscle quality and physical performance, supported cardiovascular health, and produced improvements in participants' reported well-being.
They also suggest that this strategy could be especially relevant for people planning a pregnancy or who may become pregnant.
However, the researchers caution that longer studies are needed to determine whether the benefits can be sustained. In particular, future research must establish how well participants maintain their weight loss, muscle mass, and diabetes remission after returning to everyday life outside a closely monitored clinical trial.
The authors conclude: "By focusing specifically on early-onset type 2 diabetes, our trial addresses a growing clinical population, characterized by elevated cardiovascular disease risk, greater cumulative complication burden, and poor long-term outcomes…In summary, RESET for Remission demonstrated that in early-onset type 2 diabetes, combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low-calorie diet produces high remission rates, induces fat loss while preserving muscle mass, improves muscle quality and function, enhances cardiovascular health, and leads to meaningful improvements in patient-reported outcomes. As the prevalence of early-onset type 2 diabetes rises globally, our findings highlight an opportunity to re-evaluate treatment paradigms and support scalable implementation of integrated dietary and exercise interventions for remission. Our approach may be particularly valuable in those seeking or with potential for pregnancy. It warrants further evaluation in longer term studies in real-world settings."

Yemen war makes reaching assistance too dangerous for many
More than 280,000 people have now been displaced by fighting in Yemen and many vulnerable people are unable to access lifesaving relief because it is too dangerous to do so, the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) said on Friday.
In an alert, the agency said that tens of thousands of refugees and asylum seekers were struggling to survive.
It described a rapidly worsening humanitarian crisis for more than 65,000 refugees and asylum seekers in Yemen, as “escalating insecurity, economic collapse, depleting resources and severe humanitarian access constraints leave tens of thousands with nowhere to turn”.
Despite intensifying conflict between Houthi opposition fighters and Government forces which escalated last month and ended a four-year ceasefire, thousands of people continue to risk dangerous sea crossings from the Horn of Africa to Yemen, said UNHCR spokesperson Matthew Saltmarsh.
Access heavily restricted
Aid teams are particularly worried about the situation in Kharaz refugee camp in the southwestern governorate of Lahj, close to the front line.
The camp shelters around 9,500 refugees from Somalia and Ethiopia in a Government-controlled area. Although no refugee casualties have been verified so far, “nearby shelling has disrupted services and led to movement restrictions for those in the camps…who have already previously fled conflict”, Mr. Saltmarsh noted.
UNHCR partners have distributed food inside the camp in coordination with local authorities, and health assistance and water provision continue, with significant difficulty. But most other services are on hold, with schools suspended, legal and documentation services interrupted and the rising prices of fuel and staple foods making it increasingly difficult for refugees to cover their basic needs.
“When access allows, we do move in that assistance, but it has been challenging,” Mr. Saltmarsh said. “We’ve been hearing a lot that a number of displaced people have been unable to get to places where we have our supplies and our assistance… in many cases, it’s been too dangerous for us to get to them.”
According to UNHCR, more than 280,000 people in Yemen have been displaced by the fighting. The significant increase in humanitarian needs has coincided with severe supply chain shocks in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab El-Mandeb Strait, linked to the US-Iran war, while resources available to help them are falling short. Today, the agency’s appeal for Yemen only 19 per cent funded.
Relief supplies on the way
In a positive development, the agency announced that it has secured pro bono transport support for 11 containers of emergency relief items from Dubai to Yemen, “although shifting security conditions and logistical constraints are challenging those delivery efforts”, Mr. Saltmarsh noted.
“Those 11 containers should arrive tomorrow, bringing 3,000 relief kits to over 20,000 people in Yemen,” he added, before warning that the agency’s operations in Sudan, Djibouti and Ethiopia are among the most exposed to disrupted trade and shipping in the Red Sea.

content:
The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
Date:
October 30, 2026
Source:
University College London
Summary:
Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact.
Share:
Why did crocodiles survive the asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago? New research suggests that their preference for warm environments may have given them a crucial advantage during one of Earth's greatest mass extinctions.
Scientists led by UCL (University College London) found that crocodiles and their ancient relatives spent much of their 250 million years of evolutionary history following warm climates rather than adapting to dramatically different temperatures. When Earth grew hotter, they expanded into new regions, sometimes reaching as far as Antarctica. As temperatures fell, they moved back toward the tropics.
Published in Science Advances, the study analyzed more than 7,000 fossils and records from over 400 living and extinct species. Researchers combined this evidence with computer models that reconstructed Earth's climate and geography across 245 million years.
The results suggest that tropical and subtropical regions remained suitable for crocodile relatives after the asteroid struck, even as the environments available to many dinosaurs deteriorated. Only the most extreme climate simulations eliminated these potential refuges.
Why Crocodiles Survived the Dinosaur Extinction
The researchers examined how conditions on Earth may have changed following the asteroid impact 66 million years ago. Their simulations indicated that areas near the equator could have remained warm enough to support crocodile relatives, providing places where surviving populations could persist and eventually recover.
Previous modeling by members of the same research team found that suitable habitats for non-avian dinosaurs (i.e., the ones that went extinct) contracted much more severely after the impact.
Lead author Dr. Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza, based at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "The asteroid did not make the whole planet equally hostile to every group.
"Crocodiles' long-standing preference for warm environments may have placed survivors exactly where suitable climates held up best, like around the equator. These refuges could have sheltered populations that later recovered and radiated out."
The discovery offers a possible explanation for how a group of animals that appeared around the same time as dinosaurs managed to endure two of Earth's five major mass extinctions.
Ancient Crocodiles Were Far More Diverse
Modern crocodiles and their close relatives share many recognizable features, but their evolutionary history reveals a much wider variety of body shapes, sizes, and lifestyles.
The broader crocodile lineage, known as pseudosuchians, once included heavily armored plant eaters, predators that hunted entirely on land, and enormous animals weighing more than a metric ton.
Among the most remarkable was Sarcosuchus, a giant predator nicknamed the "super croc" that could reach 12 meters in length. Another prehistoric relative, Postosuchus, was a land dwelling hunter capable of moving on either two legs or all four.
Dr. Chiarenza said: "Crocodiles are often called living fossils, but their ancestors and relatives changed enormously throughout their history, ranging from giants the size of a bus that could have devoured a T. rex, to small, cute animals with the face of a pug.
"Our study shows that, despite all this diversity, what stayed surprisingly consistent was their relationship with climate."
Fossils Reveal 245 Million Years of Climate History
To investigate that relationship, the scientists reconstructed the temperature and rainfall preferences of 400 crocodile species and their ancient relatives. They used fossil evidence, evolutionary family trees, and detailed maps of where living crocodile species are found today.
The team then compared these preferences with reconstructions of ancient geography and climate to identify where suitable habitats existed at different points in Earth's history.
A clear pattern emerged. Crocodile relatives generally followed warmer conditions as the planet's climate changed, expanding their ranges during hot periods and retreating when temperatures cooled.
About 50 million years ago, during the particularly warm early Eocene, global temperatures were approximately 10°C higher than today, and the polar regions had no permanent ice. Crocodile relatives lived at high latitudes across North America, Europe, and even Antarctica.
Over the following millions of years, global cooling gradually reduced the areas where they could thrive. Their geographic range contracted toward warmer tropical regions.
Two Surprising Exceptions
Although this preference for warm environments remained remarkably consistent, the researchers identified two important exceptions.
During the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum, approximately 94 million years ago, global temperatures climbed as much as 14°C above modern levels. One branch of the crocodile family tree evolved the ability to tolerate hotter conditions than the broader lineage could withstand at other times.
A separate adaptation occurred around 34 million years ago in Australia. As a prolonged cooling period reduced rainfall and dried out the continent, an extinct group of crocodiles adapted to increasingly arid, desert-like environments.
These exceptions show that some crocodile relatives could evolve to handle different climates, even though most continued to follow their preferred warm conditions.
What Happened After the Dinosaur-Killing Asteroid?
The researchers also used climate simulations to investigate the decades and centuries immediately following the Chicxulub asteroid impact, which triggered the extinction of most dinosaurs.
They explored several possible environmental consequences, including sunlight being blocked by dust and ash and rising carbon dioxide levels associated with volcanic eruptions.
When the simulations reduced sunlight by 5% or 10%, warm regions near the equator remained suitable for crocodile relatives. These areas could have provided critical refuges during the environmental disruption.
However, a more severe scenario involving a 15% reduction in sunlight left those regions unsuitable as well. The researchers noted that this extreme level of reduced sunlight is now considered unlikely.
Other simulated changes, including increased atmospheric carbon dioxide, did not alter the availability of suitable climates for crocodiles.
Together, the results suggest that crocodiles may have benefited from living in regions where temperatures remained within their preferred range, even as conditions became much less favorable for many dinosaurs.
The Survival Strategy That Could Now Become a Weakness
The researchers emphasized that favorable temperatures were probably only one reason crocodiles survived the mass extinction.
Other characteristics likely improved their chances, including relatively small body sizes, the ability to live partly in water, flexible diets, and modest energy requirements. As ectothermic ("cold-blooded") animals, crocodiles need less food to maintain their bodies than many animals that generate their own body heat.
The findings also raise important questions about how crocodiles will respond to modern climate change.
For millions of years, moving into regions with suitable temperatures appears to have been one of their main responses to a changing planet. Today, however, expanding cities, agricultural land, and roads increasingly limit where wildlife can move.
Professor Philip Mannion, based at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "These findings have implications for species today. If crocodiles mostly coped with past climate change by moving towards suitable habitats, today's species will need room to move as the planet warms, and the loss of suitable areas to roads, farms and cities is making that harder."
The research was funded by The Royal Society, the Leverhulme Trust, and the National Environment Research Council (NERC).

content:
Why some “lower-risk” childhood cancers turn deadly
Date:
October 30, 2026
Source:
Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute
Summary:
Scientists have uncovered hidden aggressive cancer cells in children whose tumors were previously considered lower risk, revealing why some cases of rhabdomyosarcoma become unexpectedly deadly. The discovery could help doctors identify dangerous tumors earlier and develop personalized treatments that improve survival while reducing unnecessary chemotherapy.
Share:
Some childhood cancers may be far more dangerous than their initial risk classification suggests. Scientists have discovered that certain tumors considered less threatening can contain hidden populations of highly aggressive cancer cells, potentially explaining why some children experience devastating outcomes despite lacking the usual genetic warning signs.
The discovery could change how doctors identify children at risk of life-threatening cancer, allowing treatment to be better matched to the true aggressiveness of their disease.
The findings, published in Cancer Research, come from scientists at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the University of Cambridge, Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), University College London, and collaborating institutions. Their research focused on rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), an aggressive cancer that develops from muscle tissue and is among the most common soft tissue cancers affecting children younger than 15. Approximately 55 children are diagnosed with the disease in the United Kingdom each year.[1]
Unlike many adult cancers, which can develop after years of aging or exposure to environmental factors, childhood cancers often result from genetic changes that occur during early development.
Why Some Childhood Cancers Defy Risk Predictions
Doctors generally divide rhabdomyosarcoma into two main categories based on whether a tumor carries a particular genetic warning sign. This marker occurs when two genes that are normally separate become fused together, creating an abnormal genetic combination associated with especially aggressive disease.[2]
Children whose tumors contain this fusion have substantially lower survival rates than those without it, even when they receive intensive treatment.
But this classification has a troubling limitation. Some children whose tumors lack the high-risk genetic marker still develop aggressive cancers that can prove fatal. Until now, scientists have struggled to explain why these supposedly less dangerous tumors sometimes behave so aggressively.
To investigate this mystery, the research team compared tumors from children with different forms of rhabdomyosarcoma, looking beyond the genetic markers traditionally used to estimate risk.
The researchers examined tumor samples from 16 children, including four whose cancers lacked the fusion marker but proved fatal, four with fusion-positive tumors, and eight children with fusion-negative disease who remained alive.
Hidden Aggressive Cancer Cells Revealed
Using advanced genetic analysis, scientists studied the tumors at a level of detail that conventional techniques cannot easily achieve.
One of their main tools was single-cell RNA sequencing, a technology that measures gene activity in individual cells. Rather than examining a tumor as a single mass, this approach allows researchers to investigate the behavior of its different cell populations and identify potentially dangerous cells that might otherwise go unnoticed.
The scientists also used spatial transcriptomics, a technique that maps gene activity to specific locations within a tumor. This provided a clearer picture of where aggressive cancer cells were concentrated and how they were distributed throughout the tissue.
The results revealed a striking similarity between tumors that had previously been placed in different risk categories. Some cancers classified as non-high-risk contained cells with gene activity patterns closely resembling those found in high-risk tumors.
Even more surprisingly, these aggressive tumors did not need the same genetic mutations to produce similar behavior. Researchers identified rare genetic changes that affected many of the same cellular pathways involved in the most dangerous forms of the disease.
This suggests that different genetic abnormalities can ultimately push cancer cells toward a shared aggressive state. In other words, tumors can reach a similarly dangerous biological condition through multiple genetic routes, even when they lack the warning sign typically used to identify high-risk disease.
Dr. Karin Straathof, co-senior author at UCL Cancer Institute and GOSH, said:
"By studying tumors one cell at a time, we uncovered hidden populations of aggressive cancer cells that conventional methods miss. Although these tumors carry different genetic changes, many converge on the same aggressive pathways. This helps explain why some children who appear to have lower-risk disease can still have a devastating outcome."
A New Path Toward More Precise Cancer Treatment
The findings could have important implications for how childhood cancer is diagnosed and treated.
If doctors can identify the distinctive biological signatures of aggressive cancer cells at diagnosis, they may be able to recognize children who face a greater risk of relapse or death, even when standard genetic tests suggest otherwise.
Such an approach could also help prevent unnecessary treatment. Children with genuinely lower-risk tumors might avoid some of the harmful side effects associated with intensive chemotherapy, while those with hidden aggressive disease could receive stronger or more targeted treatment earlier.
The researchers are particularly interested in identifying markers that could be used to develop therapies aimed specifically at the most dangerous cancer cells.
One possible direction involves immunotherapy, including CAR-T cell therapy. This treatment uses specially modified immune cells to recognize and attack cancer cells. Although such treatments would require further development and testing for rhabdomyosarcoma, they could eventually offer a more precise alternative to conventional chemotherapy, potentially reducing damage to healthy tissues.
Scientists are now expanding their research to include hundreds of additional tumor samples. By studying a much larger group of patients, they hope to uncover more of the rare genetic changes capable of producing aggressive cancer and accelerate the development of personalized treatments.
Sara Wakeling, Chief Executive Officer and co-founder of Alice's Arc, said:
"Every child with cancer deserves the best possible chance of survival. We're proud to support research into rhabdomyosarcoma, showing how cutting-edge technologies can uncover the biology driving aggressive childhood cancers. These discoveries bring us closer to more personalized treatments and better outcomes for children."
Dr. Laura Danielson, Children's and Young Person's Lead at Cancer Research UK, said:
"Discovery research like this is essential to understand the unique biology of these cancers. This important study demonstrates that aggressive tumors may share similar features, even if they carry different genetic changes. By helping researchers understand what these high-risk cancers have in common, this work adds a vital piece to the puzzle and could help guide future efforts to improve treatment for children and young people with rhabdomyosarcoma."
Rethinking How Doctors Identify Dangerous Childhood Cancers
Beyond its potential treatment applications, the discovery challenges a fundamental assumption about how rhabdomyosarcoma should be classified.
Instead of viewing aggressive disease primarily through the presence or absence of one genetic abnormality, the researchers suggest that doctors may need to consider the broader biological state of the cancer cells themselves.
This distinction is important because tumors with different mutations can behave in remarkably similar ways. Identifying the shared features of aggressive disease could provide a more reliable way to recognize children who need intensive treatment, regardless of the particular genetic changes driving their tumors.
Professor Sam Behjati, co-senior author formerly at the Wellcome Sanger Institute and Head of the Department of Paediatrics at the University of Cambridge, said:
"This work changes how we think about rhabdomyosarcoma. Rather than a single, abnormal gene, we've shown that there is an overarching cell state of aggressive disease that defies conventional classification systems. Understanding this shared biology could help identify children who need more intense treatment to improve their survival."
Although further research is needed before these findings can change routine clinical care, they provide a promising foundation for more accurate risk assessments and treatments tailored to each child's cancer.
By revealing aggressive behavior hidden beneath seemingly reassuring genetic classifications, scientists hope to improve survival for children with the most dangerous tumors while sparing others from treatment they may not need.

The research received support through a Cancer Research UK -- Children with Cancer UK Innovation Award, with additional co-funding from Alice's Arc and funding from Wellcome.

content:
"เขาบอกว่าน้ำจะไม่มี ชาวนาก็เลยรีบทำนากัน" ชาวนาอยุธยาอ่วมถูกน้ำท่วมช่วงที่พยากรณ์ว่าจะเกิดภัยแล้ง
ที่มาของภาพ, THAI NEWS PIX
ตั้งแต่เมื่อช่วงกลางปี ชาวนาใน ต.มารวิชัย อ.เสนา จ.พระนครศรีอยุธยา ได้รับคำเตือนว่าช่วงปลายปี 2569 จะเกิดภาวะแล้งจากปรากฏการณ์เอลนีโญ (El Niño) พวกเขาจึงตัดสินใจหว่านข้าวเร็วขึ้นหวังเก็บเกี่ยวก่อนแล้ง แต่ตอนนี้นาข้าวเหล่านี้ถูกน้ำท่วมมิดมาตั้งแต่ช่วงปลายเดือน ก.ย.
"[มีคำเตือนว่า]น้ำจะไม่มี ฝนก็จะแล้ง ก็เลยบอกกับลูกว่าเราทำนาสักรุ่นเถอะ เราจะได้เก็บเกี่ยวจะได้เอามาลงทุนรุ่นใหม่... พอข้าวกำลังสวย พอใส่ปุ๋ย ฉีดยา ทีนี้ฝนมันเริ่มตก ตกถี่ ๆ บางทีสามวันสามคืน แล้วตกไม่ใช่เม็ดเล็ก ๆ เม็ดใหญ่ ๆ" นางทองดี บุญศิริ เกษตรกรชาว อ.เสนา จ.พระนครศรีอยุธยา บอกกับบีบีบีซีไทย
ไร่นาราว 10 ไร่ ที่เกษตรกรวัย 80 ปีรายนี้เช่ามาหว่านข้าวหวังทำกำไร ปัจจุบันจมอยู่ใต้น้ำลึก 3 เมตร มานานกว่าหนึ่งเดือนแล้ว
ชาวนาในพื้นที่อีกรายบอกกับบีบีซีไทยเช่นกันว่า เขาตัดสินใจหว่านข้าวนอกฤดูเพราะกลัวภัยแล้งท้ายปีตามคำเตือนของทางการ แต่ตอนนี้นาข้าวของเขาก็ถูกน้ำท่วมมิดเช่นกัน
"พอเกี่ยวหนสองแล้ว เราก็ว่างไปอีกประมาณเดือนสองเดือนพอจะทำนาได้ เราก็เลยทำ แล้วเขาบอกว่าน้ำจะไม่มี ชาวนาก็เลยทำนาเพราะมันว่าง กว่าจะปีใหม่ก็ว่างอยู่ตั้ง 4-5 เดือน… เอลนีโญอะไรของเขา เตรียมให้ชาวบ้านรับภัยแล้ง" นายภูนนท์ ชางเนียม ชาวนาใน อ.เสนา จ.พระนครศรีอยุธยา บอกกับบีบีซีไทย
เขาเสริมด้วยว่าตนเป็น "คนรุ่นใหม่" นับเป็นรุ่นที่สี่ของตระกูลที่ทำอาชีพชาวนา แต่ก็ไม่ทราบแน่ชัดว่า "เอลนีโญ" คืออะไร
ด้าน ดร.ธนพล พิมาน หัวหน้าฝ่ายบริหารจัดการน้ำจากสถาบันสิ่งแวดล้อมสตอกโฮล์ม (Stockholm Environment Institute – SEI) บอกกับบีบีซีไทยว่า เหตุน้ำท่วมบริเวณภาคกลางผิดจากที่คาดไว้ว่าวิกฤตซูเปอร์เอลนีโญจะทำให้พื้นที่เกิดภัยแล้ง
"ซูเปอร์เอลนีโญตามวิชาการมันเริ่มตั้งแต่มิถุนายนหรือกรกฎาคมแล้ว แต่คราวนี้ความยากที่ผมมองคือความไม่แน่นอนมันสูง ปกติเราเข้าใจว่าซูเปอร์เอลนีโญมันจะทำให้เกิดภัยแล้ง… ทำให้หลายภาคส่วนเตรียมการเพื่อที่จะรองรับภัยแล้ง ไม่ว่าจะเป็นเรื่องของน้ำหรือเกษตร แต่กลายเป็นว่าสิ่งที่เกิดขึ้นมันกลายเป็นอีกข้างหนึ่งเลย คือฝนตกแช่ ฝนตกหนัก"
นักวิชาการรายนี้ระบุด้วยว่าแม้ไม่ได้เกิดภัยแล้งตามคาด แต่ก็มีความเป็นไปได้ว่านี่ก็คือผลกระทบของเอลนีโญที่ทำให้สภาพอากาศแปรปรวนหนักจนแทบคาดการณ์ไม่ได้
"เตือนเราสักหน่อย เราก็จะได้ไม่ทำ[นา]"
ที่มาของภาพ, THAI NEWS PIX
ย้อนไปเมื่อเดือน มี.ค. สำนักงานเกษตรและสหกรณ์ จ.พระนครศรีอยุธยา ได้ออกประกาศขอความร่วมมือเกษตรกรงดปลูกข้าวนาปรัง รอบสอง เนื่องจากคาดการณ์ว่าน้ำต้นทุนในเขื่อนมีจำกัด
"ประชาสัมพันธ์ถึงพี่น้องเกษตรกรขอความร่วมมือพิจารณาสถานการณ์น้ำ ก่อนตัดสินใจทำนาปรังรอบที่ 2 โดยเฉพาะในพื้นที่ลุ่มน้ำเจ้าพระยา เหตุผลสำคัญที่ขอความร่วมมือเพื่อป้องกันการขาดแคลนน้ำ ปริมาณน้ำในเขื่อนหลักมีจำกัดในช่วงฤดูแล้ง"
หนึ่งในบุคคลการเมืองที่ออกมาเตือนเรื่องภัยแล้ง คือนายปะดิธ สังขจาย สมาชิกสภาผู้แทนราษฎร (สส.) จ.พระนครศรีอยุธยา เขต 5 พรรคภูมิใจไทย ที่โพสต์ผ่านเฟซบุ๊ก เมื่อ 9 ส.ค. ว่าปีนี้อยุธยาจะไม่เกิดเหตุน้ำท่วมแน่นอน

"มันเดาไม่ได้ เดี๋ยวร้อน เดี๋ยวหนาว เดี๋ยวมีฝน เดี๋ยวแดดแจ๋...[ทำนา]ยาก เช่นว่าจะฉีดยาฆ่าแมลง พอฉีดไป ฝนตกก็ล้างยาออกอีกแล้ว มันก็ต้องฉีดใหม่อีก" นางทองดีบอก
"รู้สึกว่าปีนี้ลำบาก อากาศมันไม่อำนวย ฝนฟ้าตกไม่ตามฤดูกาล นึกจะตกก็ตก" เธอเสริม
ด้าน นายภูนนท์ ก็บอกเช่นกันว่าแต่ละปีสภาพอากาศไม่แน่นอน ไม่สามารถคาดเดาอะไรได้ เช่นในปีนี้ฝนมาเร็วกว่าฤดูกาล
"บางทีน้ำก็ท่วมมากท่วมน้อย เราก็คาดหวังอะไรไม่ได้... ธรรมดาน้ำจะท่วมปลายตุลาคม แต่ปีนี้น้ำมันมาก่อน มาตั้งแต่ปลายกันยายน" นายภูนนท์ บอก
กระทบผลผลิตข้าวไทยยังไม่มาก แต่ชาวนา "หนี้สินพะรุงพะรัง"
ที่มาของภาพ, THAI NEWS PIX
แม้เหตุอุทกภัยจะกระทบไร่นาของพื้นที่ จ.พระนครศรีอยุธยา จำนวนมาก แต่สมาคมผู้ส่งออกข้าวไทย ระบุว่าเหตุน้ำท่วมปีนี้จะไม่ส่งผลกระทบต่อผลผลิตข้าวไทยมากนัก
นายชูเกียรติ โอภาสวงศ์ นายกกิตติมศักดิ์ สมาคมผู้ส่งออกข้าวไทย เปิดเผยกับสำนักข่าวฐานเศรษฐกิจ เมื่อ 5 ต.ค. ว่าสถานการณ์น้ำท่วมในปีนี้ส่งผลกระทบต่อผลผลิตข้าวไทยในระดับน้อยมาก
ข้อมูลจากศูนย์ติดตามและแก้ไขปัญหาภัยพิบัติด้านการเกษตร กระทรวงเกษตรและสหกรณ์ ระบุว่า มีพื้นที่นาข้าวได้รับผลกระทบจากอุทกภัยประมาณ 1.3 ล้านไร่ แต่พื้นที่ที่เสียหายสิ้นเชิงมีเพียงประมาณ 4,000-5,000 ไร่ และเมื่อเทียบกับพื้นที่ปลูกข้าวทั่วประเทศที่มีประมาณ 60–70 ล้านไร่ ถือว่าพื้นที่เสียหายยังไม่มีนัยสำคัญต่อภาพรวมผลผลิตข้าวไทย
อย่างไรก็ตาม ผลกระทบต่อตัวเกษตรกรดูจะเป็นที่ประจักษ์กว่ามาก
"หนี้สินที่เราไปกู้มาลงทุน พอเราลงทุนไปแล้วไม่ได้เกี่ยว มันก็พอกเป็นคูณสอง เราก็ต้องหาเงินมาใช้ แล้วพอเราเริ่มทำนาใหม่ เราก็ต้องหาทุนใหม่ ก็ต้องไปกู้ยืมใหม่อีก หนี้สินพะรุงพะรัง" นายภูนนท์บอก
เช่นเดียวกันเมื่อสอบถามนางทองดีว่าหลังน้ำลดเธอจะทำอย่างไรต่อไป เธอก็ตอบด้วยน้ำเสียงเศร้าสลดว่าต้องทำการกู้เงินเพิ่มเพื่อมาปลูกข้าวรอบใหม่
"ก็ต้องหาเงินกู้เพิ่ม เราตอนนี้ก็หมดตัวแล้ว... รู้สึกท้อนะ ท้อแล้วจะทำยังไงได้ เราอาชีพทำนา เราก็ต้องสู้ไป" เธอกล่าวทิ้งท้าย

（德国之声中文网）这名中国籍女子名叫黄乐（Huang Le，音译），又名爱丽丝（Alice Huang）。美国政府从2024年底、拜登任内尾声，开始调查总部位于新加坡的公司Megaspeed，怀疑它协助中国规避美国的高科技禁令，替中国企业获取 英伟达的先进芯片 。黄乐是Megaspeed公司的高管。美国政府对她的电子监控已持续一段时间。
监控黄乐的过程中，美国情报机构发现她跟黄仁勋有往来。 《纽时》的报导称，由于黄仁勋对美国总统特朗普在中美核心关切议题上的思考有深入了解，加上美国几乎完全依赖英伟达等企业，维持尖端AI大模型研发领域的主导地位，因此，黄乐与黄仁勋的关系“让人不得不怀疑黄女士是否也在搜集英伟达的内部信息”。
该报导引述多位知情者说法，称黄乐曾在个人社群媒体上发布多张跟黄仁勋的合照，还曾向投资人炫耀两人的关系，借此募集资金。 2024年6月一张被发布在领英（LinkedIn）的照片显示，黄仁勋和黄乐曾在台北的酒吧参加过同一场科技业高层的聚会；隔年5月在台北的一场 人工智能 供应商的商务晚宴后，他们也曾被看到一起走出餐厅。
英伟达发言人里佐（John Rizzo）回应， 黄仁勋 身为执行长，跟客户企业的高层见面是他的工作，他与黄乐的互动并不反常。他还表示，像Megaspeed这样的客户，不会接触到英伟达内部敏感的商业机密，更是完全碰不到涉及国安的资讯。
黄仁勋本人29日接受彭博新闻采访，强调英伟达已经进行查核，确保Megaspeed没有非法向中国出口AI处理器，至于他和黄乐的往来，跟他与其他中国客户并无二致：“我们的关系和互动都是跟Megaspeed有关的，而且都完全正常，没有异常之处。”他称黄乐目前已不在Megaspeed任职。
针对此争议，Megaspeed公司向《纽时》表示其现任领导阶层非常严肃看待这件事，已外聘顾问来彻查内部，并全力配合美国政府。黄乐并未回应置评请求。中国驻华盛顿大使馆发言人刘畅则批评美国对中国展开一场“毫无根据的抹黑和诽谤”行动。有记者在周五（10月30日）的中国外交部例行新闻会上问及该报道，发言人郭嘉昆说，有关报道捕风捉影，纯属是对华的污蔑抹黑。

(เว็บไซต์ Deutsche Welle Chinese) หญิงชาวจีนชื่อ Huang Le (ทับศัพท์) หรือที่รู้จักในชื่อ Alice Huang รัฐบาลสหรัฐฯ เริ่มสืบสวน Megaspeed ซึ่งเป็นบริษัทที่มีสำนักงานใหญ่ในสิงคโปร์ ณ สิ้นปี 2024 ซึ่งเป็นการสิ้นสุดวาระของ Biden และสงสัยว่าสิ่งนี้ช่วยให้จีนหลีกเลี่ยงการแบนเทคโนโลยีขั้นสูงของสหรัฐฯ และรับชิปขั้นสูงของ Nvidia สำหรับบริษัทจีน Huang Le เป็นผู้บริหารของ Megaspeed รัฐบาลสหรัฐฯ ติดตามเธอทางอิเล็กทรอนิกส์มาระยะหนึ่งแล้ว
ในขณะที่ติดตาม Huang Le หน่วยข่าวกรองของสหรัฐฯ พบว่าเธอมีการติดต่อกับ Huang Renxun The New York Times รายงานว่าเนื่องจาก Huang มีความเข้าใจอย่างลึกซึ้งเกี่ยวกับความคิดของประธานาธิบดีสหรัฐฯ Trump ในประเด็นหลักที่น่ากังวลระหว่างจีนและสหรัฐอเมริกา และเนื่องจากสหรัฐอเมริกาพึ่งพาบริษัทเกือบทั้งหมด เช่น Nvidia เพื่อรักษาความเป็นผู้นำในการวิจัยและพัฒนาโมเดล AI ขนาดใหญ่ที่ล้ำสมัย ความสัมพันธ์ระหว่าง Huang Le และ Huang “ทำให้ผู้คนสงสัยว่า Ms. Huang กำลังรวบรวมข้อมูลภายในจาก Nvidia ด้วยหรือไม่”
รายงานอ้างแหล่งข่าววงในหลายคนว่า Huang Le ได้โพสต์รูปถ่ายหลายรูปกับ Huang Renxun บนโซเชียลมีเดียส่วนตัวของเขา และยังได้แสดงให้เห็นถึงความสัมพันธ์ของพวกเขากับนักลงทุนเพื่อระดมทุนอีกด้วย ภาพถ่ายที่โพสต์บน LinkedIn ในเดือนมิถุนายน 2024 แสดงให้เห็นว่า Huang Renxun และ Huang Le ได้เข้าร่วมการประชุมเดียวกันของผู้บริหารอุตสาหกรรมเทคโนโลยีที่บาร์แห่งหนึ่งในไทเป ในเดือนพฤษภาคมของปีถัดมา มีคนเห็นพวกเขาเดินออกจากร้านอาหารด้วยกันหลังงานเลี้ยงอาหารค่ำเพื่อธุรกิจให้กับซัพพลายเออร์ปัญญาประดิษฐ์ในไทเป
John Rizzo โฆษกของ Nvidia ตอบว่าในฐานะ CEO มันเป็นหน้าที่ของ Huang ในการพบปะกับผู้บริหารระดับสูงของบริษัทลูกค้า และการปฏิสัมพันธ์ของเขากับ Huang Le ก็ไม่ใช่เรื่องผิดปกติ นอกจากนี้เขายังกล่าวอีกว่าลูกค้าอย่าง Megaspeed จะไม่สามารถเข้าถึงความลับทางธุรกิจที่ละเอียดอ่อนภายในของ Nvidia และจะไม่สามารถเข้าถึงข้อมูลที่เกี่ยวข้องกับความมั่นคงของชาติเลย
Huang Renxun เองยอมรับการสัมภาษณ์กับ Bloomberg News เมื่อวันที่ 29 โดยเน้นว่า Nvidia ได้ทำการตรวจสอบเพื่อให้แน่ใจว่า Megaspeed ไม่ได้ส่งออกโปรเซสเซอร์ AI ไปยังประเทศจีนอย่างผิดกฎหมาย สำหรับการติดต่อกับ Huang Le นั้น ก็ไม่ต่างจากลูกค้าชาวจีนรายอื่น: "ความสัมพันธ์และการโต้ตอบของเราล้วนเกี่ยวข้องกับ Megaspeed และสิ่งเหล่านี้เป็นเรื่องปกติโดยสมบูรณ์และไม่มีอะไรผิดปกติ" เขาบอกว่า Huang Le ไม่ได้ทำงานที่ Megaspeed อีกต่อไป
เพื่อตอบสนองต่อข้อโต้แย้งนี้ Megaspeed บอกกับ New York Times ว่าผู้นำในปัจจุบันให้ความสำคัญกับเรื่องนี้เป็นอย่างมาก ได้ว่าจ้างที่ปรึกษาภายนอกเพื่อดำเนินการสอบสวนภายในอย่างละเอียด และให้ความร่วมมืออย่างเต็มที่กับรัฐบาลสหรัฐฯ Huang Le ไม่ตอบสนองต่อการร้องขอความคิดเห็น หลิว ชาง โฆษกสถานเอกอัครราชทูตจีนในกรุงวอชิงตัน วิพากษ์วิจารณ์สหรัฐฯ ที่ดำเนินโครงการรณรงค์ "ใส่ร้ายป้ายสีและใส่ร้ายอย่างไม่มีมูลความจริง" ต่อจีน ผู้สื่อข่าวถามถึงรายงานดังกล่าวในงานแถลงข่าวประจำกระทรวงการต่างประเทศจีนเมื่อวันศุกร์ (30 ต.ค.) โฆษกกัว เจียคุน กล่าวว่ารายงานที่เกี่ยวข้องนั้นมีพื้นฐานมาจากข่าวลือ และเป็นการใส่ร้ายและใส่ร้ายจีนล้วนๆ
"ชายสี่ล้านล้าน" Huang Renxun พูดอะไรในประเทศจีน?

Astronauts just gave the International Space Station a powerful upgrade
Date:
October 30, 2026
Source:
NASA
Summary:
Two astronauts completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk to install a new solar array on the International Space Station, bringing NASA one step closer to a major power upgrade. Once the final array is installed on November 5, the station will have up to 30% more available power, supporting critical operations and its eventual controlled deorbit.
Share:
NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk have completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk outside the International Space Station, marking another important step in a major upgrade to the orbiting laboratory's power system. The astronauts finished their work at 3:08 p.m. EDT.
During the spacewalk, Menon and Kutryk installed and deployed a new International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on the station's 2A electrical power channel. This is the seventh such array added to the station, providing additional electricity for essential operations, including the station's eventual safe and controlled deorbit.
Final Spacewalk Will Complete Solar Array Upgrade
The astronauts also performed several preliminary tasks to prepare for another spacewalk scheduled for Thursday, Nov. 5. During that mission, astronauts will install the eighth and final solar array on the station's 3B power channel. NASA plans to begin live coverage at 6:45 a.m., with information on how to watch available through the agency.
Once the final array is installed, the International Space Station's solar power expansion will be complete. Together, the eight new arrays will increase the station's available power by as much as 30%, raising its electricity generation capacity from 160 kilowatts to approximately 215 kilowatts.
A Milestone for Space Station Operations
The completed mission, designated U.S. spacewalk 100, marked Menon's fourth spacewalk and Kutryk's first. It was also the 285th spacewalk conducted to support the assembly, maintenance, and improvement of the International Space Station.

content:
Eating fruit and vegetable scraps such as peels and stalks could provide a health boost that most of us are missing, say UK researchers, external.
They say scraps are an overlooked source of dietary fibre and are encouraging people to try "root-to-tip" eating, including watermelon rind, pineapple core and butternut squash seeds.
Most adults do not get enough fibre. Official figures, external show only 4% meet the recommended 30g a day, despite its well-known benefits for gut health.
Fibre aids digestion, helps you feel fuller for longer and is linked to a lower risk of heart disease and bowel cancer., external
Stalks, pips and rind on
Skin and pips can be beneficial, the fibre researchers say
As a rule of thumb, the skins of fruit and veg pack more fibre than the insides.
Eating a kiwi with the skin on, external provides 50% more fibre than having a peeled one, for example.
For their study, the scientists at King's College London analysed 12 raw or uncooked fresh foods - beetroot, bell pepper, broccoli, butternut squash, cauliflower, celeriac, curly kale, fennel, kiwi fruit, leek, pineapple and watermelon.
They found many discarded parts contained more fibre than the sections people typically eat.
For example:
watermelon rind contained 2.10g of fibre per 100g – roughly equivalent to the fibre in a slice of wholemeal bread
butternut squash skin and seeds contained 9.25g per 100g – nearly as much fibre as a bowl of bran flakes
pineapple skin and core contained five times more fibre than the flesh
broccoli stalks contained fibre, although a bit less than the florets
Fibre is essential for your gut to work properly and helps prevent constipation.
Project lead Dr Rachel Gibson said the findings suggested people are throwing away a significant amount of fibre.
"This isn't just a nutritional loss, it's also a financial one - you're effectively throwing away a substantial portion of what you've paid for."
Banana peel curry?
King's College London has been experimenting in its canteen, external, offering staff and students root-to-tip meals, such as banana skin curry.
At home, people might want to try leaving skins on kiwi fruit, using broccoli stalks in stir-fries or adding bell pepper seeds to dishes, the researchers suggest.
While cooking can change the fibre content, it doesn't usually destroy it all.
Steaming, microwaving or quick sautéing tends to preserve nutrients best.
Gibson said: "This isn't about perfection and this isn't about forcing people to eat unpalatable food – it's about recognising the nutritional value in components we've been conditioned to discard."
She acknowledges some may be hesitant to try it.
Some diners raised concerns during the canteen trial.
Over the nine-week period, "root-to-tip" dishes made up a third of total daily hot menu sales at the university.
Those choosing the new dishes were less likely to finish their meals than diners eating from the conventional menu.
Kirsten Jackson, a dietitian with the British Dietetic Association who specialises in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), says the food hacks are useful as long as produce is washed thoroughly.
She suggests blending pineapple cores into smoothies, but says the tough skins are not something she would recommend.
Some stalks may need to be cooked or finely chopped to make them more palatable, she adds.
"Just because a broccoli stalk doesn't fit into tonight's meal doesn't mean it needs to go in the bin. Chop it up, freeze it and add it to a soup or stir-fry another day," she said.
She advises increasing fibre intake gradually to avoid bloating, noting that people who have IBS may find it harder to tolerate.
And there are some things to avoid entirely, said the British Nutrition Foundation.
Green potatoes and rhubarb leaves contain toxic compounds, while tough stalks and seeds may not be suitable for young children.

Watch: "My low Vitamin D levels hit me like a truck"
Published
Twenty-three-year-old Saskia Reeves-Priestley was at work when she suddenly collapsed.
"I just felt really dizzy, really nauseous, was having heart palpitations and was really hot," she says.
Saskia, a special educational needs teacher, was a keen goalkeeper who played football four times a week and felt fit and healthy. While her symptoms are not directly linked to vitamin D deficiency - she realised something was wrong.
Blood tests later showed her level was so low - it was "next to nothing".
In the UK, low vitamin D rates are increasing in some age groups, external - particularly in girls and young women.
According to data from the National Diet and Nutrition Survey, last year nearly a quarter of 11- to 18-year-olds were classed as deficient.
Vitamin D can come from our diet, in foods such as oily fish and meat, or supplements.
But most is made by our body when UV light in sunlight hits the skin. Lower levels of sunlight - depending on where in the world you live or the time of year - decrease the body's ability to produce it.
Covering parts of the body and wearing sunscreen also has an impact - despite their protective advantages.
Those with darker skin need exposure to stronger light to produce the same amount of vitamin D as lighter skin.
Doctors don't routinely offer blood tests to check for vitamin D deficiency, but will offer a supplement if a patient is concerned they might be high risk.
What are the symptoms - and their daily impact?
Vitamin D deficiency is linked to the bone disease rickets in babies and infants. In adults it causes a similar weakening of the bone called osteomalacia, external.
"They call it the silent disease," says Dr Suma Uday, a paediatric endocrinologist who wants to raise awareness of the problem.
She warns that vitamin D deficiency in young people and adults is difficult to spot and can be missed or misdiagnosed. Symptoms include fatigue and joint and bone pain.
Uday says: "It's basically silently eating away at the bones, leaving them softened and prone to breaks."
Amaka Osu says she doesn't think many of her friends realise what the symptoms are
Amaka was in the middle of making dinner at her university house in Liverpool when she started shaking.
"I couldn't really see in front of me," she says. Her housemate took her to A&E - later she too would be diagnosed as vitamin D deficient.
Other than feeling tired, she says she had no symptoms: "I'm a 21-year-old student. I've got work and uni - I'm always feeling tired."
She remembers her mother suffering from low vitamin D but says she did not realise it could happen to her.
After taking supplements, Amaka feels a lot better, but she is anxious in case it happens again. "It was scary and I don't want to experience that again."
Lifelong deficit in girls
Uday joins other clinicians and academics who have formed a group - ACT NOW Vitamin D - calling for the threshold at which you are classified as deficient to be raised.
She says that would "catch" more people with low vitamin D and give a more accurate picture of how widespread the issue is. It would also mean they can treat the deficiency earlier, she says.
Uday warns of "a lifelong deficit" in women - in adolescence, then pregnancy, and then the newborn is affected.
"If you don't correct it from the very beginning," she says, "this is going to affect multiple generations."
Saskia Reeves-Priestley plays football four times a week - and had no previous symptoms
"It's shocking," says Prof Martin Hewison, from the University of Birmingham.
He tells me that despite being 100 years on from the discovery of vitamin D "rickets hasn't gone away".
"If we have rickets in the community, there are going to be many more people who are vitamin D deficient."
He says the government should look into wider fortification of food in which vitamins are added to foods during production. Countries like Canada and Sweden have mandatory policies.
In the UK, some foods such as breakfast cereals and spreads are already fortified with vitamin D, but it is voluntary.
During the winter months, people start to lose their vitamin D levels.
"We might have to accept that for certain groups vitamin D supplementation is a matter of course," says Hewison.
Saskia is now taking vitamin D supplements regularly - and is back in goal.
Published24 August

content:
Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal
Date:
October 29, 2026
Source:
University of California - San Diego
Summary:
A surprising discovery at UC San Diego suggests that chronic lower back pain may become deeply embedded in the brain's sense of personal identity. Researchers found that movement-triggered pain activates a brain network associated with self-awareness and memories, even though ordinary acute pain typically shuts this network down. This unexpected difference could explain why conventional pain medications often provide limited relief and why fear, anticipation, and past experiences can intensify chronic pain.
Share:
For people living with chronic back pain, even a simple movement can trigger a sudden surge of pain. Now, scientists have discovered that these painful episodes activate a surprising part of the brain, one closely connected to our sense of identity and how we think about ourselves.
Researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine found that movement-triggered pain in people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) activates a brain network that normally becomes less active during ordinary pain. The discovery suggests that persistent back pain may become deeply intertwined with a person's sense of self, potentially helping explain why conventional pain treatments often provide limited relief.
According to the World Health Organization, low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide. When pain persists for more than 12 weeks, it is considered chronic. For many patients, everyday movements can provoke sudden flare-ups that make an already difficult condition even harder to manage.
Although the brain plays a central role in how pain is experienced, researchers have struggled to identify the precise brain circuits responsible for pain triggered by movement.
Chronic Back Pain Activates the Brain's Sense of Self
The new study, published on October 5, 2026, in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, identified an unexpected response involving the brain's Default Mode Network (DMN).
Sometimes called the "self network," the DMN consists of interconnected regions in the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. These areas are especially active when our attention turns inward, such as when we reflect on personal experiences, think about our identity, or consider our thoughts and emotions. In contrast, the network generally becomes less active when we direct our attention toward something happening around us.
The researchers discovered that sudden back pain caused by movement switched this network on rather than off. This unusual response suggests that chronic pain involves more than the processing of physical sensations. It may also engage the brain systems that shape how people experience themselves.
The findings could help researchers understand why treatments that focus primarily on suppressing pain symptoms do not always work well for chronic low back pain. They also raise the possibility that targeting the DMN could offer a different approach to treatment.
Brain Scans Reveal a Surprising Difference Between Chronic and Acute Pain
To investigate what happens in the brain during a pain flare, the researchers recruited 114 patients with chronic low back pain.
Each participant completed a "leg raise test," a standard clinical procedure used to provoke back pain. During the test, researchers monitored changes in brain blood flow using a specialized functional MRI method called arterial spin labeling. This technique allows scientists to track patterns of brain activity by measuring blood flow without relying on an injected contrast agent.
The team also examined how participants responded to a separate painful stimulus. They applied a harmless but uncomfortable heat sensation to the calf, similar to the brief pain someone might experience when accidentally touching a hot stove.
Comparing these two situations revealed a striking difference.
When movement triggered a flare of chronic back pain, the DMN became more active. However, when participants experienced the painful heat stimulus, the same network became less active, following the brain's typical response to acute pain.
The researchers also identified several other important patterns:
Patients with more severe chronic back pain showed stronger connections between the DMN and the primary somatosensory cortex, a brain region responsible for processing physical sensations, including signals from the back.
Greater pain intensity during the leg raise test was associated with increased activity in brain regions involved in sensation and movement.
Increases in heart rate during the test reliably reflected the intensity of the pain flare.
Together, these findings provide new evidence that chronic pain flares involve brain processes associated with personal identity, not just the physical experience of pain.
Why the Brain Reacts Differently to Chronic Pain
During ordinary acute pain, the brain generally reduces activity in the DMN so it can concentrate on the immediate source of danger. This response helps shift attention away from internal thoughts and toward an external threat.
But the UC San Diego researchers found that movement triggered chronic back pain produced the opposite effect.
"In every pain study, when you're experiencing pain, the DMN deactivates," said corresponding author Fadel Zeidan, PhD, professor in the Department of Anesthesiology, endowed professor at the Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion, and director of the Pain Health and Mindfulness Laboratory at UC San Diego School of Medicine. "What we show for the first time ever is that when you have a pain flare, it turns on instead. You start to identify the experience with who you are."
The findings suggest that chronic back pain can become closely connected with the brain's internal representation of the self. Rather than processing pain solely as a physical warning signal, the brain may also link it to personal memories, expectations, and emotional experiences.
For someone living with chronic pain, this means the experience can extend far beyond the moments when the pain is physically present. Worry about the next flare, memories of previous episodes, and fear of movements that might trigger pain can all become part of everyday life.
"The moment-to-moment experience is contaminated not only by the feeling of pain, but by the anticipation of it and recovery from it. It's contaminated by past experiences like embarrassment about not being able to participate in normal activities and fear of movement when trying to avoid the pain."
This connection between pain and personal identity may help explain why chronic back pain can be especially difficult to treat.
A New Direction for Chronic Back Pain Treatment
Because movement-triggered chronic back pain engages different brain networks from ordinary acute pain, researchers believe traditional treatments may fail to address some of the processes that sustain the experience of chronic pain.
Medications such as opiates primarily target pain signaling, but they may not adequately address the brain networks involved in the emotional and personal dimensions of persistent pain.
"Current pain medicine is fixated on ridding patients of their pain symptoms, but that's not the source of chronic pain. These data suggest that a chronic pain flare also encompasses one's identity."
The discovery points toward treatments that address not only the sensation of pain but also the brain's relationship with that sensation.
Recent work by Zeidan and his colleagues has explored two potential approaches: mindfulness meditation and the psychedelic compound psilocybin.
Both approaches are being investigated for their ability to help people experience physical pain without allowing it to become as closely tied to their identity. Early findings suggest that changing this relationship may reduce pain intensity, although additional research is needed to confirm the results and determine how effective these treatments may be.
"These types of mind-body and psychedelic medicine approaches target the whole person," Zeidan said. "Mindfulness is a meditation technique that's about cultivating non-judgmental awareness of the present moment that dramatically reduces pain in a very unique way. Psilocybin seemingly resets the pain system that integrates trauma, past experiences and future worries to facilitate a restart, if you will. They're not a silver bullet -- you're not necessarily getting rid of the pain, but you're changing the relationship you have with that pain so it doesn't contaminate your everyday life."
Can Mindfulness and Psychedelics Change How the Brain Experiences Pain?
Rather than attempting to eliminate every pain signal, these approaches aim to change how the brain interprets and responds to the experience.
Mindfulness meditation encourages people to observe their thoughts, emotions, and physical sensations without immediately judging or reacting to them. Psilocybin, meanwhile, is being studied for its potential to alter brain processes that connect pain with earlier experiences, emotional distress, and expectations about the future.
The goal is not necessarily to remove pain altogether, but to reduce how much it influences a person's thoughts, emotions, and daily functioning.
Zeidan's laboratory is currently conducting several clinical trials using brain imaging to investigate whether mindfulness meditation and psychedelic treatments can change the neural processes involved in self-reflection. Researchers hope to determine whether these approaches can reshape brain activity and improve how people subjectively experience chronic pain.
Although the research remains at an early stage, the findings offer a different way to think about persistent back pain. Understanding why the brain connects chronic pain with a person's sense of self could eventually help scientists develop treatments that address aspects of pain that conventional therapies often miss.
Additional study authors from UC San Diego School of Medicine include Morgan Gianola, Jon Dean, Conan Chen, Daniel Barrows, Gabriel Reigner, and Thomas Liu.
Funding was provided in part by the National Institutes of Health's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (Grant #R01AT009693) and the UC San Diego Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion. The researchers reported no conflicts of interest.

content:
Seabirds returning from foraging trips can be thrown hundreds of miles off course by a form of jet lag that arises when their body clocks get out of sync with local time, researchers say.
Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation.
The impact was limited on adult shearwaters because the birds were able to correct their bearings in flight. At most, the birds veered off course by about 15 degrees. After correcting their course, this added only an estimated 3 miles to a 600-mile journey.
But less experienced birds were likely to have a tougher time, the study found, with first-time foragers at risk of flying off course by hundreds of miles.
Most studies on birds’ biological clocks have been conducted under laboratory conditions but Dr Patrick Lewin, a behavioural and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford, set out to investigate wild birds with the help of his colleagues.
Their analysis of 20 years of GPS tracking data revealed a clear effect when the Manx shearwaters flew east across lines of longitude as they returned home, leading their clocks to run up to an hour or so behind local time. “The bird’s internal clock can be subject to a jet lag phenomenon, manifesting as birds flying off course,” Lewin said.
Like many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. Because the sun moves across the sky as the Earth rotates, reading its position correctly relies on the birds adjusting their heading relative to the sun, using their body clock to keep track of the time of day. Sunset and sunrise keep the bird’s body clock in sync, helping them adjust to changes in local time.
Writing in Science, Lewin said the mismatch between local time and the birds’ internal clocks could make them drift off course when the sun lay farther around the sky than expected. Surprisingly, the errors remained when birds followed the coastline, where landmarks could have guided them, further supporting the idea that the sun plays a central role in anchoring their sense of direction.
“For adult shearwaters, this lag has very limited impact on their overall journey, with errors adding a calculated 5km to a 1,000km journey,” Lewin said. “However, for first-time migrant birds, such orientation shifts due to sun compass errors could result in deviations of hundreds of kilometres as they lack a map sense to help reorient them when they lose their way.”
Prof Richard Holland of Bangor University, who was not involved in the study, said it was a significant finding: “It seems to confirm in wild animals what more controlled experimental studies have shown: reliance on the sun compass for animals that move during the day, even when it is not accurate.”
after newsletter promotion
Manx shearwaters spend most of their lives far out at sea. They cover enormous distances but return each year to islands off the west coast of the UK to breed in burrows.
“It’s not clear from the study what the consequences of these errors are, since the birds return to their colony and the errors are small,” Holland said. “Nonetheless, it highlights the importance of understanding the role of biological rhythms across multiple contexts in animal behaviour, as more and more we are starting to realise just how important these are for numerous biological functions.”
summary: Oxford study shows Manx shearwaters get lost when their body clocks get out of sync Seabirds returning from foraging trips can be thrown hundreds of miles off course by a form of jet lag that arises when their body clocks get out of sync with local time, researchers say. Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation. content:
Patients in many parts of the country have been left unable to access their GP surgery online after a tech firm went into administration.
Silicon Practice ran digital services, including websites, online booking and consultations, for around 500 practices in England – just under 10% of the total.
Practices across the country, including in London, Gloucestershire and Norfolk, have reported problems. Services in Wales are also affected.
GP leaders said the problem would cause huge disruption, given the scale of online booking that now takes places.
Patients in areas that are affected are being advised they will have to make appointments via the phone. The NHS app is working.
Since last year, all practices in England have had to offer online appointment booking. Currently, more than 40% of appointments are made that way.
An NHS England spokesperson said while "the majority" of GP practice websites were running as normal, some using Silicon Practice will be affected.
"If your GP practice website is unavailable and you need help, you should contact your practice by phone or in person as usual."
'Hugely disruptive'
Affected practices have been contacted by NHS England with advice on how to maintain business continuity and minimise the impact on patient care.
Silicon Practice ran the digital tool FootFall, which it advertised as reducing patient phone calls to practices by 30%, by working to "free your reception team from routine admin and manage demand more efficiently. Proven in 1,000+ GP practices across the UK".
Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs, said: "GP practice websites are an increasingly important way for patients to access care, book appointments and find information about the services available to them.
"When websites are not working, it can be hugely disruptive for patients and place additional pressures on already stretched practice teams.
"It is vital that any disruption to practice websites is addressed promptly to ensure patients are able to access care."
She said affected practices must receive prompt, practical support from NHS England and local NHS organisations to restore their websites, minimise disruption and ensure patients know how to contact their practice and access the care they need in the meantime.

content:
A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms
Date:
October 29, 2026
Source:
McGill University
Summary:
Scientists have identified a weakened brain signal that may connect several seemingly unrelated symptoms of schizophrenia, including sensory processing difficulties, disorganized speech, and greater symptom severity. The surprising discovery could help explain the disorder's underlying mechanisms and potentially lead to earlier detection and new treatments.
Share:
Scientists have identified a brain signal that may help explain why schizophrenia produces such a wide variety of symptoms, including difficulties with perception, movement, and speech. The discovery suggests that problems that appear unrelated could actually stem from a shared disruption in how the brain processes information.
Schizophrenia is a complex psychiatric disorder that can affect how people experience the world, interact with their surroundings, and communicate with others. These symptoms are typically studied as separate features of the condition, but new research suggests they may have more in common than previously recognized.
The study, published in Science Advances, was conducted by scientists from McGill University, the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre, the University of Montreal, the Research Centre of the University of Montreal Health Centre, and the Douglas Research Centre. Their findings point to a common brain mechanism that may help explain several distinct symptoms of schizophrenia.
A Weakened Brain Signal Links Multiple Schizophrenia Symptoms
To investigate this connection, researchers examined beta-band brain activity in 25 people diagnosed with schizophrenia and 25 healthy participants. Beta-band activity refers to rhythmic patterns of electrical activity in the brain that are involved in coordinating information processing, perception, and movement.
Participants completed tasks designed to test how accurately they could judge the timing of visual and auditory information. The researchers also analyzed their speech to look for signs of disorganized thinking and communication.
The results revealed a striking pattern. People with schizophrenia showed weaker and slower beta-band activity than those in the control group. More importantly, the participants with the most pronounced abnormalities in this brain signal also tended to have greater difficulty processing the timing of sights and sounds, more disorganized speech, and more severe clinical symptoms.
These three features of schizophrenia are usually investigated independently. Finding that they were all associated with changes in the same brain signal suggests that a shared underlying process may contribute to the disorder's diverse effects.
A New Window Into How the Brain Processes Reality
"This gives us early but compelling evidence that measuring the brain's operations, especially how it builds and revises its own model of the world, may help us appreciate that there is a common thread behind the confusing array of symptoms we see in disorders like schizophrenia," said Dr. Lena Palaniyappan, senior author of the study, Professor of Psychiatry at McGill and director of the Centre of Excellence in Youth Mental Health at the Douglas Hospital.
The brain constantly uses incoming sensory information to develop and update its understanding of the surrounding environment. This process helps people interpret what they see and hear, anticipate events, and coordinate their actions. The new findings suggest that disruptions in this process could help explain why schizophrenia affects several different aspects of behavior and perception.
The researchers used high-resolution magnetoencephalography, or MEG, to measure brain activity. This imaging technique detects the tiny magnetic fields generated by electrical activity in the brain, allowing scientists to track changes in neural signals with exceptional precision. The scans were performed at the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre at the Montreal Neurological Institute-Hospital (The Neuro).
"What struck us was that the same weakened brain signal kept showing up wherever we looked, whether patients were processing a sound, a sight or completing a movement," said Hsi (Tiana) Wei, lead author of the study and postdoctoral scholar in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and the Douglas Research Centre. "Seeing the same pattern across these different domains suggested there may be a common underlying process linking the symptoms."
Could the Discovery Help Detect Psychosis Earlier?
Beyond providing new insight into schizophrenia, the findings could eventually help researchers identify young people who are at greater risk of developing psychosis. Psychosis involves a disruption in how someone perceives or interprets reality and can include experiences such as hallucinations or delusions.
Early identification is particularly important because the first signs of schizophrenia often appear during adolescence but may go unrecognized for an extended period.
"The very first sign of schizophrenia begins in our adolescence, but this often gets missed for a long time. If this finding is confirmed in larger samples, we may have a potentially useful method to identify who, among youth seeking help for mental health, needs extra support to prevent psychosis," Palaniyappan said.
However, the researchers emphasized that the results are preliminary. The study included only 50 participants, and additional research involving larger, independent groups will be necessary to determine how reliably the brain signal is associated with speech disturbances and overall symptom severity.
"This is a first, modest-size study, and the associations with speech and clinical severity will need to be tested in larger independent samples before we can be confident in them," Wei said.
If future studies confirm the findings, measuring beta-band activity could potentially become a useful tool for identifying people who need earlier support. Wei also suggested that the brain signal may deserve investigation as a possible target for future schizophrenia treatments.

Materials provided by McGill University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
