Kaepernick คุกเข่าประท้วงครั้งแรกในเดือนกันยายน 2559
หลังจากการฆาตกรรมจอร์จ ฟลอยด์ ขณะถูกตำรวจควบคุมตัวในมินนิแอโพลิสในปี 2020 การคุกเข่ากลายเป็นเหตุการณ์สำคัญในการประท้วง Black Lives Matter และแพร่หลายไปทั่ววงการกีฬา
ทีมฟุตบอลชายและหญิงของอังกฤษเป็นหนึ่งในทีมที่ต้องปฏิบัติตาม
“นั่นเป็นช่วงเวลาที่น่าประหลาดใจสำหรับฉัน” Kaepernick กล่าว
“ฉันคิดถึงการประท้วงที่เกิดขึ้นนอกสหรัฐอเมริกา และวิธีที่มันจะเกิดขึ้นในประเทศอื่นๆ การได้เห็นทีมชาติออกมาประท้วง มันน่าน้อยใจ ฉันดีใจที่พวกเขากำลังทำอยู่
“ฉันรู้ด้วยว่ายังมีงานอีกมากที่ต้องทำเกี่ยวกับการเหยียดเชื้อชาติในสหราชอาณาจักรและในวงกว้างมากขึ้น และนี่คือความท้าทายระดับโลกที่เรากำลังต่อสู้ร่วมกัน
“ฉันตื่นเต้นมากที่ได้เห็นผู้เล่นเรียกร้องสิ่งนั้น และเต็มใจที่จะเริ่มดำเนินการเพื่อแก้ไขปัญหาดังกล่าว”
แม้จะไม่ค่อยเป็นที่รู้จักเกือบตลอดทศวรรษที่ผ่านมา แต่ Kaepernick ยังคงเป็นผู้ถือมาตรฐานสำหรับขบวนการสิทธิพลเมือง
แต่ในขณะที่การสำรวจชี้ว่านักกีฬามืออาชีพส่วนใหญ่ตั้งใจที่จะใช้ช่องทางโซเชียลมีเดียเพื่อสร้างความตระหนักรู้เกี่ยวกับความอยุติธรรมทางเชื้อชาติภายนอก เขายอมรับว่าแรงผลักดันเบื้องหลังการเคลื่อนไหวของนักกีฬาดูเหมือนจะชะลอตัวลงในช่วงไม่กี่ปีที่ผ่านมา
เป็นที่น่าสังเกตว่าผู้เล่นหลายคนจากห้าสโมสรเลือกที่จะยืนหยัดต่อไปเมื่อผู้เล่นในพรีเมียร์ลีกคุกเข่าซึ่งเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของแคมเปญ No Room for Racism ในเดือนตุลาคม
กลุ่มรณรงค์ต่อต้านการเลือกปฏิบัติ Kick It Out บอกกับ BBC Sport ว่าท่าทาง “ยังคงมีคุณค่าในการสร้างความตระหนักรู้ถึงความไม่เท่าเทียมกันทางโครงสร้างที่มีอยู่ในฟุตบอลและสังคม” แต่เสริมว่าสามารถ “เข้าใจเหตุผลที่ผู้เล่นอาจหงุดหงิดกับก้าวของการเปลี่ยนแปลง”
รายงานการเลือกปฏิบัติที่ได้รับจากองค์กรการกุศลเพิ่มขึ้นกว่าสองเท่าในช่วงห้าปีที่ผ่านมา ซึ่งแตะระดับสูงสุดเป็นประวัติการณ์ในฤดูกาลที่แล้ว
“ฉันคิดว่าเราอยู่ในช่วงเวลาที่เรียกร้องให้มีการประท้วงมากขึ้นกว่าเดิม” แคเปอร์นิคกล่าว
“เหตุใดฉันจึงคิดว่าการประท้วงไม่ดังในตอนนี้ [เป็น] เนื่องจากความพยายามร่วมกันที่ดำเนินการโดยองค์กรต่างๆ เช่น NFL เช่นฝ่ายบริหารของทรัมป์ และองค์กรต่างๆ ที่ติดตามและยอมจำนนในกระบวนการนั้น
“ในขณะที่สิ่งเหล่านั้นกำลังเกิดขึ้น ผมคิดว่าความเป็นจริงของสถานะของสหรัฐฯ และในวงกว้างมากขึ้นนั้น เรียกร้องให้เราปรากฏตัวในวิธีที่สำคัญกว่านี้”
'การเมืองเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของกีฬาโดยเนื้อแท้'
Kaepernick ต่างคุ้นเคยดีว่าการแบ่งขั้วในการยืนหยัดทางการเมืองในวงการกีฬานั้นเป็นอย่างไร
ผู้คัดค้านการคุกเข่าอ้างว่าเป็นแถลงการณ์ทางการเมืองและสร้างความแตกแยก และแทนที่จะสนับสนุนขบวนการ Black Lives Matter กลับแสดงการสนับสนุนองค์กรที่ใช้ชื่อเดียวกัน
ในปี 2018 นักวิจารณ์สนับสนุนให้ผู้คนทำลายสินค้าของ Nike หลังจากที่ยักษ์ใหญ่ด้านชุดกีฬาใช้ Kaepernick เป็นพรีเซนเตอร์ของแคมเปญโฆษณาที่มีคำบรรยายว่า "เชื่อในบางสิ่งบางอย่าง" แม้ว่ามันจะหมายถึงการเสียสละทุกสิ่งทุกอย่างก็ตาม'
แล้วเขาพูดอะไรกับคนที่โต้แย้งว่ากีฬาและการเมืองควรแยกออกจากกัน?
“พวกเขาดูไร้สาระและรู้สึกหน้าซื่อใจคดมาก เพราะการเมืองเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของกีฬาโดยธรรมชาติ” เขากล่าว
“เราเห็นใน [อเมริกัน] ฟุตบอล เราเห็นผู้เสียภาษีให้ทุนสนับสนุนสนามกีฬา NFL เราเห็นเจ้าของ NFL ออกไปสนับสนุนผู้สมัครทางการเมือง... ดังนั้นการพยายามวางจุดยืนนี้ราวกับว่ากีฬาไม่ใช่เรื่องการเมือง ในหลาย ๆ ด้านฉันรู้สึกว่ามันน่าหัวเราะและถูกตัดการเชื่อมต่อ
“ตอนนี้ คำถามที่เข้ามาสำหรับผู้คนคือ: 'เราไม่ต้องการให้นักกีฬาเป็นเรื่องการเมือง ทุกสิ่งรอบตัวพวกเขาสามารถเป็นเรื่องการเมืองได้ แต่ตัวนักกีฬาเอง เราไม่ต้องการให้พวกเขามีเสียงในการเมือง เพราะมันขัดขวางความบันเทิงของเราและความสามารถของเราในการตัดการเชื่อมต่อ' สำหรับฉัน นั่นคือสิ่งที่สังคมมีความท้าทาย"
เมื่อเผชิญการต่อต้านที่สำคัญจากนักกีฬาชื่อดังในช่วงวาระแรก ดูเหมือนว่าทรัมป์จะเผชิญกับความท้าทายน้อยลงจากโลกแห่งกีฬาในช่วงสมัยที่สอง โดยเฉพาะอย่างยิ่งการกลายเป็นประธานาธิบดีคนแรกของสหรัฐฯ ที่เข้าร่วมการแข่งขันซูเปอร์โบวล์
เขายังเคยปรากฏตัวในรายการกอล์ฟไรเดอร์คัพ และรอบชิงชนะเลิศของฟุตบอลคลับเวิลด์คัพและฟุตบอลโลก แม้ว่าเขาจะถูกโห่เมื่อเข้าร่วมการแข่งขัน NBA Finals ที่นิวยอร์กในเดือนมิถุนายนก็ตาม
“มันเชื่อมโยงกับบทสนทนาที่ว่า 'กีฬาเป็นเรื่องการเมืองหรือเปล่า' เมื่อเขาออกไปข้างนอกและพยายามใช้สิ่งเหล่านั้นเพื่อให้ได้รับความโปรดปรานและความนิยม” เคเปอร์นิคกล่าว พร้อมเสริมว่าการตัดสินใจอันขัดแย้งของฟีฟ่าในการมอบรางวัล 'รางวัลสันติภาพ' ครั้งแรกเมื่อปีที่แล้วนั้น "น่าเสียใจ"
“ส่วนที่ฉันคิดว่าเป็นเรื่องดีที่ได้เห็นคือตอนที่เขาปรากฏตัวต่อเหตุการณ์เหล่านี้และถูกฝูงชนโห่ ซึ่งพูดถึงสภาพแวดล้อมทางการเมืองที่เขาสร้างขึ้น ซึ่งคนส่วนใหญ่ของประเทศไม่เห็นด้วยกับ…เมื่อพูดถึงเรื่องกีฬา ผู้คนจำเป็นต้องตอบสนองต่อไปตามนั้น”
แม้จะฟันเฟืองกลับ แต่ Kaepernick ก็คุกเข่าซ้ำก่อนการแข่งขัน NFL ฤดูกาลปกติ 11 รายการ
'เรามีงานต้องทำอีกมาก'
ปัจจุบันอายุ 38 ปี Kaepernick ได้ตีพิมพ์บันทึกความทรงจำชื่อ The Perilous Fight โดยมีรายละเอียดเกี่ยวกับวัยเด็กของเขาในแคลิฟอร์เนียที่ได้รับการเลี้ยงดูจากครอบครัวคนผิวขาว การเผชิญหน้ากับการเหยียดเชื้อชาติ การศึกษาและวิวัฒนาการของเขา “ผู้คนมองเห็นช่วงเวลานั้น แต่พวกเขาไม่เห็นช่วงเวลาหลายปีที่ทำให้มันเกิดขึ้นได้” เขากล่าว “คำถามว่าฉันเป็นใคร ความอยุติธรรมที่ฉันไม่สามารถเพิกเฉยได้อีกต่อไป เสียงของผู้ที่อยู่ตรงหน้าฉันที่พาเข้าไปในสนามนั้น...เมื่อฉันคุกเข่า มันไม่ใช่การกระทำกะทันหัน มันเป็นผลมาจากหลายปีของการเป็น”
แล้วเขาค้นพบกระบวนการของการเดินทางครั้งนั้นอีกครั้งได้อย่างไร?
"มีช่วงเวลาที่ท้าทายในการย้อนกลับไปหรือไม่ มี แต่ฉันหวังว่าข้อมูลเชิงลึกจะช่วยให้ผู้อื่นสามารถนำทางสถานการณ์...ที่ช่วยให้พวกเขาก้าวไปข้างหน้าหรือช่วยให้พวกเขาทำสิ่งต่างๆ ได้สำเร็จ"
Kaepernick ยังสนับสนุนองค์กรชุมชนผ่านแคมเปญการศึกษา Know Your Rights ของเขา เป็นผู้ใจบุญ และได้เขียนหนังสือสำหรับเด็กหลายเล่ม
แม้กระทั่งตอนนี้ เขายังคงรักษาระบบการออกกำลังกายที่เขามีในช่วงเวลาที่เขาอยู่กับทีม 49ers เผื่อในกรณีที่มีโอกาสที่ไม่น่าจะกลับมาเล่น NFL ของเขาต่อได้
แคเปอร์นิคอาจไม่ได้ขว้างลูกบอลด้วยความโกรธมาเกือบทศวรรษ แต่เขาได้รับการยกย่องอย่างกว้างขวางว่าเป็นหนึ่งในนักกีฬาที่สำคัญที่สุดในประวัติศาสตร์สมัยใหม่
วิธีที่เขาใช้เวทีเพื่อส่งเสริมการเปลี่ยนแปลงนั้นเทียบได้กับนักมวยในตำนาน มูฮัมหมัด อาลี ที่สนับสนุนขบวนการต่อต้านสงคราม และนักกีฬาของสหรัฐอเมริกา ทอมมี่ สมิธ และจอห์น คาร์ลอส กล่าวแสดงความยินดีต่อพลังสีดำในโอลิมปิกปี 1968
“การได้สนทนาแบบเดียวกันกับ [พวกเขา] เป็นเรื่องที่น่าถ่อมใจอย่างยิ่ง” เขากล่าว “แต่ที่สำคัญกว่านั้น ฉันแค่พยายามมีสมาธิกับงาน”
"เราสามารถทำอะไรได้บ้างเพื่อช่วยเหลือผู้คน และเราจะร่วมกันก้าวไปข้างหน้าในฐานะสังคมได้อย่างไร และท้ายที่สุด เราจะสร้างสังคมที่เหมาะกับทุกคนได้อย่างไร นั่นให้ความรู้สึกเหมือนเป็นหลักการง่ายๆ ที่สูญหายไป
“ฉันรู้โดยเฉพาะในสหรัฐอเมริกา เรามีงานต้องทำมากมายที่นั่น ฉันหวังว่าเราจะเริ่มดำเนินการเพื่อกลับไปยังจุดที่เรากำลังตอบสนองความต้องการของผู้คนอย่างแท้จริง และสร้างสังคมที่มีความเท่าเทียมสำหรับทุกคน”

content:
For a very long time, I dreamed of being cured. I was born in 1981. I learned to walk early enough, but I stumbled and fell more easily than other children. My parents began to worry that something was wrong, that my muscles were weaker than they should be. Eventually, at the age of three, I was diagnosed with a form of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). In the 1980s, the precise mechanics were not yet understood, but the condition was known to be hereditary, probably linked to a recessive gene. It was also known to be progressive. As I aged, my muscles would not keep pace. At eight, I began to use a wheelchair for longer distances. By the time I was 18, I rarely walked outdoors any more.
It is hard to be young and to know that you are growing weaker rather than stronger. I had all the same aspirations that my nondisabled friends did, but I lived in fear of the future in a way they did not. I spent a lot of time thinking about what my life would have been like if I didn’t have SMA. The images in my head were of something like a double: myself, only rid of this one deficit, imprecisely defined, but encoded somewhere in my body.
In the 1990s, the human genome began to be mapped. Medical genetics grew ever more precise. I was vaguely aware of this, of the fact that genetic conditions such as mine were being better understood with every year. With that understanding came the possibility, however faint, that there might be some form of treatment for me beyond the interminable hours of painful, barely-worth-it physical therapy I took after school.
At some point, it did strike me that before medical genetics could even begin to pursue a treatment, an SMA gene would be identifiable in embryos. My other self might be me, cured. Or he might be someone living in my stead, while I’d never been born at all.
As science progressed, this other self came to seem more concrete, more knowable than ever. It was an immensely attractive image. In almost every other respect, I was happy to be me. I didn’t bother to ask who I might have been if my eyes were blue, like my sister’s, instead of brown. I didn’t ask whether I’d have been happier with a talent for music instead of languages. Only this one error in my genome would need to have been corrected, and I would have been me, only better.
Eventually, this perfect shadow-self faded away, for many reasons. But last year it came back to haunt me, as I read about a series of adverts placed by a company called Nucleus Genomics. Throughout the New York City subway system, Nucleus promised prospective parents that they could now have their “best baby”. By way of posters claiming that “height is 80% genetic” and “intelligence is 50%”, potential customers were led to a website detailing an expensive, comprehensive IVF procedure. Up to 20 embryos would be screened for every genetic disorder under the sun, but also for eye and hair colour, and for traits ranging from strength and longevity to insomnia and male-pattern baldness.
It was a sales pitch perfectly tailored to the present moment. We already seek to optimise ourselves in every way, through healthy, precisely monitored living. Through the measurement and quantification of exercise routines, nutrition and even sleep patterns, we can assess whether we are living our lives in the best possible way, so why not have the best baby as well? Although we may not be immortality-seeking billionaires, we are all constantly living under the relentless imperative to strive for human perfection, in our own generation and the next. And although it has taken on a new, consumerist form, centred on the individual self, that imperative has a familiar name: eugenics.
Genomics companies tend to avoid the label eugenics, and for good reason. Although the word derives from the Greek for “good birth”, in the wake of the second world war, eugenics was broadly disavowed as a racist, pseudo-scientific movement. Its stated aim was to improve the human species, but its most tangible results were the involuntary sterilisation and forcible institutionalisation of “inferior” people in many countries and, in Nazi Germany, the mass murder of people deemed a threat to the master race.
In the preceding decades, however, eugenics was popular among scientists, politicians and the general public. Although many of its champions were elitist, sexist and racist reactionaries, there were eugenic progressives, eugenic socialists and eugenically minded feminists. While some eugenicists advocated the forced sterilisation of people deemed unfit to reproduce, some advocated women’s right to birth control as a means of social improvement. After all, the belief that many traits in human beings were strongly hereditary was not incompatible with the belief that humans also needed good sanitary conditions, public health and welfare systems, and access to education if they were to realise their full potential.
It is impossible to understand the appeal of eugenics without realising that it held both utopian and dystopian elements. This is particularly important, because the return of eugenics also involves both. And eugenics really has returned, including under its old name. What may be called the neo-eugenic revival sometimes takes an explicitly racist, white-supremacist form. It talks about birthrates, IQ levels and the impending “civilisational collapse” of the west. It focuses on what it sees as distinct, unequal racial groups. It harkens back to classical eugenic dystopias, such as the influential American writer Madison Grant’s The Passing of the Great Race, published in 1916, an inspiration for Tom Buchanan’s racist rants in The Great Gatsby.
This form of neo-eugenics is easy to dismiss for people who think of themselves as enlightened. However, another form of neo-eugenics is arguably much more pervasive. It is careful about words and labels, and it eschews the state management of populations for a focus on individual freedom of choice. In one sense, this form of eugenics never really went away.
Towards the end of the last century, some philosophers and bioethicists began to defend what they called “liberal eugenics”. Nicholas Agar and Julian Savulescu are among the figures who have argued that this form of eugenics, driven by parental freedom of choice, is something entirely different from the repressive eugenics of the past, which sought to mobilise the state to marginalise or even exterminate entire groups.
The origins of this reorientation are much earlier. According to the historian Nathaniel Comfort, eugenics was already beginning to shift its attention from the population to the individual during the middle of the 20th century, in tandem with the rise of medical genetics. This was partly because repressive eugenic policies were controversial, and partly because medical genetics was a burgeoning science, very different from the pseudo-scientific assumptions of the past. In the US, eugenic records offices kept a hodgepodge of observations based on prejudices about race, class and gender. Medical genetics clinics were building knowledge and tools with actual, and growing, predictive power. Today, prenatal screening procedures have been part of standard medical practice for decades, mostly directed at the identification of disabilities and illnesses. Down syndrome is becoming very rare in countries that facilitate screening. Denmark, for instance, now sees the termination of over 95% of pregnancies where Down has been identified.
Of course we want the best for our children. In a neoliberal society, one obsessed with maxxing every aspect of life, the “best” might easily come to mean competitive advantage. A company such as Nucleus knows this. Playing on the term “generational wealth”, its website suggests that customers can purchase “generational health”, providing a kind of embodied insurance policy against deteriorating public health and social services. In the 20th century, eugenics was a project for the nation state; in the 21st century, it has reinvented itself as the logical extension of capitalist individualism.
There are still problems with the science. Nucleus’s claims about height and intelligence being genetic to a particular degree refer to population-level estimates of how much of the variation in a group is due to genetics (and are contested, at that). They do not mean “you can reliably decide how smart and tall your child will be”, even if that was a likely takeaway for some people. But in a way, applying population-level logic to individuals makes perfect sense. States need to manage their populations for instrumental purposes – to keep the economy growing, to avoid public health emergencies and to have enough soldiers available to fight wars.
For a long time, this management was carried out in paternalistic or authoritarian ways. But, as the philosopher Michel Foucault argued, a signal feature of the modern state is that it operates through governmentality – by providing the incentives for citizens to manage themselves in ways that align with state interests. If we, as individuals, freely decide to treat ourselves and our families as miniature populations to be optimised for health and productivity, that saves the state quite a lot of effort. But what does this mean for our sense of ourselves?
As the biologist and historian Adam Rutherford has pointed out, eugenics was always about control. The word itself was coined in 1883 by Francis Galton, a cousin of Charles Darwin who saw evolution as a process to be managed and directed. With the discovery of natural selection, it seemed obvious to Galton that “what nature does blindly, slowly, and ruthlessly, man may do providently, quickly, and kindly”, as he put it in his seminal 1904 essay, Eugenics: Its Definition, Scope, and Aims.
An enduring image from the early decades of the movement is the “eugenics tree” commissioned for the Second International Congress of Eugenics, held in New York City in 1921. Growing from roots labelled with disciplines across the natural sciences, social sciences and humanities, the tree is surrounded by the words “eugenics is the self direction of human evolution”. In that image, the accumulation of knowledge as well as biological processes are provided with a teleology. But what are their goals? What is all the control, management and optimisation really for?
To Galton, and to the generations of committed eugenicists who succeeded him, eugenics was politically and morally necessary in order to prevent societal disaster due to degeneration. Following earlier thinkers such as Thomas Malthus, they worried that too many poor and undesirable people were reproducing. In a short time, the superior peoples, whether defined as the upper class or as “Anglo-Saxons”, “Nordic types” or “Aryans”, would be outbred and outcompeted by their natural inferiors.
Eugenics’ proposal of wholesale management of the population was thus made in service of a particular ideal of humanity, where the universal “best” was defined in a strikingly narrow way. Through the notion of “hereditary genius”, Galton presented the privileges of wealth and class as innate qualities; while he explained undesirable traits such as “vagrancy” and “criminality” as the causes, rather than the consequences, of poverty, deprivation and marginalisation. Galton’s eugenic utopia was an idea that reflected the prejudices of a particular place and time.
The same is true of liberal eugenics in our own time. We may question whether the genomics companies’ promises of “best babies” are credible. But it may be more important to ask what their notion of the “best” is. What do they see as valuable and worthless in a human life?
Liberal eugenics accentuates the positive. In an attempt to distance itself from the forced sterilisations of the past, it prefers to focus, as Nucleus does, on human improvement and enhancement. But as Rutherford notes, in biology you cannot select for something without selecting against something else. Positive eugenics and negative eugenics are two sides of the same coin; without an idea of what is undesired, there can be no notion of the desirable.
For the Victorian eugenicists, the “best” was an amalgam of racial fantasies about “Nordic” or “Aryan” types conflated with the privileges of the upper classes, defined against the undesirable character of brown and black people, and the underclass. For the new eugenics in its liberal form, positive qualities coalesce around productivity and competitive advantage. The ideal human is strikingly close to the ideal worker, someone who is smart, efficient and unlikely to ever take a sick day.
Against this ideal stand the unwanted lives of people with disabilities and chronic illnesses. Intellectual disability was among eugenics’ biggest bugbears, but a range of other conditions recur as targets to be eradicated. In a way, this is unsurprising. Disability really does mean disadvantage. That is something I know in my bones – and my muscles. Disability, as the scholar Tom Shakespeare has written, is a predicament. It means limitation and restriction; it can mean pain and suffering. There are simple reasons why I longed so deeply for a cure. The reasons why and how that longing began to fade are more complex.
As it turned out, medical genetics really did produce an effective treatment for spinal muscular atrophy. About a decade ago, a drug called nusinersen was being developed. Some studies suggest that if it is administered early enough, it can wholly counteract the symptoms of the condition, while arresting its progression in adults. But medical genetics also proved that I didn’t have SMA after all. The original diagnosis was made on the basis of muscle biopsies and clinical guesswork. When a test for the genetic markers for SMA became available, mine came back negative. Instead, I was shown to have an even rarer condition – rarer, and less likely to attract research funding. I am tempted to quote Franz Kafka, who once remarked that there is infinite hope in the universe, only not for us.
But, in truth, that isn’t quite apt. Losing both the original diagnosis and the possibility of a treatment felt like a wave of sorrow, tinged with relief. Strange as it may seem, it also gave me a greater sense of freedom, that my life was really my own.
Don’t get me wrong. If there was an actual cure for my condition, I would take it. But there won’t be one, at least not for me. Too much time has passed; too much of my life is behind me. It is my life as it unfolded, and I try my best not to compare it to lives I didn’t live.
It is easier to think this way in your forties than in your teens. In the company of my nondisabled friends, I see plenty of injuries, illnesses and vaguely defined aches. We all have the markings of life. It’s not exactly that my disability ceases to matter as I grow older. In one way, it’s quite the opposite, as I feel the physical impact of the world on my muscles and joints. But I do feel a sense of convergence with my kith and my kin about the tenuousness and frailty of it all, about the need to take care of each other, as we hurtle towards what is coming.
Call it a kind of realism. Those of us who have kids know another side of it. If you plan to have a particular kind of child, you are setting yourself up for failure. Every parent I know has had to abandon their notions of what they thought their children would be for the reality of their particular children. I don’t think any one of them subscribed to the idea of an ideal baby. I hope they didn’t. Such an ideal is a terrible thing for parents as well as children to live up to.
This is the most corrosive effect of liberal neo-eugenics: in positing that an individual ideal of embodiment is something that can be specified, quantified and realised, it creates a framework for torturing both our children and ourselves. Why are we not this perfect thing? Why are we not fitter, happier, more productive? I’m not particularly sentimental about the value of disability in any particular case, but I think it is crucial to acknowledge disability as part of human variation. In treating ever more traits and qualities as things to be measured, ranked and diagnosed, we are doing the opposite – turning variation itself into something like disability.
For me, hope comes from working to change the world so that it accommodates imperfection. One of the reasons I dislike liberal eugenics is that its individualist ethos runs counter to political measures that have mattered immensely in my lifetime. I believe we should direct our efforts toward making better societies rather than making better people.
During the postwar era, in parallel with the eugenic shift from the population level to the individual level, disability began to become a socio-political issue rather than a medical one. What the sociologist Mike Oliver once called the “personal tragedy theory” of disability was challenged by a social model that explained how people with a range of different impairments and illnesses were made disabled by societal structures.
Essentially, what constitutes “disability” varies with place and time. Although dyslexia can be hugely disadvantageous in the modern world, in a nonliterate society it amounts only to neurological difference. The kind of mobility impairment that I have – that is, being unable to walk for more than a few steps, or get up from the floor – is restricting under any circumstances. But it is orders of magnitude more disabling in a society without wheelchairs, or wheelchair accessibility. In between these extremes, there are conditions, illnesses and impairments that amount to disability in some contexts but not in others.
The goal is not to abolish cures, but to abolish the idea that only cures, or the prenatal optimisation of an embryo, can make for a life worth living. For the disability movement, the aim has always been to make a better world for everyone: a world where people with all kinds of bodies can thrive and flourish. That includes both people who were born disabled and people who had disability thrust upon them. It is a project that accounts for human variation, and the variability of life.
That is why it stands opposed to the neo-eugenic notion that there is a “best baby”; the best, in the singular, is not something the human species should be striving towards at all. It also bears remembering that the majority of disabilities do not stem from wholly genetic causes, but from an interaction of human genetic variation with the wear and tear of the world. There are good reasons to research cures, treatments and interventions whenever possible; there are equally good reasons to temper our expectations for how the human species may be perfected.
Rosemarie Garland-Thomson, a scholar of disability and bioethics, has put forward the “case for conserving disability”. It is a provocative case, for the obvious reason that disability, and chronic illness, are qualities which entail vulnerability and dependence on others. But, then again, so does the human condition. We are born helpless, and we age into helplessness. Even if we come into the world equipped for perfect health, we are always at risk of illness and injury. Neo-eugenics offers a vision of total independence, of a disconnect from society. Measured against such an ideal, all of us fall short. However strong and self-reliant we may think ourselves to be, we are a social species, with few prospects of surviving, let alone thriving, on our own.
The aim of control, and so of predictability, is intrinsic to eugenics’ notion of the ideal society. But who wants to live in a fully controlled, fully predictable world? A world where an external entity tells you how to live your life down to the last detail, what to eat, when and where to move, what to watch, all in the name of becoming your best possible self? Oh, right.
Against this vision of total algorithmic control, we must appeal to the unpredictability of the human condition. Shortly after the second world war, Hannah Arendt wrote her magnum opus The Origins of Totalitarianism, in which she traced the construction of “superfluous people” – whole swathes of the population made disenfranchised and killable by states that saw them as useless at best and dangerous at worst. Eugenics was central to this idea of superfluousness: of people who were incidental to the future of the species, or the nation, or the race.
Arendt described totalitarianism as, among other things, a vision for the absolute closure of the future, against all alternatives. In a subsequent book, titled The Human Condition, she laid out the alternative principle, by which human societies could grow and develop. That principle was plurality – the encounter with difference. Only this encounter provided the possibility for what Arendt saw as humanity’s highest calling – namely action: something with unforeseeable consequences and unpredictable results.
With her notion of plurality, Arendt was not referring to disability as such. But the concept can be extended to human embodiment. As humans, we are very much alike, but we are not the same. We may share the same bodily needs that must be met if we are to flourish, but our varying capabilities, talents and preferences mean that flourishing may look very different from one case to the next. Against the narrow-minded eugenic idea of “the best baby”, we can perhaps set another concept of Arendt’s: what she called natality. With each birth, with each new person, something wholly unique comes into being. And the world is made anew.

summary: For decades the idea of eugenics has been taboo. Now it is returning in a new commercial guise For a very long time, I dreamed of being cured. I was born in 1981. I learned to walk early enough, but I stumbled and fell more easily than other children. My parents began to worry that something was wrong, that my muscles were weaker than they should be. Eventually, at the age of three, I was diagnosed with a form of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). In the 1980s, the precise mechanics were not yet understood, but the condition was known to be hereditary, probably linked to a recessive gene. It was also known to be progressive. As I aged, my muscles would not keep pace. At eight, I began to use a wheelchair for longer distances. By the time I was 18, I rarely walked outdoors any more. It is hard…

content:
Earlier today, I set a puzzle by UCLA professor Terry Tao, who is widely regarded as one of the world’s top mathematicians.
Here it is again with solutions.
The magic money plant
In an online game, you earn coins by harvesting from plants. There are two types of plant:
a regular plant produces a single coin per day
a mother plant produces a single coin and two seeds per day. (A seed will grow into a regular plant the following day.)
At the start of the game, a player has a certain number of mother plants, regular plants and coins, but not more than nine of each.
Suppose that I begin on Day 1 with a mother plants, b regular plants and c coins.
1. How many coins do I have in total at the end of days 2 and 3?
2. Find an expression for how many coins I have at the end of Day X.
3. At the end of Day 10 I have 427 coins. What are a, b and c?
Solution
1. Day 2: 4a + 2b + c. Day 3: 9a + 3b + c
Workings: At the end of day 1 the number of coins is is a + b + c. Each mother plant has also produced 2 seeds, but these have not yet grown into regular plants. On day 2, these plants produce a coin each, so there are 2a of these, added to another a from the mother plant and the a from day 1, makng 4a. The regular plants produce another coin each, making b in total to add to the b from day 1. This gets us 4a + 2b + c for day 2, and the same reasoning gets us the above expression for day 3.
2. aX2 + bX + c
We calculated for X = 1, 2 and 3. You hopefully saw the pattern emerge. The number of coins produced by the mother plant and her descendants is the square of the day.
3. a = 4, b = 2, c= 7.
When X = 10, there are 427 coins. Thus
100a + 10b + c = 427. So a, b and c must be 4, 2 and 7. The answer was in the question!
Tao said he suggested this puzzle because he likes the way it naturally introduces algebraic ways of thinking as the most efficient way to solve a problem.
“It turns out that the number of coins at day X is given by a polynomial, aX2 + bX + c. In modern algebra, we have realized that polynomials are very similar to numbers in many ways: for instance, one can add and multiply two polynomials together much as one can add and multiply numbers. For this problem, it is more than an analogy: on day 10 (X=10), the value of the polynomial aX2 + bX + c is just the three-digit number abc (assuming that a,b, and c are at most nine). So one can now read off the desired unknowns a, b, c just by inspecting the digits 4, 2, and 7 of the given coin value 427.”
The idea that polynomials behave like numbers is one of the themes of Tao’s first book for a general audience, Six Maths Essentials.
I hope you enjoyed today’s puzzle. I’ll be back in two weeks.
Six Maths Essentials by Terence Tao is out tomorrow. You can buy it at the Guardian Bookshop.
I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

content:
Meg Hamon says she hopes her story might help others who struggle with excessive drinking and partying
Published
Meg Hamon was struggling with her self-confidence after she began to rely on partying and drinking to get by.
The problems began to develop during the Covid-19 pandemic and then continued until the start of this year when Hamon decided a change was needed as she was going to turn 30, she said.
Since then, she had focused on exercising through activities such as gym workouts and running, as well as going to therapy to improve her wellbeing, she added.
Hamon said: "Exercise has helped me massively with my confidence... If I'm ever feeling low, a good gym session will always help."
'I was struggling'
Hamon felt her problems had been growing for some time before she decided to take action to make a change in her life.
She said: "I think my lowest was Covid. I think that was like a struggle for everyone and I just had gone through quite a bad breakup.
"I was struggling with that and I just think I'd never really processed my emotion.
"I really neglected myself mentally and physically... but I just never really noticed how unhappy I was until I started to make a change."
Hamon said she had felt the benefits on focusing on her physical and mental wellbeing since making lifestyle changes.
She said: "Even if I had just done the therapy – it would be incredible... but I think the exercise side has just helped me massively with my confidence."
Hamon has been sharing her experiences on social media as well, adding : "If it inspires one person to make a change, then I think it's really important to do that as well.
"If you get stuck in the same cycle... I just think you can find so many other things to do than going out and just drinking excessively."
Therapist Sally Agathangelou says younger people are more open to getting support
Hamon has been going to therapist Sally Agathangelou as part of her work to improve her wellbeing.
Agathangelou said: "It could be various issues, it can be drinking, it can be gambling, it can be drugs, it can be self-harm - but it's all bridges for coping."
"I'm really quite proud of this generation because they are very open to therapy," she added.
"I'm very, very proud of them because I can support, but it's down to them at the end of the day to make that change."

content:
Consultant doctors in England are to stage a two-day strike next month in a dispute over pay and working conditions.
The walkout will begin on 25 November at 06:59 GMT, with consultants staffing emergency care only.
This is known as Christmas Day cover and is likely to have a major impact on most routine and elective or planned services.
The announcement comes after talks had been taking place with the government over the past month, following the vote in favour of strike action by British Medical Association members in July.
Consultants – the most senior doctors in hospitals – were given a 3.5% pay increase this year.
But the BMA argues pay has fallen by a quarter over the past 17 years, once inflation is taken into account.
The union also wants a reduction in the standard working week, from 40 to 35 hours, and higher pay for out-of-hours work, alongside changes to pensions, including greater flexibility over when they can be taken.
Expect disruption
In a joint statement, BMA consultants committee co-chairs Dr Helen Neary and Dr Shanu Datta, said they had tried to negotiate with the government in "good faith", but "time-and-time again ministers have kicked the can down the road".
"Unfortunately, that road has now run out, and we have been forced to announce strikes.
"Consultants take their responsibilities incredibly seriously, and striking does not come naturally, but we are hearing loud and clear from the profession that they have had enough."
Average earnings for consultants top £150,000 a year.
Basic pay starts at £113,500, with the most experienced getting £150,500.
But many earn tens of thousands in extra payments and awards.
In the strike ballot, 76% of consultants who took part voted in favour of strike action, with just over half of eligible BMA members taking part.
The government says this represents only around one in five consultants employed by the NHS in England voting for strike action, as nearly half are not BMA members.
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the government had been in "constructive discussions" with the BMA so it was "disappointing" the strike dates had been announced.
She said taking strike action would be "irresponsible" and "place the health service under even greater pressure".
The strike announcement comes as consultants and other doctors are taking part in strike action during November in Northern Ireland.
Consultants last took strike action in England in 2023. The long-running dispute involving resident doctors in England came to an end earlier this year after more than three years of on-and-off strike action.

content:
Today’s puzzle is set by Terence Tao, who may be the world’s most famous mathematician.
Tao, aged 51, has been a global phenomenon since the age of ten, when he became the youngest competitor at the International Maths Olympiad, a record he still holds. For the last three decades he has been a professor at UCLA, where he has been garlanded with prizes, and where one of his colleagues famously said: “Terry is like Mozart: mathematics just flows out of him.”
Tao is a very visible leader of the field, not only because of his scientific contributions and collaborations, but also because he writes the most widely-read blog in research level maths. When Open AI earlier this month stunned the community with the release of hundreds of proofs of long-standing open questions – the “mathpocalypse” – his blog has become one of the most important forums for the community’s response.
This week Tao publishes Six Maths Essentials, his first work aimed at a general audience. The puzzle below reflects ideas in the book.
He said: “I like this puzzle in that it naturally introduces algebraic ways of thinking as the most efficient way to solve the problem: working out small examples by hand can give some valuable initial intuition, but it will be algebra that lets you solve the entire problem in a civilized amount of time.”
The magic money plant
In an online game, you earn coins by harvesting from plants. There are two types of plant:
a regular plant produces a single coin per day
a mother plant produces a single coin and two seeds per day. (A seed will grow into a regular plant the following day.)
At the start of the game, a player has a certain number of mother plants, regular plants and coins, but not more than nine of each.
Suppose that I begin on Day 1 with a mother plants, b regular plants and c coins.
1. How many coins do I have in total at the end of days 2 and 3?
2. Find an expression for how many coins I have at the end of Day X.
3. At the end of Day 10 I have 427 coins. What are a, b and c?
I’ll be back at 5pm UK with the solutions – and Tao will explain what it all means.
PLEASE NO SPOILERS Instead discuss the mathpocalypse.
Six Maths Essentials by Terence Tao is out tomorrow. You can buy it at the Guardian Bookshop.
I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

content:
Lucy says she noticed changes in her skin and hair (left photo) alongside symptoms including fatigue and hair loss when her ferritin levels were low. Lighting and shadows also play a part
Published
"Do you have ferritin face?" a young woman asks on TikTok, pointing to dark circles, washed-out skin and brittle hair, alongside before-and-after style photographs. The content creator puts these features down to her iron levels.
It is one of a growing number of videos and posts on TikTok and Instagram claiming that low ferritin - a protein which stores iron in the body - can leave visible clues on your face.
Users list pale or grey-looking skin, dark under-eye circles, dry or cracked lips, hair shedding and weak nails, while others share portraits claiming stark visual differences.
The phrase "ferritin face" has spread widely across social media, with videos attracting millions of views.
But doctors say appearance alone cannot diagnose iron deficiency.
"Ferritin face is not a medical diagnosis," said GP Dr Aziza Sesay, who is based in the West Midlands. "However, it may be a clue to tell us that something is going on."
Pale skin, hair shedding or brittle nails can accompany low iron, but can also be signs of other conditions, she told BBC News.
What is ferritin?
Your ferritin levels show how good your body's iron stores are, while haemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells which carries oxygen. When haemoglobin is low, the blood cannot carry as much oxygen - a condition known as anaemia.
But iron stores can become depleted before that happens, meaning someone can be iron-deficient and have symptoms without being anaemic.
Can you tell your ferritin levels from your face?
"You've got no stored iron but you're maintaining your haemoglobin. That's the big disconnect," said consultant haematologist Dr Drew Provan.
Dr Sue Pavord, also a consultant haematologist, said iron deficiency is common and often under-diagnosed in women.
UK guidelines from the British Society of Gastroenterology say ferritin below 15 micrograms per litre indicates absent iron stores, while below 30 generally indicates low iron stores.
Social media users have shared posts and videos claiming that low ferritin can cause visible changes to the face
Lucy M, 32, who posts about hair loss as @marvluceskin on Instagram and TikTok, said "ferritin face" seemed to describe changes she had noticed in herself.
In 2021 she developed heart palpitations, fatigue and hair loss. After being told her blood tests were normal and being diagnosed with generalised anxiety disorder, a later test showed her ferritin was 12 micrograms per litre.
Lucy said she looked "grey" and her hair had become dull and brittle.
She shared photographs with the BBC from when her ferritin was low, compared to when it had recovered, and said the difference between how she felt and looked was "night and day".
Can low iron change your face?
Videos about "ferritin face" often encourage viewers to look for a combination of physical signs - from dark circles and pale skin to dry lips, thinning hair and brittle nails - and compare them with their own appearance.
"You're not ugly, your ferritin is low", one creator says, pointing to the camera.
Provan said it was "impossible" to determine someone's ferritin levels from how their face looks.
People who are significantly anaemic may look pale, he explained, while fatigue can contribute to dark circles, but these visual signs are "subjective and unreliable".
In people with darker skin, changes in skin colour may be less obvious, Sesay added, meaning someone looking specifically for the signs described online could miss iron deficiency.
Doctors say appearance alone cannot tell you whether your ferritin is low, and that iron deficiency should be confirmed with a blood test
Awareness or misinformation?
For doctors, symptoms and how someone feels are more useful than appearance.
Blood tests matter not only to confirm iron deficiency, Provan and Sesay said, but to establish the cause and guide treatment.
Both said treatment should also address the cause. Heavy periods, low dietary iron, gastrointestinal blood loss and problems absorbing iron through the gut can all play a role.
Iron deficiency is commonly treated with oral iron. Pavord said iron tablets are best taken on an empty stomach, ideally first thing in the morning, and advised avoiding tea or coffee around the time they are taken because they can inhibit iron absorption.
Iron can also be obtained naturally from foods including meat, beans, lentils, leafy green vegetables and fortified cereals.
Taking iron supplements without a diagnosis can be harmful, while self-treating could delay the investigation of an underlying problem.
Lucy said social media has nevertheless helped women take symptoms more seriously, and has given some the confidence to ask questions when something feels wrong.
"There are so many women saying, 'Oh my gosh, this is me," she said, adding that she is not a doctor and presents her content as her own experience.
For her, doing so has been empowering - giving women information with which to advocate for themselves.
Sesay called social media a "double-edged sword" - it can encourage people to seek help, but can also lead them to incorrectly diagnose themselves from a short video.
For Lucy, the useful part is not diagnosing yourself from your appearance, but knowing when something doesn't feel right, and when to ask questions.

หมายเหตุประเพทไทยสัปดาห์นี้ ปองขวัญ สวัสดิภักดิ์ และ ต่อศักดิ์ จินดาสุขศรี ชวนอ่านบทความ “Birds of a Feather: Anand Panyarachun, Elite Families and Network Monarchy in Thailand” ของ Yoshinori Nishizaki จากมหาวิทยาลัยแห่งชาติสิงคโปร์ (NUS) ตีพิมพ์ใน Journal of Southeast Asian Studies ปี 2020 บทความนำสำนวน “Birds of a Feather” หรือคนที่มีลักษณะคล้ายกันมักรวมกลุ่มกัน มาใช้สำรวจความสัมพันธ์ระหว่างตระกูลชนชั้นนำของไทย และขยายความเข้าใจแนวคิด “Network Monarchy” หรือ “สถาบันกษัตริย์เชิงเครือข่าย” ที่ Duncan McCargo เสนอไว้ก่อนหน้านี้
Nishizaki เสนอว่า การทำความเข้าใจเครือข่ายดังกล่าวไม่ควรมองเฉพาะความจงรักภักดี อุดมการณ์ หรือระบบอุปถัมภ์ แต่ต้องพิจารณา สายเลือด การแต่งงาน และความสัมพันธ์ระหว่างตระกูลเชื้อพระวงศ์กับตระกูลขุนนางและข้าราชการชั้นสูง ที่สืบเนื่องมาหลายชั่วอายุคน เครือข่ายเหล่านี้มีรากมาก่อนการเปลี่ยนแปลงการปกครอง พ.ศ. 2475 และสามารถปรับตัวเข้าสู่ระบบราชการ กองทัพ ศาล และสถาบันทางการเมืองหลังเปลี่ยนระบอบ ผู้เขียนจึงเสนอว่า Network Monarchy หลัง พ.ศ. 2516 ไม่ได้ถูกสร้างขึ้นใหม่ทั้งหมด แต่เติบโตต่อยอดจากเครือข่ายชนชั้นนำที่มีอยู่เดิม
บทความใช้ อานันท์ ปันยารชุน เป็นกรณีศึกษาหลัก เพื่อติดตามว่าเครือญาติของครอบครัวหนึ่งเชื่อมโยงไปยังราชสกุล ตระกูลข้าราชการ นักการเมือง กองทัพ และองค์กรสำคัญได้อย่างไร ก่อนขยายไปสำรวจตระกูลอื่น ๆ เพื่อให้เห็นโครงสร้างที่กว้างกว่าความสัมพันธ์ของบุคคลสำคัญเพียงไม่กี่คน อย่างไรก็ตาม ผู้เขียนไม่ได้เสนอว่าคนในเครือข่ายทั้งหมดมีอุดมการณ์เดียวกัน หรือได้รับคำสั่งจากศูนย์กลางเดียว เพราะสมาชิกในครอบครัวเดียวกันอาจอยู่คนละฝ่ายทางการเมืองได้ ประเด็นสำคัญคือ ความสัมพันธ์ทางครอบครัวสามารถทำหน้าที่เป็นโครงสร้างพื้นฐานที่ช่วยให้ชนชั้นนำรักษาความต่อเนื่องของสถานะและอิทธิพลข้ามยุคสมัย
จากแนวคิด Network Monarchy บทความจึงไปถึงข้อเสนอเรื่อง “Royalist Family Network State” หรือรัฐที่เครือข่ายครอบครัวฝ่ายนิยมเจ้ามีส่วนเป็นรากฐานของโครงสร้างอำนาจ ชวนมองการเมืองไทยไม่เพียงมองผ่านรัฐบาล รัฐสภา กองทัพ หรือศาล แต่รวมถึงสายสัมพันธ์ทางสังคมและครอบครัวที่เชื่อมบุคคลในสถาบันเหล่านั้นเข้าหากัน คำถามสำคัญจึงอยู่ที่ว่า เครือญาติ การแต่งงาน และตระกูลชนชั้นนำช่วยอธิบายความต่อเนื่องของอำนาจทางการเมืองไทยได้มากน้อยเพียงใด และแนวคิด Network Monarchy จะเปลี่ยนไปอย่างไร เมื่อเรามองผ่าน “ครอบครัว” มากกว่าบุคคลเพียงไม่กี่คน ติดตามได้ใน #หมายเหตุประเพทไทย #อานันท์ปันยารชุน

content:
A report found complementary therapy sessions rose from 405 in 2021 to a record 965 in 2025
Published
A cancer charity has seen an increase in demand for wellbeing support over the past five years, a reports says.
Macmillan Cancer Support Jersey published its annual report, external which looked back at the charity's work during 2025 and the progress made over its five year strategy period from 2021 to 2025.
The charity said counselling and higher-level emotional-support sessions more than doubled in Jersey from 407 in 2021 to 835 in 2025 - an increase of 105%.
Steph Gibaut, chief executive officer of Macmillan Jersey, said: "Behind every figure in this report is a person, a family and a moment when support mattered".
She added: "Over the past five years, we have transformed the way we support people affected by cancer.
"We are identifying needs earlier, offering more personalised care and providing a wider range of emotional, practical and wellbeing support."
The report found complementary therapy sessions rose from 405 in 2021 to a record 965 in 2025, representing an increase of 138%.
It also found the charity delivered 4,253 support sessions to Islanders affected by cancer in 2025.
Additionally, 308 people accessed its drop-in cancer support and wellbeing centre without a referral.
The charity said over its five-year strategy period it generated £4.38m in income and invested £3.44m in delivering and developing services for Islanders affected by cancer.
'Demand continues to grow'
Macmillan Cancer Support Jersey said a major development was the introduction of holistic needs assessments which was formally launched after a pilot.
It said these helped identify a person's "physical, emotional, practical and financial needs earlier in their cancer experience, allowing an individual care plan to be put in place"
The report also showed the charity raised £963,090 in 2025 and invested £890,352 in its work.
The charity said fundraising highlights included the Tour des Pyrénées, which saw 52 cyclists complete a coast-to-coast challenge and raise a "record-breaking" £236,000 for the charity.
Gibaut said: "We are incredibly proud of what has been achieved, but we also know that demand continues to grow and people's needs are changing."
It said the new 2026 to 2030 strategy would focus on expanding emotional, wellbeing and group support and expanding services for people living with and beyond cancer.

Dr Sarah Redvers brought a claim of constructive dismissal
Published
A doctor who raised concerns about the treatment of children questioning their gender has told the BBC she was accused of transphobia, bullied and harassed out of her child protection job in the NHS.
Dr Sarah Redvers, who was a named safeguarding GP, said she faced a brutal investigation after she passed on complaints brought to her by other doctors.
Speaking publicly for the first time, Redvers said she felt she was "silenced" for doing her job after questioning whether another GP was appropriately assessing the needs of young people who were distressed about their gender identity.
She has brought a claim of constructive dismissal against the NHS Sussex Integrated Care Board (ICB), which managed health services in the county, and Adam Doyle, who was the ICB's chief executive until 2025.
Redvers told a three-week employment tribunal hearing that she felt the focus on investigating her meant issues of patient safety had been sidelined.
"I was just bewildered really that the medical and safeguarding issues were completely lost," she said. "It's really risky," she told the BBC.
NHS Surrey and Sussex said: "We recognise that some employment processes should have been handled differently." They have apologised to Redvers.
In June 2026, nearly six years after she first raised concerns, a separate NHS safety investigation found that dozens of children, some as young as 13, had been inappropriately prescribed drugs at the WellBN practice, the clinic where the other doctor worked.
The report said 78 children had potentially been harmed after puberty-blocking drugs and cross sex hormones were prescribed to them without proper checks.
The report said it was in response to a drug review carried out in autumn 2024, not to the concerns first raised by Redvers years earlier.
NHS England said: "It is totally unacceptable young people were put at risk of harm because some practitioners at the WellBN practice provided care they were not commissioned to deliver by the NHS."
"To read about a medical scandal knowing it could have been stopped was upsetting," said Redvers, "because concerns were raised appropriately and leaders knew about it".
Redvers, who has many years of experience working with vulnerable groups, was a named safeguarding GP for Sussex, which meant other doctors who had safety concerns about patients could turn to her for advice and help.
The tribunal heard that in July 2020, a doctor got in touch because she was worried about a patient who had gone to an online clinic which was registered overseas.
It wanted the GP to take over prescribing testosterone to a vulnerable 18-year-old female, who was distressed about her gender.
The doctor was also given advice on such prescriptions by a Brighton GP, Dr Sam Hall.
"The concerns to me were that Hall was recommending treatment for patients that he hadn't assessed, that he hadn't met, and that other GPs were uncomfortable with prescribing," Redvers said.
Redvers spoke to NHS England (NHSE) and was advised to make the complaint as a whistleblower.
It was investigated and NHSE said it was satisfied with Hall's practice.
Over the following months several other GPs voiced their concerns to Redvers about the quality of assessments, the prescription of puberty blocking drugs and cross sex hormones, and the lack of specialist supervision at the WellBN clinic, where Hall was based.
Again, the NHS investigated her concerns. She said she was also told by the investigator that there was a "general worry" that there "would be allegations of transphobia."
Hall, who is a trans man and was born female, qualified as a GP in 2019 and is known as a campaigner for transgender rights in Brighton.
Publicly, he had said that his own pain had shown him the importance of "affirmative care" - support for a patient in a way which accepts rather than challenges their preferred gender and treatment decisions follow from that.
He was also working with the NHS locally on setting up a Trans Health hub and with a Brighton trans support charity called The Clare Project.
The second NHS investigation considered "the full scope" of Hall's work and concluded there was no cause for concern. It also said there was "one colleague whose persistent interest in the issue appeared disproportionate." Redvers took that to mean her.
The concerns she said she and others were raising were about the quality of care being provided, and whether it had the necessary medical evidence to underpin it, not her views on gender.
"It's about medical assessment and treatment of patients, which is something we have to get right, particularly in this complex group of vulnerable patients," she said.
She said she viewed any suggestion of transphobia as "appalling," and it was "dangerous" that such claims were obscuring the medical and safeguarding issues she was raising.
In 2021, whilst waiting for the outcome of the second investigation and prompted by a concern raised by local mental health services about the care of a vulnerable 15-year-old, Redvers referred Hall to the medical regulator, the GMC.
Hall emailed Adam Doyle, then CEO of NHS Sussex, directly to complain.
"I am being victimised here, and I need proper protection from this individual and their repeated attempts to disrupt my career" he said.
Adam Doyle, was chief executive of the NHS Sussex Integrated Care Board until 2025
Although Doyle at first denied to the tribunal he knew Hall before this, it emerged during the tribunal that he had previously had a number of mentoring meetings with the GP.
The GMC investigation was not taken forward. However, the NHS launched an investigation into Redvers, bringing in an external investigator.
The tribunal heard she was called to what she described as a "brutal" four-hour interrogation.
"It was oppressive, very upsetting. I didn't feel I had the chance at all to explain what had happened," she said. "I broke down at one point".
She said she was off sick for several months as a result and received treatment for trauma.
Other colleagues who were interviewed as part of the investigation into Redvers also complained about the process and the NHS upheld most of their complaints.
The investigation concluded the CEO and trust should apologise to Redvers.
It also warned that Redvers' treatment would have a "broader negative impact" on the willingness of staff to raise concerns.
In 2023, a year after the grievance outcome, when a trans campaigner suggested in an NHS meeting that she was transphobic, Redvers told the tribunal she felt the NHS did not do enough to support her. She felt she had no choice but to leave her job as a safeguarding GP.
"I just felt there's no way I could carry on working in this organisation," she told the BBC.
At about that time, a group of parents, school governors and social workers began raising concerns about WellBn and Hall.
The co-founder of campaign group PSHE Brighton, Rachel Cashman, said: "It is a travesty that Sarah Redvers was punished for doing her job safeguarding and expecting the best standards of care for gender distressed children."
Redvers is now waiting for the outcome of her employment tribunal. She may not get the judgment for several months.
She described what has happened as "personally and professionally difficult" and said the NHS "needs to remember that patients come first" and it should "listen to staff who raise legitimate concerns."
In a statement NHS Surrey and Sussex said: "We engaged professionally and supportively with the Employment Tribunal. We recognise that some employment processes should have been handled differently and have apologised whilst Dr Redvers was employed with us, before, and during the hearings. We await the findings of the tribunal to make any further comment."
NHS England said: "When concerns about prescribing practices by an individual GP were escalated to NHS England national directors in 2023, they met directly with an affected family and asked regional professional standards leads to undertake formal investigations.
"Wider concerns were subsequently identified, and the WellBN practice was asked to stop providing a specialised prescribing service. Further new information led to NHS England and NHS Sussex initiating an independent patient safety investigation in 2025."
Dr Sam Hall and WellBN have been contacted for comment.
In response to the investigation report in June, WellBN said it recognised "the seriousness and sensitivity of the matters raised" and that its priority remained providing "compassionate, safe and effective care for all patients".

content:
Hollie Sharman spent hours searching symptoms, feeling panicked and isolated
Published
Hollie Sharman was convinced she was dying. She would go to hospital "four to five times a week" complaining of excruciating chest pain.
"I think the longest I spent in A&E was 13 hours," says the 25-year-old. But despite numerous tests, doctors could never find anything wrong.
Sharman says she had "always worried" about her health as a child and remembers "making up any excuse" to get sent home from school and get into bed.
Her 22nd birthday meal was spent in the restaurant toilets "having the worst panic attack I've ever had".
That triggered years of health anxiety, with hours spent searching symptoms, feeling panicked and isolated.
Constantly Googling symptoms
"I was constantly Googling and using ChatGPT, every source I could get that could tell me what was wrong," she says.
"I spent so long in the hospital. They'd tell me it's nothing, they'd check everything.
"I'd go home, but then my legs would feel weak, so I'd Google that and then it would say it's a sign of heart failure. So I'd go back, it was literally a constant cycle."
At its worst, she "completely disconnected from everyone" and wouldn't reply to messages from family to avoid repetitive conversations.
Sharman says her health anxiety also had an extreme affect on her relationship.
"It got to the point that nothing he said would be the right thing.
"I would get upset because he didn't understand what was going on inside my own head. How can you tell someone everything's fine when I think I'm actually dying?"
Dr Schnack says health anxiety is an "obsessional worry" about being seriously ill
Clinical psychologist Dr Kirren Schnack says health anxiety is "a constant worry about being seriously ill or becoming seriously ill when you are not".
Key signs can be "checking" behaviours, such as frequently examining your body, taking your temperature, blood pressure or researching symptoms online.
Another is constantly asking the internet, friends or family for reassurance that you are safe and healthy, she tells Complex with Kimberley Wilson.
Others may experience "avoidance" - not looking at their body or going to doctors appointments because they fear "the worst".
Some may "take on the persona of somebody who has an illness", she adds.
"You may slow down your movements and stop exercising, you're treating yourself and your body and mind as if you are already ill."
Sharman says her parents understand her condition more after watching the videos she makes about health anxiety on TikTok
Sharman was eventually diagnosed with health anxiety and health-related obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD). She says her family and partner have been "incredibly supportive" and have helped her get to a "better place" with techniques to manage her anxiety.
"I'd write down my symptoms like 'chest pain, excruciating'. And then at the end of the day, I'd write that I was fine.
"And then next time I'd have it, I'd have something to read and I'd be like, but I thought I was dying then and I wasn't."
Sharman says her health anxiety "doesn't control her life any more".
"You need to push yourself and do things when you're anxious, don't put your life on hold because I did for so many years."
How to manage health anxiety
Dr Schnack says if you have a symptom that is "new, concerning or doesn't go away", it is "responsible health behaviour" to check the NHS website.
If a symptom has not gone away within two weeks, she advises making a GP appointment. Here's when to call 111, 999 or go to A&E.
And here are some tips from Dr Schnack that might help:
Challenge worst-case thinking - give your brain other explanations for physical sensations; a stiff back might be poor posture rather than a serious illness.
Limit reassurance-seeking - set rules and time limits on how often you ask friends or family about symptoms, and stick to them.
Burn off anxious energy - take quick bursts of movement, like jumping jacks, to help process adrenaline and cortisol.
Ground yourself - use strong sensory experiences such as holding an ice cube or tasting something sour or spicy.
Breathing techniques - take a long breath through your nose, add a second inhale at the top and release it with a long sigh through your mouth.

content:
Wendy Rhein is trying to round up the sheep hanging out among the hazelnut and walnut trees of her Chutzpah Hollow farm in Tryon, North Carolina.
“Hi, Brea. Come on down. I hear you,” Rhein calls to the bleating queen of the flock. If the Barbados black belly ewe moves, the rest will follow.
Brea, a bottle-fed lamb named Hadassah and their flock mates bound down the hill when Rhein rustles a box of kosher tea biscuits. The small treat reveals something different about this farm. Rhein is remarkable for several reasons: she’s a female farmer in a male-dominated industry and a single mother who had no farming experience when she launched her farm at age 52. She’s also Jewish.
Rhein, who also works as vice-president of a faith-based advocacy organization, is part of a renewed interest among Jews in farming as an expression of their religion, culture or values. Shani Mink, co-founder of the Jewish Farmer Network, often hears “Jewish farmer – isn’t that an oxymoron?” Mink’s organization serves about 1,800 farmers, most of them first-generation agriculturalists, and offers conferences, classes and farm-to-table Shabbat dinners.
There is no solid estimate of the number of Jewish farmers in the country; the US Department of Agriculture’s census of the farming workforce doesn’t collect data on religion. But as Mink points out: “Jews have been farmers from time immemorial. The Jewish tradition is an agrarian tradition” – evidenced by how many holidays, such as the autumn harvest celebration Sukkoth, are tied to the agricultural calendar.
The Jewish Agricultural Society, chartered in 1900, helped people facing persecution in eastern Europe relocate to US farmland, where they could gain skills and independence. By 1933, more than 100,000 Jews earned some or all of their living from farming, according to Gary Moore, professor emeritus at North Carolina State University. But as the US population shifted away from agricultural work, many Jewish people moved into cities and suburbs. Some are returning to rural environments and family roots to farm, inspired by principles of their faith and building better food systems.
Rhein grew up in Detroit, the daughter of a man who was raised on a dairy farm he couldn’t wait to leave. In contrast, she loved the idea of raising livestock and being closer to her food sources; she challenged herself to prepare every ingredient she and her two sons, Nathan and Samuel, consumed, down to the ketchup, while living in a high-rise with a kitchen “the size of a postage stamp” in Washington DC. When the pandemic hit, she started to search for land and research a new venture selling starter flocks of sheep.
Her brother, who lives about 45 minutes away in Asheville, showed her properties for sale over FaceTime. “I did not step foot on to this land or into this house until the day of our closing,” she said. Now she owns a 10-acre property.
Despite rising Jewish interest in land stewardship, Mink noted that most Jewish growers are “the only Jewish person in their farming community or the only farming person in their Jewish community”. In Rhein’s case, the nearest synagogue is almost an hour away. For her, that means “how I practice being a Jew on a day-to-day basis is how I farm and how I am attached to and care for this land”.
Rhein donates 10% of everything she raises to a local food bank, a reflection of pe’ah, a Talmudic concept that describes giving part of the harvest to the needy. She prays over every duck, chicken and sheep she slaughters so her family may eat.
“It’s all God’s creation,” she said. “It is a gift that we get to be part of it. We are stewards. We are not owners.”
But she also differs in her interpretation of some principles. The concept of bal tashchit focuses on limiting waste, so she keeps a pig to eat food scraps – a controversial decision for some Jews who don’t eat pork due to kosher dietary practices, many of whom disagree with her choice online.
“I am very clear this is not a quote-unquote ‘Jewish farm’,” Rhein said, “but I do consider us to be a Jewishly inspired place.”
Blending traditions and futures
A number of Jewish farming organizations focus on both community building and skills building. The Sacred Slaughter Institute trains students to become shochets, ritual slaughterers of kosher meat; the butchering process calls for prayer, a highly sharpened knife and a single clean cut to lessen tza’ar ba’alei chayim, or animal suffering. Elsewhere, at the 20-acre non-profit Adamah Farm in Falls Village, Connecticut, Jewish people in their 20s and 30s come for three-month farming fellowships. Located at the Isabella Freedman Jewish Retreat Center, Adamah sells vegetables and herbs through membership in its community-supported agriculture (CSA) model.
Adamah Farm co-founder Shamu Sadeh said the work “is a process of reinvigorating Judaism and the Jewish community with an ecological perspective, and of reinvigorating the ecological environmental community with people who feel spiritually connected”. Graduates work in food rescue programs, food policy, environmental groups and Jewish social services, among other fields; a small percentage are farmers.
Rabbis Shoshana and Philip Ohriner run the 16-acre Ma’alot Farms in Los Gatos, California, with grants from community organizations and foundations. The farm nurtures hundreds of varieties of produce, from olives and broccolini to marionberries, a type of blackberry. Almost everything is given away to people facing food insecurity, including kids in afterschool programs and seniors with nutritional needs.
Ma’alot’s marketing doesn’t refer to Judaism. Still, “you cannot step on to Ma’alot Farms without feeling our Judaism permeate everything”, Philip Ohriner said, “from the way in which we care for our staff and provide a living wage for them and benefits, to the ways in which we seek to share our abundance to feed the hungry, to seek to bring equity and justice more fully into our world.”
At Ekar Farm, located at an eldercare community in Aurora, Colorado, executive director Jason Plotkin offers intergenerational gardening programs and donates about 20,000lb of organic produce annually to groups including Hope Communities, which serves refugees, and Spirit of the Sun, an Indigenous-led organization. The farm grows epazote, Thai hot chilies and bitter melon among its crops based on requests from recipients. Plotkin grew up Jewish but wasn’t religious. “I actually have learned more about my Jewish identity working for Ekar,” he said, “than what I brought into it.”
Non-profit farms exemplify the idea of tzedakah, or charity, a requirement in Jewish tradition. Small-scale for-profit farms strive to be community partners in their own ways.
Zalman (Robbie) Friedman operates a subscription and delivery service for local kosher meat from Robariah Farms in South Deerfield, Massachusetts. A certified shochet, he tends to about 1,000 birds, including meat chickens, egg layers and turkeys. About a quarter of his customers aren’t Jewish but appreciate Robariah’s regenerative farming practices. His birds have plenty of room to move and dine on fresh pasture every day thanks to mobile coops. “We raise a slower-growing variety that’s very active on the grass,” he said.
The laws of kashrut, or keeping kosher, outline how to slaughter an animal but are less specific about its care, Friedman said. “Why can’t it be done in a way that also honors the life of the animal, which is also a very important Jewish value and Jewish practice?”
Jewish guidance can show up even in crop selection. Ian Yosef Hertzmark grows ancient grains such as emmer, einkorn, spelt and Persian wheats, among other crops, on the 32-acre Migrash Farm in Baltimore county, Maryland. He plants ancient grains in the fall to be yoshon, or “old”, taking root before Passover (the Torah forbids eating chadash, or “new” grain). Hertzmark finds fulfillment in having “a relationship with land in an observant and seasonal context”.
Rhein agrees. She feels “more self-aware, more confident, more alive and whole as a human being here, doing this, than I ever felt living in Manhattan … This way of life – attaching yourself to land and animals and seasonality – is a constant sense of joy.”

content:
（德国之声中文网）今年秋天，美国总统特朗普政府加大外交力度，试图重启陷入停滞、旨在结束俄乌战争的谈判。
华盛顿一边向基辅及其欧洲伙伴加大施压 ，一边通过一系列让步，设法把莫斯科拉回谈判桌，其中包括一项涉及俄罗斯向美国出口柴油的协议，以及暂时放宽部分制裁。
然而，克里姆林宫似乎并不急于恢复有实质意义的和平谈判。10月21日，美国特使威特科夫（Steve Witkoff）在圣彼得堡与俄罗斯总统普京会晤后，克里姆林宫表示，莫斯科已准备好在下个月与乌克兰举行技术层面的谈判。
普京 的助理乌沙科夫（Yury Ushakov）在会晤后表示，普京同意在11月10日之后恢复由华盛顿斡旋的和平谈判。他还说，下一轮谈判可能在阿布扎比举行，重点将放在“为战争结束后的俄罗斯和乌克兰构建安全体系”上。
据乌沙科夫介绍，普京还与威特科夫交流了对一场可能举行的三方峰会的看法，参与者将包括美国总统特朗普和中国国家主席习近平。乌沙科夫指出，北京已经在为这次会晤做准备。
DW专访泽连斯基：愿去美国见普京
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
在中国举行三方峰会 乌克兰缺席
《华尔街日报》本周早些时候报道，莫斯科提议在11月18日至19日于中国深圳举行的亚太经合组织（APEC）峰会期间，另外举行一场三方会晤。据该报消息人士透露，普京希望与特朗普和习近平就以对俄罗斯有利的条件结束乌克兰战争达成协议。
莫斯科提议由俄罗斯、美国和中国举行三方峰会，却把乌克兰和欧盟排除在外， 从中可以看出克里姆林宫偏好的谈判模式。 俄罗斯坚持认为，谈判要取得进展，乌克兰必须先做好在领土问题上让步的准备。普京也一再强调，只有在俄罗斯的利益得到考虑的前提下，他才愿意谈判。
据《华尔街日报》报道，普京把拟议中的深圳会晤视为一场可能的新“雅尔塔会议”。1945年，美国、英国和苏联领导人在雅尔塔会晤，讨论击败纳粹德国以及战后欧洲秩序的问题。
该报还报道说，中国官员已通过外交渠道表示，如果特朗普同意参加，北京不会反对这种三方形式。特朗普与基辅的关系最近几周明显恶化，他也表示愿意举行这样的会谈。
乌克兰总统泽连斯基10月20日在奥斯陆访问期间指出，有关乌克兰未来的会谈， 只有在乌克兰能坐上谈判桌的情况下，才是可以接受的。
中国能从会谈中得到什么？
柏林卡内基俄罗斯欧亚中心（Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center）专门研究中俄关系的研究员乌马罗夫（Temur Umarov）对克里姆林宫的这项提议并不意外。他对德国之声表示，莫斯科希望受到华盛顿的尊重，被当作一个国际大国看待。
乌马罗夫说，美国上一届政府不愿在没有基辅参与的情况下，与俄罗斯讨论涉及乌克兰主权的问题。而现在，克里姆林宫认为，这样的谈判或许已经有了可能。
中俄关系：真朋友还是权宜合作？
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
莫斯科显然希望，拟议会晤上达成的任何协议，都能促使白宫向乌克兰和欧盟施压，迫使它们接受俄方的条件。可是，中国究竟会扮演什么角色？
乌马罗夫认为，北京参会主要是作为一个象征性的伙伴，而不是一个要为结果负责的积极调解方。他说：“北京无意为乌克兰的未来承担责任。”
单纯出席峰会，不会给中国带来任何额外的义务。乌马罗夫解释说：“克里姆林宫坚持这种形式并不奇怪。 俄罗斯想表明，它不仅与美国平起平坐，与中国也是如此。 但客观地说，在这对关系中，莫斯科并不是占主导地位的一方。”
乌马罗夫认为，中国对这样的谈判没有多少直接利益。他说，即便几位领导人发表联合声明，北京也会力求措辞尽可能模糊、不做任何承诺。这样一来，无论战争此后如何发展，中国几乎都可以说它与峰会达成的共识相符。在乌马罗夫看来，保有这种回旋余地，是北京参会的关键前提。
不过，墨卡托中国研究中心（MERICS）高级副研究员波伊塔（Yurii Poita）的看法不同。他认为，中国和俄罗斯有着相互重叠的战略利益，尤其是在推动建立一个覆盖整个欧亚大陆的替代性安全架构方面。
波伊塔认为，西方在欧洲和亚洲的军事存在减少、北约影响力削弱，对两国都有好处。他对德国之声说：“如果俄罗斯和中国能说服美国减少在欧洲的军事存在和对乌克兰的军事援助，俄罗斯就会在战场上获得更多优势。”
他补充说，这种局面还会进一步削弱欧盟对美国这个北约盟友的信任。波伊塔认为，在与华盛顿的任何谈判中，莫斯科和北京追求的正是这样的结果。
担忧征兵动员令：俄罗斯男性逃往格鲁吉亚

普京的政治存续对中国至关重要？
美国凯南研究所（Kennan Institute）所长基梅奇（Michael Kimmage）同样怀疑北京会准备在结束战争问题上扮演更积极的外交角色。
基梅奇对德国之声表示，中国或许认为这场冲突会造成不稳定，也更希望维持与乌克兰及该地区其他国家的贸易关系。但他认为，有一个更重要的优先事项压过了这些顾虑。他说：“对中国来说，更重要的是普京的政治存续。”
基梅奇认为，俄罗斯给中国带来了几项地缘政治上的好处，包括廉价的能源，以及一个很少妨碍北京的外交伙伴。
他认为， 中国会继续间接支持俄罗斯的军事行动，以免俄罗斯战败。 他说，俄罗斯取得彻底胜利未必是北京的目标， 但确保普京不输掉战争至关重要 。正因如此，基梅奇并不认为，如果普京不愿结束战争，中国会向他施压。
排除欧洲，暴露了欧盟的弱势？
无论乌克兰还是欧盟，都不会参加拟议中在中国举行的会谈。
基辅智库“新地缘政治研究网络”（New Geopolitics Network）的初级研究员克拉西娜（Kateryna Krasina）认为，把乌克兰和欧盟排除在外，或许能看出北京实际上如何看待两者的国际影响力。
她认为，从中国的做法可以看出，中国并不把乌克兰当作谈判中的独立一方，并认为欧洲相对弱势。
基梅奇则认为，把欧洲排除在峰会之外，未必会削弱欧洲对谈判进程的影响力。
他承认，欧洲各国政府或许无力阻止特朗普、普京和习近平会面。但他提到，2025年特朗普与普京在阿拉斯加举行峰会时，欧洲曾积极奔走。他认为，这些努力帮助避免了对欧洲不利的结果。
基梅奇说，欧洲通过对乌克兰的财政援助，以及广泛的国防工业合作，特别是德国和其他欧洲国家参与的合作，扩大了自身的影响力。

他认为， 欧洲的支持对乌克兰抵御俄军推进发挥了重要作用 。基梅奇说：“而这种支持就是筹码。”
他认为，俄罗斯、中国和美国或许都有意把欧洲描绘成一个次要力量，但这种描绘忽视了欧洲的实际影响力。
“表面看到的和实际情况并不完全一样，”他说。他以此区分了两件事：一边是看上去像雅尔塔会议那样的大国外交，一边是欧洲在支持乌克兰方面所起的作用。
乌马罗夫则提出了另一个角度。
他认为，美国、俄罗斯和中国之间达成的任何外交协议，都将面对战场上的现实。
他说：“中国明白，无论与美国和俄罗斯的谈判结果如何，战场上的现实都会大不相同，而且首先取决于乌克兰。”
“不管克里姆林宫喜不喜欢， 乌克兰都有自己的主动权 。无论是美国还是西方国家，都不能仅凭外交压力就完全决定战场上发生什么。”
